text:
WASHINGTON – The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) is proposing to collect additional information to enhance its compliance oversight of multiemployer pension plans that receive special financial assistance (SFA). The new requirements would expand the scope of information that must be filed as part of the Annual Statement of Compliance to include documentation of plan investment policies and procedures for locating missing participants.
“One of PBGC’s highest priorities is monitoring the stewardship of SFA funds to ensure that taxpayer dollars are used solely for their intended purpose,” said PBGC Director Janet Dhillon. “The proposed changes would give PBGC additional tools to verify that SFA funds are being managed responsibly and used to pay earned pension benefits to retirees and their beneficiaries.”
Stronger Oversight of Investment Decisions
Under the proposal, plans that received SFA would be required to submit documents that explain how investment decisions are made and monitored. These include investment policy statements, investment guidelines, asset allocation policies, committee charters, and other governing documents related to the management of plan assets, including SFA funds. The additional documentation would help PBGC assess whether plans are complying with SFA requirements, including rules governing how SFA funds are used, invested, and safeguarded.
Greater Focus on Missing Participants
PBGC is also proposing new information requirements related to missing participants. Plans that received SFA would be required to provide data on participants who may have lost contact with the plan, as well as documentation describing the procedures used to locate them.
The goal is to help ensure that retirees and beneficiaries receive the pension benefits they have earned.
The proposed revisions to the collection of information are published in today’s Federal Register and are open for public comment through December 15, 2026.
About the Special Financial Assistance Program
Enacted by legislation in 2021, the SFA Program provides funding to financially troubled multiemployer pension plans. Upon approval of an SFA application, PBGC makes a lump-sum payment to an eligible multiemployer plan in an amount projected to enable the plan to pay full plan benefits through 2051. The program is funded entirely by appropriations from the General Fund of the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Plans receiving SFA are subject to certain terms, conditions and reporting requirements, including an annual statement documenting compliance with the terms and conditions.
About PBGC
PBGC protects the retirement security of about 30 million American workers, retirees, and beneficiaries in both single-employer and multiemployer private sector pension plans. The agency’s two insurance programs are legally separate and operationally and financially independent. PBGC is directly responsible for the benefits of nearly 1.4 million participants and beneficiaries in failed single-employer pension plans. The Single-Employer Program is financed by insurance premiums, investment income, and assets and recoveries from failed single-employer plans. The Multiemployer Program is financed by insurance premiums and investment income. Special financial assistance for financially troubled multiemployer plans is financed by general taxpayer monies.
title: PBGC proposes additional information requirements for oversight of multiemployer pension plans receiving special financial assistance

This is the first time in American history that there have been zero releases at the border
WASHINGTON — The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) today announced preliminary Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 data showcasing a 95% drop in southwest border apprehensions compared to the Biden Administration, alongside the lowest annual encounters in American history and the first-ever fiscal year with zero Border Patrol releases.
Driven by President Donald J. Trump’s policies and the leadership of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FY 2026 combined historic low crossings with strengthened border infrastructure, disrupted cartels, and protected American trade. September marked the 17th consecutive month with ZERO releases.
“President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered. Over the past year, CBP recorded its lowest numbers in American history. A stark contrast to Biden, where CBP recorded its highest illegal immigration numbers ever,” said Secretary Mullin. “The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership and the hard work of CBP and DHS law enforcement personnel, we have restored control of the border and made America safer than ever.”
“FY 2026 demonstrated what focused enforcement, strong partnerships, and the commitment of our frontline personnel can achieve,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “DHS and CBP are securing the border, stopping dangerous drugs and criminals, protecting communities, and ensuring our personnel have the resources necessary for this critical mission.”
Historic Border Security Results
CBP’s enforcement posture drove U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions to their lowest level in agency history. The Border Patrol, which completed its first-ever fiscal year with no releases, recorded less than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in FY 2026—a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden. Total FY 2026 apprehensions (98,708) were 60% lower than the Biden Administration’s single highest month alone (249,740).
Additionally, preliminary data shows total nationwide encounters in FY 2026 were the lowest in agency history at 379,243, compared with 2.7 million per year under Biden (seven times higher). FY 2026 encounters were 88% lower than FY 2023 under Biden, which was the highest fiscal year ever.
These results reflect sustained enforcement and the deterrent effect of a secure border. Illegal aliens have received a clear message: don’t try to enter the country illegally, or you will be apprehended, detained, and deported.
A Safer Border
President Trump’s policies are also saving lives by reducing unlawful crossings, leading to a dramatic decline in border-related deaths.
Fewer unlawful crossings have contributed to a significant decline in border-related deaths. Preliminary data shows alien deaths identified by the Border Patrol fell nearly 80% in FY 2026 and since January 20, 2025, compared to the Biden Administration.
CBP personnel nevertheless remained ready to respond when lives were at risk. Across the nation, agents, officers, and air and marine personnel conducted search-and-rescue operations and delivered emergency medical aid. These efforts have included railcar rescues, a rescue effort following flooding at the Grand Canyon, and a CBP officer who responded to victims of a plane crash in Miami.
CBP’s Office of Field Operations responded to more than 3,000 medical emergencies during FY 2026, performing CPR on over 50 individuals in cardiac arrest and administering Naloxone for suspected opioid overdoses.
Stronger Infrastructure Along the Border
CBP reached a major construction milestone in FY 2026, completing 250 miles of new border barrier along the southwest border since January 20, 2025. This includes primary and secondary barriers, waterborne barriers, and supporting technology.
Funding from the Working Families Tax Cut Act enabled CBP to accelerate Smart Wall construction. From September 2025 through September 2026, CBP obligated $34.3 billion to support Smart Wall projects across all southwest border states, cementing a generational investment in physical security and operational control.
Drug Interdictions that Save Lives
As the frontline against drug smuggling, CBP is leading federal efforts to combat illicit trafficking.
CBP utilizes cutting-edge nonintrusive inspection technology and intelligence-driven strategies to seize deadly drugs, targeting not just finished products but precursor chemicals, tools, and pill presses.
As a result, preliminary data shows CBP’s drug seizures in FY 2026 totaled nearly 1 million pounds—63% higher than the 600,000-pound annual average of the last four years.
Trade and Tariff Enforcement
CBP plays a central role in enforcing trade law, supporting economic security, and interdicting counterfeit merchandise and goods made with forced labor.
In FY 2026, CBP stopped more than 4,000 shipments valued at over $325 million suspected of involving forced labor, and issued eight Withhold Release Orders along with two modifications.
CBP also seized nearly 55.5 million counterfeit goods valued at more than $12.6 billion, including 476,903 items infringing FIFA World Cup intellectual property valued at over $33 million.
By securing the border, intercepting dangerous narcotics, expanding physical barriers, and enforcing lawful trade, CBP has closed vulnerabilities across every front to ensure the long-term safety and prosperity of the American people.
title: Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS Announces Lowest Fiscal Year Border Crossings in American History

Coast Guard repatriates Cuban national following rescue off South Florida
Southeast Public Affairs - Southeastpublicaffairs@uscg.mil
MIAMI — Coast Guard Cutter Isaac Mayo’s crew repatriated one person to Cuba, Wednesday, following a maritime interdiction near Key Biscayne.
A good Samaritan reported to Coast Guard Sector Miami watchstanders they rescued a person after finding them on a 15-foot homemade raft without a life jacket.
A Coast Guard Station Miami Beach boat crew and U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations personnel responded to the scene and took custody of the person for further processing.
“Attempting to migrate by sea aboard homemade, unseaworthy vessels is extremely dangerous. No one should risk their life to try to enter the U.S. illegally,” said Lt. Cmdr. Jon Girot, U.S. Coast Guard Liaison Officer / DHS Attaché at U.S. Embassy Havana, Cuba. “Our crews remain committed to protecting lives at sea and preventing unlawful maritime migration.”
Once aboard a Coast Guard cutter, individuals are processed to determine their identity and are provided food, water, shelter and basic medical attention before transfer or repatriation, as appropriate.
The Coast Guard, along with its Operation Vigilant Sentry partners, maintains a continual presence with air, land and sea assets in support of Operation Vigilant Sentry. The combined, multilayered approach is designed to protect safety of life at sea while preventing unlawful maritime entry to the United States and its territories.
Visit our Newsroom for Coast Guard Southeast District press releases. Visit our DVIDS account for Coast Guard Southeast District imagery.
For breaking news, follow us on X. For additional information, find us on Facebook and follow us on Instagram.
-USCG-
title: Coast Guard repatriates Cuban national following rescue off South Florida

text:
Fast Facts
Ghost preparers are paid tax preparers who hide their identities on returns and avoid accountability for making errors, committing fraud, or stealing refunds. But ghost preparers are hard for IRS to identify—leaving taxpayers responsible for errors or fraud.
The IRS has started addressing this problem, but its efforts are fragmented. For example, relevant data is scattered across several databases. This makes it hard for IRS to use this information to better understand ghost preparer behavior and protect taxpayers.
IRS also doesn't have a strategy, goals, or ways to measure the success of its efforts.
Our recommendations address these issues.
A pen points to the paid preparer section of a tax return.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Ghost preparers are paid tax preparers who do not comply with requirements to identify themselves on tax returns they prepare for others. Ghost preparers may intentionally leave identifying information off to get away with filing fraudulent income tax returns, stealing taxpayers’ refunds, and stealing taxpayers’ identities. Courts have ordered individual ghost preparers to pay millions in restitution to the government, but according to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) officials, the total effect of ghost preparers is likely greater, in part, because ghost preparers are difficult to detect.
IRS maintains some data on identified ghost preparers, but the systems IRS uses to track ghost preparer cases and outcomes are not connected and have limitations that impede their usefulness. As a result, IRS does not know how many ghost preparers it has identified, investigated, and addressed. Better understanding existing data, including its limitations, would help IRS direct enforcement resources and protect taxpayers from fraudulent returns or stolen refunds.
IRS identifies and addresses ghost preparers through data analysis, referrals, taxpayer education, and enforcement actions such as investigations. However, these efforts are fragmented across six offices and IRS is missing opportunities to share information and better address risks. A comprehensive, coordinated preparer strategy, including efforts addressing ghost preparers, could help IRS better align resources with risks and identify additional needs.
Notional Example of Fragmented Activities Compared to a Comprehensive, Coordinated Strategy
While IRS has some activities to address ghost preparers, including data analysis and taxpayer education, it has not developed measurable objectives or performance goals. Defining objectives, goals, and performance measures could help IRS reliably assess whether its efforts are reducing ghost preparer activity and adjust its strategy and allocate resources more effectively.
Why GAO Did This Study
Paid tax preparers prepared more than half of all tax returns in fiscal year 2025 and have an enormous effect on IRS’s ability to administer tax laws effectively. However, ghost preparers may hide their identities to avoid accountability and leave taxpayers responsible for inaccurate or fraudulent returns they prepare.
GAO was asked to examine IRS’s efforts to address ghost preparers. This report (1) describes how ghost preparers have harmed taxpayers and IRS, (2) assesses the extent to which IRS maintains data on ghost preparers, and (3) evaluates IRS actions to identify and address ghost preparers.
GAO reviewed federal court cases, and IRS documentation and data. GAO compared IRS’s efforts to leading practices for evidence-based policymaking and consumer education planning. GAO also interviewed IRS and Department of Justice officials and stakeholder groups, such as IRS oversight and industry groups.
Recommendations
GAO is making three recommendations including that IRS identify opportunities to enhance data collecting, sharing, and analysis to inform its ghost preparer efforts, incorporate ghost preparer efforts within a comprehensive, coordinated paid preparer strategy, and define measurable objectives and goals. IRS agreed with GAO’s recommendations and described steps it plans to take or started taking, in response to each recommendation.
title: Tax Filing: IRS Should Enhance Ghost Preparer Identification and Compliance Efforts in a Comprehensive Preparer Strategy

Davids Urges Federal Action as Kansas Small Businesses Squeezed Out of Tariff Refunds While Large Corporations Cash In
New study shows without reckless tariffs, inflation would have declined
Today, Representative Sharice Davids demanded immediate action to ensure Kansas small businesses receive the tariff refunds they are owed. Following this year’s Supreme Court ruling overturning the president’s reckless tariffs, the federal government began processing billions of dollars in refunds. However, while major corporations get massive paydays, local Kansas mom-and-pop shops are facing bureaucratic hurdles that leave them behind.
"Small businesses should not need a team of lawyers or customs specialists to recover money they are owed," wrote Davids in a letter to the Small Business Administration (SBA) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP). "The businesses with the fewest resources should not face the greatest barriers to recovering their money while large corporations are better positioned to navigate the system... I urge the administration to ensure that the refund process works for the small businesses that need this relief most."
Data from the Center for American Progress highlights the stark disparity facing Kansas main streets: the average Kansas small business importer has recovered just $49,000 in refunds compared to the $140,000 they paid out in tariffs. Meanwhile, some of the nation’s largest corporations — which possess internal legal teams and outside specialists to navigate the complex application process — have secured refunds worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
In her letter, Davids outlined how many small businesses were forced to absorb higher costs passed down by suppliers, yet remain ineligible or unable to navigate the current non-automatic refund process. She is calling on the SBA and CBP to create a realistic, streamlined, and accessible path for small businesses, including direct guidance and a simplified application process for small firms that have not yet applied.
This action builds directly on Davids’ ongoing efforts to protect Kansas workers and small businesses from unfair trade practices. Davids previously supported the RELIEF Act, legislation designed to provide automatic, hassle-free tariff refunds to small businesses and hardworking families who bore the financial burden of reckless tariff policies.
The administration’s reckless tariff policies have hit Kansas hard, driving up costs for families and threatening small businesses and farmers. Average American households will pay $2,500 more this year because of these policies. Local industries, including agriculture, manufacturing, and retail, have faced higher costs for imported goods, forcing some businesses to raise consumer prices, cut jobs, or close entirely.
Read Davids’ full letter here or below
Dear Administrator Loeffler and Commissioner Scott,
I write to share my concerns about the impact of the Trump Administration’s trade war and tariff refund process on Kansas small businesses. Local small businesses have already paid the price of higher tariffs. Now, as the federal government works to return billions of dollars in tariffs that were collected, small businesses are at risk of being left behind.
The Center for American Progress estimates the average Kansas small business importer has only received $49,000 in refunds, compared with the $140,000 paid in tariffs (as of August 2026). At the same time, some of the nation’s largest corporations have received refunds worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Following the Supreme Court’s decision earlier this year overturning President Trump’s broad International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariffs, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) began processing refunds for eligible businesses. These refunds are not automatic. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found that larger firms are somewhat more likely to receive or seek refunds, relying on internal staff or outside firms to navigate the process.
Kansas small businesses often lack the staff to navigate a complicated federal refund process. Some may also be ineligible to apply, even though they ultimately paid higher prices because of tariffs. For example, a tariff may be passed from an importer to a small business through a supplier, but the refund may go to the original importer — not the small business that absorbed the higher cost.
Small businesses should not need a team of lawyers or customs specialists to recover money they are owed.
I urge the Small Business Administration to work with CBP and other federal agencies to create a realistic, efficient, and accessible path for small businesses to receive the tariff refunds they are owed. This should include a straightforward process for businesses that have not yet applied, as well as clear guidance and assistance for small businesses navigating the process.
The businesses with the fewest resources should not face the greatest barriers to recovering their money while large corporations are better positioned to navigate the system. I urge the administration to ensure that the refund process works for the small businesses that need this relief most.
Sincerely,
title: Davids Urges Federal Action as Kansas Small Businesses Squeezed Out of Tariff Refunds While Large Corporations Cash In

text:
Fast Facts
Critical minerals—such as lithium, copper, and zinc—are essential to the nation's economic and national security.
The U.S. relies on imports for many of these minerals. But those supply chains are vulnerable to disruptions. Amid efforts to increase domestic mineral production, concerns have been raised about foreign influence in domestic supply chains.
Mining companies aren't required to disclose foreign ownership of mines on federal land. So, the full extent of foreign ownership is unclear. But we found companies operating critical mineral mines that were subsidiaries of foreign companies, some of which had investment from Chinese entities.
Copper Mine on Federal Lands
A terraced open pit mine.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The U.S critical mineral supply chain faces numerous constraints, including the need for substantial capital investment and limited domestic processing capacity. The U.S. exports large quantities of domestically extracted ore to Canada, Mexico, and China, among other countries.
Copper Mine on Federal Lands
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and the Forest Service oversee hardrock mines on federal land. As of February 2026, there were 632 approved hardrock mining plans of operation on federal land. The 1872 Mining Law generally requires mining claimants to be U.S. citizens or business entities incorporated in the U.S. Foreign businesses can meet this requirement by having a U.S. subsidiary serve as the claimant. While there is limited available information on the full extent of foreign investment in mining on federal lands and parent-subsidiary relationships, GAO reviewed ownership information of 43 claimants and operators associated with critical mineral mines on federal lands. GAO determined ownership for 32 of those companies and found that 14 were subsidiaries of foreign entities. GAO found that none of the 14 had Chinese-owned parent companies, but in at least two cases, Chinese entities had financial interest in the foreign parent companies.
The 1872 Mining Law does not contain a provision requiring BLM or Forest Service to collect information on foreign parent companies nor does it require claimants or operators to submit information regarding foreign ownership. However, other federal agencies have some authorities and processes to identify foreign investment in mining. For example, the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, chaired by the Department of the Treasury, can review foreign investment in mining as it relates to potential national security concerns.
Why GAO Did This Study
Critical minerals are essential to the economic and national security of the United States. These minerals, including copper, lithium, and zinc, are key components in advanced technologies and have vulnerable supply chains.
As demand for these minerals increases, U.S. access to critical minerals has become a key topic in domestic policymaking and international relations. Recently, the administration and Congressional entities have expressed concerns over U.S. dependence on imports and the role of potential adversary nations, such as the People’s Republic of China (China), in the U.S. supply chain of critical minerals.
Most critical minerals that can be mined in the U.S. are obtained through hardrock mining, some of which occurs on federal lands. However, policymakers have raised questions about the full amount and extent of foreign investment in those mines.
This report provides information on hardrock mining that occurs on federal lands, foreign investment in mining on federal lands, and steps federal agencies take to identify foreign investment. It also provides information on the amount of extracted critical minerals exported from the U.S. from 2019 through 2025. GAO reviewed ownership information using a variety of sources for 43 claimants and operators associated with critical mineral mines, analyzed federal laws, and interviewed officials. In a related report (GAO-27-108196), GAO reports on BLM’s role in collecting citizenship information from mining claimants.
For more information, contact Dr. Nagla'a El-Hodiri at elhodirin@gao.gov.
title: Critical Minerals: Limited Available Information on the Full Extent of Foreign Investment in Mining on Federal Lands

text:
Fast Facts
U.S. national security and economic interests depend on technological innovation and advantage. This Q&A looks at people who collect sensitive information for other countries. This group may include university students and researchers. The FBI calls these people "non-traditional intelligence collectors" and says they pose an insider threat to the U.S.
The FBI works with academic institutions and industry to identify and address such threats, but its relationships with academia vary. According to FBI officials, good relationships can help institutions come forward with tips and requests for help.
We recommended strengthening these relationships.
Picture of the FBI's seal on a wall outside of an office.
Highlights
What GAO Found
According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), non-traditional intelligence collectors (NTCs) are individuals whose primary profession is not intelligence collection, but who actively or passively collect sensitive U.S. information on behalf of foreign entities. For example, researchers and students at universities may act as NTCs if they collect non-public research on behalf of a foreign entity. According to the FBI, unlike intelligence officers, NTCs function independently of established intelligence organizations.
FBI officials and representatives from academic associations identified several challenges in addressing threats posed by NTCs. For example, FBI officials said that it is difficult to identify and investigate NTCs because their activities may not constitute a violation of the law until information is transferred to foreign entities. Also, there are cultural differences between the FBI and academia that may impede communication, as academic institutions promote the free exchange of information, and, according to FBI officials, may not want to be perceived as “turning over” their students.
FBI offices involved in mitigating and investigating threats posed by NTCs are the Office of Private Sector, which leads information-sharing and engagement with the private sector, and the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. The FBI also uses the National Counterintelligence Task Force and field office-based Counterintelligence Task Forces to coordinate with partner agencies.
Interplay Between FBI’s Headquarters and Field Offices in Mitigating Threats Posed by NTCs
According to FBI officials, building relationships between field offices and academic institutions is important, so academic institutions come to the FBI for assistance in addressing NTCs. FBI officials also said they rely on tips from academia to identify potential NTCs. Publicly, FBI officials have stated that relationships with academic institutions need strengthening to address research security issues. Academic association representatives similarly have said the FBI could improve outreach efforts and that relationships between the FBI and universities are stronger at some universities than others. However, the FBI did not identify a plan for strengthening partnerships with academic institutions. Without strong partnerships, the FBI’s ability to counter NTC threats and protect U.S. research, intellectual property, and technological advantage is hindered.
Why GAO Did This Study
U.S. national security and economic interests are heavily dependent on technological innovation and advantage. According to FBI officials, NTCs pose a significant insider threat to U.S. information, intellectual property, and technological advantage.
GAO was asked to review the FBI’s efforts to investigate and address threats posed by NTCs. This report provides information on the challenges posed by NTCs, the FBI offices involved in mitigating and investigating threats posed by NTCs, and the relationships between the FBI and academic institutions relative to NTC threats, among other things.
To conduct this work, GAO reviewed laws and statutes related to the FBI’s authorities to investigate federal crimes and national security threats, analyzed documentary evidence to understand how key offices interact and coordinate with each other, and reviewed the mechanisms the FBI uses to coordinate its efforts with other federal agencies, academia, and the private sector. GAO also interviewed FBI officials and representatives from academic associations and private industry, selected based on their experiences in addressing NTC activities in academia and the private sector.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that the FBI develop and implement a plan to strengthen the FBI’s partnerships with academic institutions to better facilitate the exchange of information and to help address threats posed by NTCs. The FBI concurred with our recommendation.
title: National Security: FBI Should Strengthen Partnerships to Combat Non-Traditional Intelligence Collectors

This illegal alien had numerous storage devices with child sexual abuse material in his apartment, with one hidden inside a crucifix
WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued the following statement after an investigation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) led to an illegal alien being convicted for child pornography in Minnesota.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota announced that on October 8, a federal jury found Alejandro Rojas Garcia, an illegal alien from Mexico, guilty of attempted production of child pornography.
Alejandro Rojas Garcia
According to federal documents and evidence presented during the four-day trial, the investigation began in April 2024 after it was alleged that Garcia had sexually assaulted two sisters who were under the age of 13. Upon Garcia’s arrest on April 5, 2024, officers searched his apartment and found multiple cell phones, cameras, laptop computers, flash drives, and other data storage devices. They also found multiple hidden cameras throughout the apartment, including five hidden in the bathroom.
Upon searching the storage devices, officers found numerous depictions of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). One of the storage devices, a micro-SD card, was hidden inside a crucifix.
One of Garcia’s storage devices, hidden inside a crucifix in his apartment
Garcia now faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years in prison. His sentencing will be set at a later date. In addition to the federal charges, he is also facing state criminal charges for related conduct.
“This pedophile was just convicted for attempted production of child pornography in Minnesota,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Thanks to the brave men and women of HSI, as well as our local partners and the men and women at the Department of Justice, this illegal alien will face justice for his crimes. Once he finishes his sentence, he will be deported so that he cannot harm another child in America ever again.”
“Garcia is a predator,” said U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen. “A verdict cannot undo the evil he brought on two innocent girls, but it is justice.”
Garcia obtained a B-2 visa in January 2002. He entered the United States at an unknown date and location.
This case was the result of an investigation by HSI and the Stillwater Police Department, with assistance from Washington County Child Protective Services.
Under Governor Tim Walz, Minnesota has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime. Recent examples of illegal alien crime in the state include:
- In June, Governor Walz and the Minnesota Clemency Review Commission granted a pardon to Tou Lue Vang, an illegal alien from Laos, who had been convicted for first-degree criminal sexual conduct after he repeatedly sexually assaulted a 10-year-old girl. In July, ICE deported Vang back to Laos.
- In June, ICE arrested Georgii Gabiev, an illegal alien from Russia, who caused a fatal truck crash in 2024 that killed American truck driver Tim Tarnowski in Chippewa County.
- In June, Governor Walz and the Minnesota Clemency Review Commission granted a pardon to Jai Vang, an illegal alien from Laos, whose criminal record includes felony convictions for robbery and robbery of a business with a gun, as well as a conviction for driving under the influence of liquor.
- In April, ICE arrested THREE illegal aliens convicted of sex crimes against children in a single day: Rene Rosario-Miranda, an illegal alien from Guatemala convicted for third-degree aggravated sexual abuse of a minor; Axel Javier Martinez-Castillo, an illegal alien from Honduras whose criminal history includes the sexual assault of a 7-year-old; and Rene Flores-Lue, an illegal alien from El Salvador and a convicted rapist of a 5-year-old.
- In February, ICE arrested Morris Brown, an illegal alien from Liberia and serial immigration fraudster, who was working as a Minnesota correctional officer despite having no legal status in the United States.
- In June 2025, ICE arrested Roberto Carlos Munoz-Guatemala, an illegal alien from Mexico, after he dragged an ICE officer 50 yards with his car in an attempt to flee law enforcement. His criminal history includes a conviction for sex crimes against an underage teenager and an arrest for domestic assault.
# # #
title: ICE HSI Investigation Leads to Conviction of Illegal Alien for Child Pornography in Minnesota

Rep. Gillen and House Minority Whip Clark Hold Fireside Chat on Impacts of Rising Healthcare Costs on Long Island
More than 63,000 Long Islanders have lost health insurance following historic federal cuts to Medicaid and the expiration of ACA tax credits
Watch the full conversation HERE.
GARDEN CITY, NY — Today, Congresswoman Laura Gillen (NY-04) and Whip Katherine Clark (MA-05) hosted a fireside chat with Nassau County residents and leaders at Harmony Health in Garden City to discuss how rising healthcare costs are affecting Long Island and the country. Both lawmakers discussed a path in Congress to lower healthcare costs, extend the Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits and reverse the $1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
"Long Island’s hardworking families, care workers and providers are being crushed by rising healthcare costs and the GOP majority’s $1 trillion cut to Americans’ coverage,” said Rep. Gillen. “Alongside Whip Clark, we’re fighting to pass bipartisan solutions to reverse these cuts, restore the ACA tax credits, lower costs and protect the people who care for us. Together in Congress, we will continue working to ensure that quality healthcare is more affordable for all Americans.”
“Congresswoman Laura Gillen is fighting every day for the quality, affordable healthcare that Long Island families deserve," said Democratic Whip Katherine Clark. “It was a privilege to join her in the 4th District of New York and discuss House Democrats’ agenda to deliver for working families. In the 120th Congress, we will reverse this administration’s harmful cuts and pass legislation to ensure everyone can get the medical care they need, when they need it.”
“Congresswoman Gillen has been a strong and consistent advocate for healthcare and for the needs of the communities we serve, and we are deeply grateful for her continued support” said David Nemiroff, Chief Executive Officer of Harmony Healthcare Long Island. “We also extend our sincere thanks to Whip Clark for coming to Long Island and lending her voice and leadership to this critical issue. At a time when access to affordable, high-quality healthcare is more important than ever for our patients and families, this level of advocacy and engagement makes a meaningful difference. We appreciate their partnership and unwavering commitment to the health and well-being of our communities.”
During the conversation, Whip Clark expanded on House Democrats’ plan to restore expired federal ACA tax credits, which lowered health insurance premiums by thousands of dollars for some Nassau County residents. In January, Clark and Gillen helped pass a bipartisan three-year extension of the tax credits in the House, which now awaits passage in the Senate.
Whip Clark and Rep. Gillen also discussed the impact of the administration’s termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian recipients on Long Island’s healthcare workforce. In April, the House passed Rep. Gillen’s legislation to extend TPS for Haitians with bipartisan support.
Rep. Gillen highlighted the impact of rising healthcare costs on Long Island families, including Floral Park resident Karen Brandon. Brandon’s healthcare premiums tripled from $600 per month to $1,900 per month after ACA premium tax credits expired in 2025.
Since taking office, Rep. Gillen has worked to expand access to affordable, high-quality healthcare and protect critical health programs for Long Island families. She has fought against cuts to Medicaid and SNAP in the OBBBA, led and signed bipartisan letters opposing policies that would increase healthcare costs or jeopardize cancer research and safety-net hospitals and called on congressional leadership to protect Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid.
Rep. Gillen has also supported legislation to lower prescription drug costs by expanding Medicare drug price negotiations, permanently extend Affordable Care Act tax credits. Additionally, she has championed bipartisan legislation to protect safety-net hospitals, streamline Medicare Advantage prior authorization for seniors and increase transparency and affordability in dental and vision coverage.
To watch the full conversation, click HERE.
###
title: Rep. Gillen and House Minority Whip Clark Hold Fireside Chat on Impacts of Rising Healthcare Costs on Long Island

text:
Fast Facts
The National Nuclear Security Administration currently has its largest workload since the Cold War. It's overseeing a $200 billion, two-decade-long effort to modernize nuclear weapons and infrastructure.
We previously found that NNSA faced challenges recruiting and retaining skilled federal staff to meet its mission. In 2024, NNSA committed to rebuilding its workforce.
But in this Q&A, we reported that NNSA—in response to presidential directives in FY 2025—halted workforce planning and limited hiring. At the same time, employee separations increased significantly.
Consequently, NNSA has seen a 12% decrease in its federal staff since FY 2025.
Close-up of a person cutting the word jobs on paper with scissors
Highlights
What GAO Found
The National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) oversees a $25 billion annual budget and approximately 70,000 management and operating contractor personnel to maintain the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile and nuclear nonproliferation efforts. NNSA took steps to build its federal workforce to meet mission needs in 2024, with its workforce peaking at 1,991 early in fiscal year 2025. However, since then through the second quarter of fiscal year 2026, NNSA has reduced its federal workforce by 236 employees—or 11.9 percent. These reductions have impacted NNSA’s mission critical workforce, including occupations like nuclear engineers and contract specialists.
Number of National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) Federal Employees and Annual Appropriations, Fiscal Year (FY) 2023–FY 2026 Quarter (Q) 2
Note: The Federal Salaries and Expenses appropriation account funds the salaries, benefits, and other related expenses for most of NNSA’s federal workforce.
The reduction of NNSA’s workforce occurred because of two primary reasons: (1) very limited hiring and (2) employee separations—primarily employees choosing to retire or resign. Hiring was limited during the second quarter of fiscal year 2025 through the first quarter of fiscal year 2026.
Why GAO Did This Study
NNSA—a separately organized agency within the Department of Energy (DOE)—has a current workload that is at its highest level since the Cold War as the agency oversees a $200 billion, 2-decades-long effort to modernize nuclear weapons and related infrastructure.
In May 2024 (GAO-24-106167), GAO found NNSA continued to face challenges recruiting and retaining federal staff to meet the agency's mission needs, even though a statutory cap limiting the number of its federal employees was eliminated in fiscal year 2023. NNSA committed to developing a workforce planning process intended to inform future budget requests in response to its increased workload, the elimination of the cap, and consistent with GAO’s May 2024 report. The agency began building its workforce to meet mission needs in 2024. However, in response to presidential directives in early 2025, NNSA reduced the size of its federal workforce.
GAO was asked to examine NNSA’s retirements, resignations, terminations, and other voluntary or involuntary workforce reductions since January 2025. This report describes changes to NNSA’s federal workforce from the beginning of fiscal year 2023 through the second quarter of fiscal year 2026. GAO analyzed relevant NNSA data for workforce and personnel actions, including hires and separations, by program, office, and location. GAO also reviewed NNSA budget information and interviewed NNSA officials.
For more information, contact John Bumgarner at BumgarnerJ@gao.gov.
title: National Nuclear Security Administration: Reductions to Federal Workforce

text:
Fast Facts
The federal government spends billions of dollars every year to operate and maintain federal space—whether or not the space is being fully used.
A 2025 law requires agencies to collect and report data on the extent to which office space is being used. Many agencies said they were using or planning to use the data to dispose of unneeded space, which could save millions of dollars.
But the data doesn't offer a complete picture because it excludes some spaces that are vacant. And some agencies' collection and reporting of data isn't consistent with guidelines.
We recommended ways to improve future reporting to address this High Risk area.
Office area with empty cubicles.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Under the Utilizing Space Efficiently and Improving Technologies (USE IT) Act, enacted in January 2025, federal agencies are now required to collect and report occupancy data. This data is used to calculate utilization rates for agencies’ office space in federally owned buildings and leased locations. While 20 of the 23 agencies that responded to GAO’s survey reported using existing badging systems for this purpose, 16 of these 20 agencies reported supplementing that information with data from other sources such as daily check-in surveys. Nearly all agencies surveyed noted the importance of having easy to implement, cost-effective data collection approaches that they could put in place by the act’s July 2025 implementation deadline. Most agencies reported minimal costs associated with collecting and reporting USE IT Act data—collectively $16 million across 23 agencies in 2025.
Agencies’ Use of Approaches to Collect Occupancy Data, as of September 2025
Many agencies told GAO they are either using or plan to use their USE IT Act data to identify and dispose of unneeded real property. Some agency officials told GAO that they have already made decisions to consolidate or dispose of underutilized spaces, informed in part by USE IT Act data, and that they expect to save millions of dollars annually as a result.
However, the USE IT Act data submitted to Congress and the public in March 2026 does not have important context—including on GSA-controlled vacant space—needed to fully reflect office space utilization. Without this information, Congress and the public may have an inaccurate impression of the extent to which owned and leased office spaces are being utilized, including some locations that are likely being utilized at lower or higher rates than reported.
While surveyed agencies generally agreed that USE IT Act data are helpful, about one-third expressed concerns about how GSA data collection and reporting guidelines affect their utilization rate calculations. Further, some agencies described approaches to collecting and reporting their occupancy data that are inconsistent with GSA guidelines, resulting in data that are incomplete. For example, one agency reported the number of employees that are assigned to each location rather than measuring the extent to which employees were present in those spaces. By coordinating with agencies to improve the consistency and completeness of their occupancy data, GSA could better position agencies to make informed decisions about which underused spaces to prioritize for disposal, potentially leading to tens of millions of dollars in financial savings.
Why GAO Did This Study
Chronic underutilization of federal buildings is one of the main reasons that the management of federal real property has been on GAO’s High Risk list for more than 20 years. The USE IT Act requires the 24 Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Act agencies to collect and report occupancy data on the number of employees working in certain owned and leased spaces. It also contains a provision for GAO to review the costs to these agencies of this requirement to measure the occupancy and utilization rates of their spaces.
This report examines 1) the approaches CFO Act agencies reported using to collect the occupancy data required by the USE IT Act and their associated costs; 2) how agencies are using USE IT Act data to inform real property decisions and what additional information, if any, may help Congress and the public better understand federal office space utilization; and 3) agencies’ concerns about USE IT Act data collection and reporting and GSA’s actions to address these concerns.
GAO surveyed the CFO Act agencies about their data collection approaches, associated costs, and any limitations to their data or selected approaches. GAO also reviewed GSA guidelines for USE IT Act data collection, analyzed GSA data on vacant spaces, and conducted in-depth interviews with five agencies selected based on the variety of approaches to collecting occupancy data and the size of their real property portfolios.
Recommendations
GAO is making four recommendations to GSA to improve future office space utilization reporting, including that it provide data on vacant space to help fully reflect utilization. GSA did not agree or disagree but stated it would consider these recommendations.
title: Federal Real Property: New Occupancy Data Help Agencies Shed Unneeded Office Space But Gaps Limit the Full Picture

ATF and law enforcement partners conclude Operation Show Me Justice
435 dangerous offenders arrested, 166 illegal firearms seized, 81 kg illicit drugs off the streets in St. Louis
WASHINGTON — The Department of Justice, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, U.S. Marshals Service, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Missouri, and others today announced the conclusion of Operation Show Me Justice, an ATF-led high‑impact violent crime enforcement surge in St. Louis.
The DOJ-sponsored operation was a whole‑of‑government initiative led by ATF and carried out in close coordination with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Missouri and in partnership with the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, United States Marshals Service, Drug Enforcement Administration, FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, and other federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies.
“Operation Show Me Justice demonstrates exactly what happens when federal, state, and local partners unite behind a single mission: protecting communities from violent criminals,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “The results speak for themselves. Dangerous criminals are off the streets, their weapons are out of circulation, and families in St. Louis are safer today than they were before.”
“Operation Show Me Justice delivered the kind of decisive action the public should expect from ATF,” said ATF Director Rob Cekada. “We removed violent offenders from the street, cut off their access to firearms, and dealt a significant blow to the criminal networks endangering this community.”
“By removing these dangerous firearms from St Louis, together, we have achieved unprecedented results, not just for the partners who participated in Operation Show Me Justice, but for all the residents, commuters, students, and visitors to the Gateway City,” said Director Gadyaces S. Serralta of the U.S. Marshals Service.
“We in St. Louis are very grateful for the women and men of ATF who left home, came to our community, and faced daily danger to assist in this enforcement effort,” said U.S. Attorney Thomas C. Albus for the Eastern District of Missouri. “Just as important, we are grateful to all local, state, and federal law enforcement and prosecutors who fight violent crime every day and who will remain. We are in this for the long haul and want so much to help continue to drive down violence for the health and safety of our city that we love.”
“Driving down violent crime takes relentless follow-through, and our partnership with ATF and our other law enforcement partners helps us turn local intelligence into cases that hold violent offenders accountable,” said St. Louis Metropolitan Police Chief Robert J. Tracy. “Operation Show Me Justice builds on that daily collaboration and our commitment to lasting progress — so every neighborhood can experience a safer St. Louis.”
Photo of law enforcement as part of Operation Show Me Justice.
The operation focused on violent criminal conduct and the illegal supply of firearms to violent offenders. During the operation, ATF and its partners arrested more than 435 violent offenders, including individuals with histories of possessing machine guns illegally, carrying stolen firearms, resisting arrest, violating felon‑in‑possession laws, engaging in straw purchasing, and committing other serious weapons-related offenses.
Agents, officers, analysts, and prosecutors combined local intelligence with ballistic leads from the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network (NIBIN) and insights from crime‑gun tracing to drive investigations forward. This coordinated approach enabled investigators to connect shootings, link firearms to multiple crime scenes, identify gun and drug trafficking patterns, and develop leads that otherwise would remain isolated across jurisdictions.
Photo of illegal guns, ammunition, and narcotics seized as a result of Operation Show Me Justice.
Photo of an illegal gun seized as a result of Operation Show Me Justice.
NIBIN compares ballistic evidence from crime scenes with test‑fired shell casings from recovered firearms, generating actionable leads. Crime‑gun tracing tracks a firearm’s commercial history, from the manufacturer or importer to its first retail sale. When paired with traditional investigative work, these tools help investigators identify shooters, associates, firearms traffickers, and sources of crime guns fueling violence.
Operation Show Me Justice has delivered significant enforcement results in St. Louis, with 435 criminal arrests and 166 firearms seized to date. Participating agencies have cleared 412 warrants, including the execution of 32 search warrants, and seized 81 kilograms of drugs, six machine gun conversion devices, and more than $1.25 million in currency related to suspected illegal firearms and drug transactions.
Photo of individual arrested during Operation Show Me Justice.
Photo of illegal guns seized as a result of Operation Show Me Justice.
###
ATF protects American communities from violent crime driven by the illegal use of firearms, explosives, and acts of arson. Through crime gun intelligence, forensic analysis, and relentless investigation, we identify and arrest violent offenders and gang members, dismantle trafficking networks, and sever the supply chains arming cartels, prohibited persons, and terrorist organizations. We defend the rights of law-abiding citizens by safeguarding lawful commerce and upholding the Constitution of the United States. Learn more about what ATF is doing to reduce violent crime in your community by following us on X @ATFHQ, Instagram @ATFHQ, LinkedIn @ATF, and Facebook @HQATF, or on the web at www.atf.gov.
title: ATF and law enforcement partners conclude Operation Show Me Justice

U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), Kweisi Mfume (D-MD-07), and Wesley Bell (D-MO-01) introduced the U.S.S. Doris Miller Act and the Department of Defense Renaming Integrity and Ethics (DORIE) Act. These two pieces of legislation would honor the legacy of Mess Attendant Third Class Doris “Dorie” Miller and ensure that the Navy aircraft carrier currently under construction retains his name.
The U.S.S. Doris Miller Act would express the sense of Congress regarding the naming of a naval aircraft carrier in Miller’s honor. Miller famously manned an anti-aircraft gun during the attack on Pearl Harbor in World War II, despite having never been trained to operate the weapon, and helped carry wounded soldiers to safety even after being ordered to abandon ship. He was the first Black service member to receive the Navy Cross, the Navy’s second-highest award for valor.
The Department of Defense Renaming Integrity and Ethics (DORIE) Act would prohibit the naming of Department of Defense assets, including military bases, ships, and other military installations, after sitting presidents. The DORIE Act would amend Title 10 of the United States Code, which is the section of federal law that outlines the legal framework, roles, missions, and organization of the U.S. Armed Forces and the Department of Defense. This comes after an unprecedented proposal by Navy leadership to rename the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Doris Miller in honor of President Donald Trump.
“Doris Miller represented courage, sacrifice, and the essential role African Americans have played in defending this country,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “Naming this carrier after him is more than honoring one extraordinary sailor—it recognizes that African Americans are an essential part of American history. No sitting president has ever been able to, nor should they be able to, name a vessel after themselves. I am proud to support the U.S.S. Doris Miller Act to ensure American heroes are honored for their sacrifice.”
“Black history is American history, and you cannot tell the story of the Second World War without the story of Doris (Dorie) Miller,” said Congressman Kweisi Mfume. “Doris Miller’s life was one of extraordinary bravery and patriotism, and I will continue to fight against any and all efforts to minimize or denigrate that history. The aircraft carrier that was scheduled to be named in his honor represents a fitting tribute to the estimable legacy of Dorie Miller. It is the very least that we owe to this great American hero who like so many before him, laid down his life for his country. Taking his name off that ship to instead name it for President Trump while he is still in office would be a disgrace. That has never been the practice of our government, nor should it be now. No sitting President, of any party, should have a ship, a base, or any other military asset named after them while in office. That is just one of the many reasons why I am proud and honored to support the DORIE Act. It's the right thing to do.”
“Doris Miller put himself in harm’s way to save his fellow sailors, and he did it at a time when segregation limited what Black servicemembers were allowed to do. His courage deserves to be celebrated, not forgotten,” said Congressman Bell. “As a member of the House Armed Services Committee, I will continue working to ensure our sailors are honored for their service, and that their legacy is never erased. Our warships should carry the names of those who gave something to this country, and few gave more than Dorie Miller. That’s why I’m proud to champion these bills.”
Bill text for the DORIE Act can be found HERE.
Bill text for the U.S.S. Doris Miller Act can be found HERE.
title: Dingell, Colleagues Introduce Legislation Honoring Doris Miller and Prohibiting Renaming of Naval Vessels After Sitting Presidents

This is the first time in American history that there have been zero releases at the border
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection today announced preliminary Fiscal Year 2026 data showcasing a 95% drop in southwest border apprehensions, compared to the Biden Administration, alongside the lowest annual encounters in American history and the first-ever fiscal year with zero Border Patrol releases.
Driven by President Donald J. Trump’s policies and the leadership of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FY 2026 combined historic low crossings with strengthened border infrastructure, disrupted cartels, and protected American trade. September marked the 17th consecutive month with ZERO releases.
“President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered. Over the past year, CBP recorded its lowest numbers in American history. A stark contrast to Biden, where CBP recorded its highest illegal immigration numbers ever,” said Secretary Mullin. “The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership and the hard work of CBP and DHS law enforcement personnel, we have restored control of the border and made America safer than ever.”
“FY 2026 demonstrated what focused enforcement, strong partnerships, and the commitment of our frontline personnel can achieve,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “DHS and CBP are securing the border, stopping dangerous drugs and criminals, protecting communities, and ensuring our personnel have the resources necessary for this critical mission.”
Historic Border Security Results
CBP’s enforcement posture drove U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions to their lowest level in agency history. The Border Patrol, which completed its first-ever fiscal year with no releases, recorded less than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in FY 2026—a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden. Total FY 2026 apprehensions (98,708) were 60% lower than the Biden Administration’s single highest month alone (249,740).
Additionally, preliminary data shows total nationwide encounters in FY 2026 were the lowest in agency history at 379,243, compared with 2.7 million per year under Biden (seven times higher). FY 2026 encounters were 88% lower than FY 2023 under Biden, which was the highest fiscal year ever.
These results reflect sustained enforcement and the deterrent effect of a secure border. Illegal aliens have received a clear message: don’t try to enter the country illegally, or you will be apprehended, detained, and deported.
A Safer Border
President Trump’s policies are also saving lives by reducing unlawful crossings, leading to a dramatic decline in border-related deaths.
Fewer unlawful crossings have contributed to a significant decline in border-related deaths. Preliminary data shows alien deaths identified by the Border Patrol fell nearly 80% in FY 2026 and since January 20, 2025, compared to the Biden Administration.
CBP personnel nevertheless remained ready to respond when lives were at risk. Across the nation, agents, officers, and air and marine personnel conducted search-and-rescue operations and delivered emergency medical aid. These efforts have included railcar rescues, a rescue effort following flooding at the Grand Canyon, and a CBP officer who responded to victims of a plane crash in Miami.
CBP’s Office of Field Operations responded to more than 3,000 medical emergencies during FY 2026, performing CPR on over 50 individuals in cardiac arrest and administering Naloxone for suspected opioid overdoses.
Stronger Infrastructure Along the Border
CBP reached a major construction milestone in FY 2026, completing 250 miles of new border barrier along the southwest border since January 20, 2025. This includes primary and secondary barriers, waterborne barriers, and supporting technology.
Funding from the Working Families Tax Cut Act enabled CBP to accelerate Smart Wall construction. From September 2025 through September 2026, CBP obligated $34.3 billion to support Smart Wall projects across all southwest border states, cementing a generational investment in physical security and operational control.
Drug Interdictions that Save Lives
As the frontline against drug smuggling, CBP is leading federal efforts to combat illicit trafficking.
CBP utilizes cutting-edge nonintrusive inspection technology and intelligence-driven strategies to seize deadly drugs, targeting not just finished products but precursor chemicals, tools, and pill presses.
As a result, preliminary data shows CBP’s drug seizures in FY 2026 totaled nearly 1 million pounds—63% higher than the 600,000-pound annual average of the last four years.
Trade and Tariff Enforcement
CBP plays a central role in enforcing trade law, supporting economic security, and interdicting counterfeit merchandise and goods made with forced labor.
In FY 2026, CBP stopped more than 4,000 shipments valued at over $325 million suspected of involving forced labor and issued eight Withhold Release Orders along with two modifications.
CBP also seized nearly 55.5 million counterfeit goods valued at more than $12.6 billion, including 476,903 items infringing FIFA World Cup intellectual property valued at over $33 million.
By securing the border, intercepting dangerous narcotics, expanding physical barriers, and enforcing lawful trade, CBP has closed vulnerabilities across every front to ensure the long-term safety and prosperity of the American people.
title: Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS announces lowest fiscal year border crossings in American history

REP. HOYLE JOINS REP. ZINKE AND REP SCHRIER TO INTRODUCE BIPARTISAN NORTHWEST WETLANDS VIP ACT
Eugene, OR – This week, during National Wildlife Refuge Week, Representative Val Hoyle, Rep. Ryan Zinke (MT-01) and Rep. Kim Schrier (WA-08) joined conservation partners in the Pacific Northwest to introduce the bipartisan Northwest Wetlands Voluntary Incentives Program (VIP) Act.
“Conservation is a team effort, and everyone needs to play their part,” said Rep. Hoyle. “Our bipartisan bill supports habitat restoration and active management of invasive species across Northwest wetlands that support Tribes, farmers and other local economies. This work will strengthen our climate resilience, supporting these lands for the next generation.”
“Good conservation starts by bringing everyone to the table,” said Rep. Zinke. “The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act gives farmers, ranchers, Tribes, sportsmen and local communities a way to work together on voluntary projects that restore wetlands and keep working lands working. That’s how we protect habitat and water for the next generation. I'm proud to support this legislation.”
“Farmers, Tribes, and local communities across our region rely on wetlands and the species they protect,” said Congresswoman Schrier. “I am proud that this bipartisan bill will take a meaningful step to make sure Washingtonians continue to benefit from these important habitats that are a critical part of our ecosystem.”
The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act would create a new grant program under the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) to provide critical water infrastructure and on-the-ground habitat needs for birds in the Columbia River Basin and along the Washington and Oregon coasts. 
This legislation is supported by a host of nonpartisan, regional conservation organizations, including. Ducks Unlimited the Coalition of Oregon Land Trusts (COLT), Montana Wildlife Federation, Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership (TRCP), Pacific Birds Habitat Joint Venture (Pacific Birds), Trout Unlimited, Oregon Agricultural Trust, Washington State Audubon, and more. 
“We’re thankful to Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for introducing the Northwest Wetlands VIP Act in the House of Representatives. The future of conservation is on private working lands. This important legislation will bring much-needed resources for landowners to more effectively provide multi-benefits for people, wildlife, agriculture, and wetlands in the Northwest and the Columbia River Basin.” said Jeff McCreary, Ducks Unlimited Director of Operations for the Western Region.
"The Columbia River?Basin holds critical habitat for migratory birds and other wetland-dependent species,” said Joe Buttafuoco, COLT Executive Director. “COLT and our members are thrilled about the bipartisan NW?Wetlands VIP?Act. This bill would offer grants that land trusts, Tribes, private landowners, and nonprofits can use to improve habitat, manage invasive species, and restore floodplain connectivity. Thank you to Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for advancing this important legislation." 
“Wetlands on the coast of Oregon and Washington and within the Columbia River Basin are vital for millions of waterbirds and wetland-dependent species. Support for durable ecosystems, strong partnerships, and natural and working landscapes will deliver real benefits for wildlife, communities, and the economy of the Pacific Northwest. The NW Wetlands VIP Act emphasizes collaboration — consistent with Pacific Birds’ partnership-driven approach. This bill will provide resources for the installation, maintenance, and replacement of critical infrastructure, which aligns with Pacific Birds’ goal to support long-term habitat management while emphasizing multi-species benefits and multi-benefit projects, and empowering collaborative on the ground action,” said Glenn Lamb, Vice Chair of the Pacific Birds Habitat Joint Venture Management Board.  
“The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act would bring critical infrastructure dollars to Pacific Northwest farmers and ranchers. These water management projects not only enhance and restore wetland habitat for migratory birds, but also help producers improve agricultural production on parts of their properties. The Act also provides funding to support conservation easements, which protect farms and ranches for agriculture and associated habitat,” said Nellie McAdams, Executive Director of Oregon Agricultural Trust.  
“Montana’s waterfowl hunters and anglers depend on healthy, connected wetlands, and the birds we chase each fall rely on habitat across the entire Columbia River Basin. The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act gives ranchers, farmers, and Tribes a voluntary way to restore that habitat while keeping working lands working, so our kids and grandkids still have ducks in our skies and fish in our rivers,” said Frank Szollosi, Executive Director of the Montana Wildlife Federation.  
"TRCP appreciates Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier introducing the NW Wetlands VIP Act,” said Michael O’Casey, Director of Public Lands for the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership. “As someone who learned to hunt and fish among the many wetlands and sloughs at the mouth of the mighty Columbia River, and who has seen firsthand the impact of development and fragmentation, this legislation would provide a healthy boost to wetland conservation for both private landowners and the public.” 
“The Association of Northwest Steelheaders strongly supports S.1615 and the continued commitment to policies that protect and strengthen the future of our fisheries, waterways, and outdoor heritage," said James Adkins, Executive Director, Association of Northwest Steelheaders. "Healthy rivers and responsible stewardship are essential to sustaining wild fish populations, supporting local communities, and preserving opportunities for future generations of anglers. Prime habitat for migrating waterfowl also provides critical rearing habitat for juvenile salmon, steelhead and other endangered aquatic species of the Pacific Northwest. We appreciate congressional leadership in advancing this important legislation.” 
“The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act recognizes the importance of investing in wetland infrastructure and habitat restoration projects that benefit both working lands and wild places,” said Christopher Borgatti, Policy & Conservation Manager for Backcountry Hunters & Anglers. “BHA applauds Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for championing this commonsense investment in the future of wetlands, waterfowl, and public access throughout the Columbia River Basin and coastal wetlands.” 
“Healthy wetlands provide a critical foundation for healthy rivers,” said Lindsay Slater, Trout Unlimited Vice President of Government Affairs. “By incentivizing voluntary restoration and conservation, the bipartisan Northwest Wetlands VIP Act will improve water quality, sustain coldwater fisheries, and benefit the communities that depend on them. Trout Unlimited supports this collaborative approach that helps landowners, sportsmen, and conservation partners work together in the Columbia River Basin and along the coast of Oregon and Washington to restore habitat while keeping working lands working.” 
“Healthy wetlands are essential to birds, coastal ecosystems, and the people and communities who help care for these landscapes,” said Amanda Kaplan, vice president for the National Audubon Society’s Washington state office. “The Northwest Wetlands Voluntary Incentives Program Act would give landowners, Tribes and conservation partners resources to restore and improve wetland habitat that shorebirds and waterfowl depend on across the Columbia River Basin and the Pacific Northwest coast. By supporting voluntary conservation efforts, this legislation would also strengthen Audubon’s work with ranchers and other landowners to improve habitat on working lands throughout the region. We thank Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for introducing this bipartisan bill.” 
“Healthy wetlands are essential to healthy river systems, supporting fish, waterfowl, and other bird species while helping ensure clean drinking water,” said Liz Hamilton, Policy Director for the Northwest Sportfishing Industry Association. “We thank Representatives Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for working with Ducks Unlimited to advance this important legislation. These projects will create jobs during implementation and support long-term employment across the region through the outdoor recreation economy.”
"Healthy wetlands are foundational to Washington’s economy, ecosystems, and communities,” said Washington Association of Land Trusts (WALT) Executive Director Erik Kingfisher. “The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act would provide much needed investments in enhancing, maintaining and restoring these vital lands across the Columbia River Basin, Washington coastal zone, and throughout the Puget Sound. As land trusts with the skills to make these projects happen across our beautiful state, we support this bipartisan legislation that would empower landowners through a voluntary, partnership-based approach to establish an open space legacy and enable the care and restoration of these lands to sustain them for future generations."

text:
Fast Facts
Critical minerals–like copper and lithium–are vital to the U.S. economy and national security. The U.S. relies on imported critical minerals to meet its needs, raising concerns that have prompted the President to call for expanding mining on federal lands.
To extract minerals from federal lands, individuals must generally be U.S. citizens and companies must be incorporated in the U.S. However, the Bureau of Land Management, which oversees mines on federal lands, rarely collects information to know if these requirements are being met.
We recommended that BLM do so to help ensure that only those qualified can extract minerals from federal lands.
Photo of a copper mine on federal lands.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management (BLM) administers mining claims that grant the exclusive right to extract critical and other hardrock minerals from most federal lands. U.S. mining laws include citizenship requirements for individuals and business entities holding such claims, known as mining claimants. Under these laws, mining claimants generally must be U.S. citizens, which can include individuals as well as business entities incorporated in a U.S. state or territory. Foreign entities are not qualified to be claimants, but their subsidiaries can hold claims if they are incorporated in the U.S. Mining claimants are not required to disclose to BLM if they are a subsidiary of another entity, foreign or domestic, and they do not have to provide information on any foreign investment they may receive.
Under BLM’s regulations and guidance, the agency collects basic identifying information from individuals and business entities holding mining claims. However, BLM generally does not collect citizenship information and does not document if mining claimants meet the U.S. citizenship requirements. In addition, BLM officials said the agency rarely verifies the citizenship of mining claimants. As a result, BLM generally does not know whether mining claimants are qualified to hold mining claims.
Information the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Collects from Mining Claimants
GAO analyzed a nongeneralizable sample of 15 mining claimants that appeared to be business entities and could not find evidence that seven of the claimants were incorporated in the U.S., as required. BLM was unable to help determine if these entities met the requirement to be incorporated in the U.S. because it did not have the necessary information to do so. Until BLM directs staff to collect citizenship information and document that mining claimants meet the U.S. citizenship requirements, BLM lacks reasonable assurance that only qualified individuals and business entities hold mining claims that allow them to extract and profit from the minerals produced on federal lands.
Australia and Canada—examples of top mineral-producing countries—collect detailed information on foreign investors in businesses in their countries. They can use this information to restrict foreign investments in mining and other sectors by prohibiting certain investments or imposing conditions, as each country has done in some cases in recent years. In addition, both countries limit the ability of foreign state-owned enterprises and other foreign investors to acquire control of businesses involving critical minerals.
Why GAO Did This Study
Critical minerals are vital to the U.S. economy and national security. Federal lands are a significant source of hardrock minerals and include some mining operations supported by foreign investments, according to BLM officials. The administration and Congress have expressed concern about U.S. reliance on foreign sources for critical minerals, and the President has called for expanding mineral production from federal lands.
GAO was asked to review issues related to foreign entities’ involvement in mining on federal lands. This report examines (1) the extent to which BLM collects, documents, and reviews mining claimants’ citizenship information and (2) how selected mineral-producing countries address foreign investments in mining. GAO was also asked to report on the extent of foreign investment in mining on federal lands (see GAO-27-108094).
GAO reviewed U.S. laws and regulations; analyzed a nongeneralizable sample of mining claimants to assess if they appear to meet citizenship requirements; examined BLM documents; visited three BLM state offices; and interviewed officials and representatives from BLM and other federal and nonfederal entities. GAO also reviewed Australian and Canadian laws, guidance, reports, and written responses to questions.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that BLM direct staff to collect citizenship information from mining claimants and document that they meet the citizenship requirements to hold mining claims. Interior did not provide comments on this report.
title: Critical Minerals: BLM Should Ensure Individuals and Businesses Meet Citizenship Requirements for Hardrock Mining Claims

San Diego Man Pleads Guilty to Tax Evasion
A California man pleaded guilty yesterday to tax evasion.
According to court documents and statements made in court, Peter L. Roper, of San Diego, operated various La Jolla-based businesses that marketed and sold purported federal tax credits throughout the United States. Between 2010 through 2021, Roper and his businesses received nearly $19 million in income, on which he owed more than $6.7 million in federal income taxes. Roper and his businesses, however, did not report any of this income on tax returns or pay taxes to the IRS. Throughout this period, Roper used his businesses’ bank accounts to pay personal expenses and concealed assets by titling them in the names of others. Instead of paying taxes, Roper spent $187,432.34 on a 2015 McLaren 650S Spider and another $277,698.50 on a 2021 Aston Martin DBX, among other things.
Roper pleaded guilty to one count of tax evasion. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 8 and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the case.
Trial Attorneys John C. Gerardi and Charles A. O’Reilly of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathan Brooks for the Southern District of California are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: San Diego Man Pleads Guilty to Tax Evasion
