Bosnian National Sentenced for Violating International Sanctions Against North Korea
A Bosnian national was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to federal export and sanctions violations by conspiring and attempting to broker the sale of Man Portable Air Defense Systems, which are anti-aircraft missiles.
“U.S. sanctions mean little if those who knowingly evade them face no consequences,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison for the District of New Mexico. “This defendant helped carry out an international scheme to conduct business that U.S. law prohibited, and this sentence holds him accountable for his role. I am proud of the investigators and prosecutors whose hard work and dedication brought this case to sentencing in New Mexico. Their commitment to seeing this prosecution through is a testament to the caliber of the people who serve in this district.”
“Those who knowingly attempt to circumvent U.S. export controls and international sanctions to facilitate the illicit trafficking of military weapons pose a serious threat to our national security and global stability,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Ryan G. McRae of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) El Paso. “Their willingness to profit from prohibited weapons transactions demonstrates blatant disregard for the law. HSI aggressively pursues those who traffic in restricted military technology and hold them accountable for their actions.”
According to court documents, Sasa Micev, 43, a citizen of Bosnia, is an international arms dealer. Micev worked with a co-conspirator based in New Mexico and others to violate and evade restrictions imposed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury under the North Korea Sanctions Regulations by brokering the purchase of SA-18 Igla portable surface-to-air missiles from North Korea without the required license or approvals from the Department of Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control.
On multiple occasions in 2020, Micev and a co-conspirator discussed unlawfully acquiring the Igla missiles and Micev provided pricing information, participated in efforts to obtain the items through falsified documentation, and worked to procure the weapons from North Korea despite knowing that such transactions were prohibited under U.S. and international laws.
In late 2020, Micev and the co-conspirator traveled to Ankara, Turkey to meet and complete the sale of the Igla missiles. However, after a price dispute with the North Koreans, the sale fell through.
Micev pleaded guilty to violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the North Korean Sanctions Regulations.
HSI’s Albuquerque and Phoenix Field Offices investigated this case.
Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tavo Hall and Holland Kastrin for the District of New Mexico are prosecuting the case with the assistance of the Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.
title: Bosnian National Sentenced for Violating International Sanctions Against North Korea

NEW ORLEANS – RAYMOND T. KNESEL (“KNESEL”) , age 60, of Abita Springs, Louisiana was indicted on October 9, 2026, for attempted coercion and enticement of a minor, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 2422(b), announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle.

According to the indictment, between September 24, 2026, and September 28, 2026, KNESEL persuaded and enticed an individual he believed to be a fifteen-year-old female to engage in illegal and illicit sexual activity.

U.S. Attorney Courcelle praised the work of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in investigating this matter. Assistant United States Attorney Mary Anne Flippo of the Public Integrity Unit and Human Trafficking and Child Exploitation Task Force is in charge of the prosecution.

text:
Fast Facts
The Department of Housing and Urban Development has undergone a number of changes since 2025.
For example:
HUD reduced its workforce by 29% between December 2024 and December 2025, mostly through deferred resignation programs
Over half of employees who left had worked at HUD for at least 10 years; over 40% had worked there for over 20 years
We interviewed 20 stakeholder organizations about these changes. Nearly all said that experienced points of contact had left, making it harder to navigate HUD programs. Some stakeholders had to reduce services or staffing during funding gaps; others reported delays with physical inspections of properties.
Sign that reads "U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development".
Highlights
What GAO Found
The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) reduced its workforce by 29 percent in 2025 and modified the types of programs it funds in response to presidential directives and executive branch guidance. HUD largely achieved workforce reductions through deferred resignation programs. Over half the employees who separated had at least 10 years of service at HUD, including 41 percent with more than 20 years of service. HUD did not publish notice of any reorganization plans that led to field office closures in 2025, though in 2026 it announced plans to consolidate one field office into a nearby regional office.
Workforce Changes at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in 2025
Note: Percentages may not sum to 100 due to rounding.
About half of HUD’s 68 active grant programs made new awards in fiscal year 2025, but the median value of those awards was higher than in previous years. HUD also terminated about 21 percent of its active contracts in 2025, valued at about $367 million. Most terminated contracts involved professional or IT services.
Representatives of 20 stakeholder organizations GAO interviewed—including fair housing grantees and agencies, public housing agencies, and Section 8 project-based rental assistance property managers—reported confusion, delays, and operational disruptions following HUD’s changes. Nearly all said that experienced points of contact had left, making it harder to navigate HUD programs. Fair housing stakeholders reported reducing services or staffing during monthslong funding gaps. Stakeholders also reported delays with physical inspections of HUD-assisted properties.
Since January 2025, HUD has reported launching initiatives aimed at increasing efficiency and streamlining operations. For example, HUD reported developing a unified grants system to standardize grant administration and a project voucher initiative to automate aspects of rental assistance processing. HUD did not respond to GAO’s requests to discuss these initiatives or provide supporting documentation. As a result, Congress and the public have limited information on the status or effectiveness of these initiatives.
Why GAO Did This Study
HUD administers programs related to housing assistance, community development, and fair housing. To carry out these programs, HUD headquarters and field staff work with public housing agencies, private property owners, nonprofit organizations, and other stakeholders.
Executive orders and other actions issued in 2025 called for workforce and program changes at HUD. GAO was asked to examine the effects of these changes. This report describes (1) changes HUD made to its workforce, field office structure, and grant and contract spending in 2025; (2) effects of those changes on selected HUD functions reported by housing stakeholders; and (3) steps HUD has publicly reported to manage the changes.
HUD did not respond to GAO’s requests for information throughout the audit. GAO analyzed publicly available 2025 data on HUD’s workforce, terminated contracts, and grant spending. GAO selected three HUD functions for review, chosen to reflect a mix of funding levels and other criteria: (1) enforcement of the Fair Housing Act and Violence Against Women Act of 1994, (2) administration of the Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance Program, and (3) coordination of inspections of HUD-assisted properties.
GAO also conducted four site visits and interviewed representatives of a nongeneralizable selection of 20 local and national housing organizations, including public housing agencies and fair housing organizations. GAO also reviewed court documents and publicly available data, and agency documentation related to HUD’s workforce and efficiency planning.
For more information, contact Jill Naamane at naamanej@gao.gov.
title: Department of Housing and Urban Development: 2025 Workforce and Spending Changes

text:
HHS Launches Health Center Healthy Lifestyle Commitment to Advance Nutrition, Prevention, and Healthy Living
CHATHAM, VA—OCTOBER 14, 2026—U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., joined by Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) Administrator Tom Engels, today launched the HHS Health Center Healthy Lifestyle Commitment, a voluntary initiative that encourages health centers nationwide to put nutrition, prevention, and healthy living at the center of patient care.
Secretary Kennedy announced the initiative during a visit to Piedmont Access to Health Services (PATHS) health center in Chatham, Virginia, where he highlighted the role health centers play in preventing chronic disease and helping patients build healthier lives.
“We will not reverse chronic disease by waiting until Americans get sick,” said Secretary Kennedy. “HHS is equipping health centers to make nutrition, physical activity, healthy sleep, and prevention part of everyday care. This commitment will help doctors and families act earlier, build healthier habits, and prevent disease before it starts.”
Through the voluntary Health Center Healthy Lifestyle Commitment, HRSA-supported health centers are encouraged to advance evidence-based best practices that support:
- Prioritizing prevention and healthy lifestyles by encouraging healthy eating, physical activity, adequate sleep, limited screen time, and other behaviors that can help prevent, delay, and better manage chronic disease;
- Promoting healthy eating by helping patients and families understand and apply the new Dietary Guidelines for Americans, including choosing whole, nutrient-dense foods and limiting highly processed foods and added sugars;
- Empowering patients and families with practical, actionable information about nutrition, preventive care, and healthy behaviors that support lifelong health;
- Connecting patients to community health activities, including community gardens, fresh produce programs, nutrition education, and physical activity opportunities;
- Strengthening the prevention workforce by equipping health center staff with tools, training, and resources to integrate nutrition and healthy living into everyday patient care; and
- Building a culture of health that encourages healthy choices and empowers patients to take an active role in improving their health.
As part of the initiative, HHS is encouraging participating health centers to display the new food pyramid and use it as a resource to help patients and families understand the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025–2030 and make healthier food choices.
“Health centers are trusted partners in their communities, caring for millions of Americans every year,” said HRSA Administrator Tom Engels. “They are uniquely positioned to help patients and families make healthier choices and prevent chronic disease before it starts. This commitment builds on the important work health centers are already doing by giving them additional tools and resources to make nutrition, prevention, and healthy living part of everyday patient care.”
HRSA is also making resources available on the new Health Centers and Nutrition webpage, including nutrition education materials, tools for patients and providers, and practical guidance to support conversations about healthy eating and disease prevention.
The Health Center Healthy Lifestyle Commitment builds on the Trump Administration’s Make America Healthy Again Strategy by recognizing the critical role of community-based primary care in addressing chronic disease and improving the health of American families.
Participation in the commitment is voluntary and does not establish new federal requirements or standards of care. A health center’s decision to participate will not affect its eligibility for or receipt of HRSA funding.
Learn more about the HHS Health Center Healthy Lifestyle Commitment.

WASHINGTON, D.C./October 14, 2026 – Today, Special Counsel Charles Baldis formally presented Dr. Brett Wyrick, Deputy Federal Air Surgeon at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), with the Office of Special Counsel’s 2026 Outstanding Public Servant Award. OSC announced the award on July 30, 2026, National Whistleblower Day.
In connection with the presentation, Special Counsel Baldis issued the following statement:
“I am pleased to present Dr. Brett Wyrick with the 2026 Outstanding Public Servant Award.
“Dr. Wyrick saw a risk to the people who fly, and to the people who keep them safe in the air, and he would not look past it. As Deputy Federal Air Surgeon, he identified that medical officers in the FAA’s Office of Aerospace Medicine were too few for the work before them. Certificates and clearances for pilots and air traffic controllers were falling behind. Hundreds of airmen continued flying while flagged medical issues had not been fully reviewed. Some personnel were discouraged from reporting an illness, injury, or new medication because a report could ground them for months. New controllers, hired to ease shortages in the towers, were waiting on medical clearances that should not have taken so long.
“He put that warning on the record because safety in the national airspace is not an internal matter. It belongs to everyone who boards a plane, and to the families waiting for them on the ground.
“His disclosure moved the FAA to hire additional medical officers and to clear these cases with more care and more speed. Those changes made a real difference. That is what this award recognizes: not simply the difficulty of speaking up, but the good that followed from it.
“On behalf of the Office of Special Counsel, I thank Dr. Wyrick for his service to the flying public.”
title: Office of Special Counsel Presents 2026 Outstanding Public Servant Award to FAA Deputy Federal Air Surgeon

text:
Thompson, Correa, Thanedar Release Government Report on Problems with DHS Body Camera Program
Legislation to Be Introduced to Address ICE’s Refusal of Automatic Camera Activation
(WASHINGTON) – Today, Democratic Members of the House Committee on Homeland Security announced the release of a U.S. Government Accountability Office report they requested on the Department of Homeland Security’s Body-Worn Camera program for its immigration officers and agents. Recent tragic shootings have shown that not only do these cameras need to be deployed, they need to be activated with proper controls.
In the report, entitled “Federal Law Enforcement: CBP and ICE Should Improve Body-Worn Camera Program Management,” the GAO found while DHS has rushed deploying body-worn cameras, both CBP and ICE lack updated program plans, results oriented performance measures, and sufficient controls to ensure cameras are activated and used consistently. GAO concludes that these gaps limit DHS’s ability to achieve the core objectives of the program—transparency, accountability, and strengthened public trust.
GAO also found that ICE, unlike CBP, relies on manual camera activation and that the absence of automated controls – which GAO recommends – puts ICE at greater risk of missing critical recordings.
“With shootings by DHS officers on the rise, the American people – and Congress – have rightfully demanded DHS use body-worn cameras when its officers are out in the field. However, this government report shows that DHS’s body-worn camera program is deficient and needs to be revamped if DHS is going to be transparent and accountable,” said Rep. Bennie G. Thompson (D-MS), Ranking Member of the Committee on Homeland Security. “Worse yet, ICE – which has shown time and again it thinks it is immune to accountability – is unwilling to implement automatic activation for its cameras, increasing the risk of missing critical recordings, just like what happened when Wilber Garces Perez was shot by an ICE agent in Austin last month. This is completely unacceptable and I will be introducing legislation in the coming days to close this gap and ensure all DHS body-worn cameras have the recommended automatic activation.”
"Since January, federal immigration agents have shot at least 25 people. Six are dead, three of them American citizens. These are not just numbers – they are real lives lost, and the public deserves transparency and accountability from DHS,” added Rep. Lou Correa (D-CA), Ranking Member of the Border Security and Enforcement subcommittee. “DHS has been turned into a tool for political ends, and that has to stop. This report confirms the DHS body-camera program is lacking, even though the department has had more than enough time to get it right. Transparency and accountability aren't optional."
“ICE is violently terrorizing Americans left and right. To help with transparency and accountability, they need to have body cameras that are automatically activated. This latest GAO report shows DHS's current body camera program is unacceptable, plagued with old plans and no performance goals,” added Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-MI), Ranking Member of the Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability subcommittee. “DHS must reverse course immediately and implement additional automatic activation controls for body cameras as well as issue transparent operations guidance for this program. DHS's continued attempts to avoid accountability for their horrific actions are unacceptable, and I will continue to work with my Homeland Security Committee colleagues to hold this department accountable.”

text:
BOSTON – A Raynham, Mass. man has been sentenced in federal court in Boston for the armed robbery of a cash courier in Swansea, Mass.

Christopher White, 39, was sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Patti B. Saris to 154 months in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release. In May 2026, White pleaded guilty to one count of robbery interfering with interstate commerce, commonly referred to as Hobbs Act robbery; one count of conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act robbery; one count of brandishing a firearm in the commission of a crime of violence; one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm; and one count of possession with intent to distribute cocaine. In May 2024, White was arrested and charged.

In the early morning hours of Feb. 19, 2024, White and another individual, Steven Madison, were seen on video stealing a rental van from a U-Haul Moving & Storage location in Abington, Mass. Later in the day an armed courier who worked for a company that provides secure cash transportation services for licensed cannabis companies arrived at a bank in Swansea. carrying approximately $436,200 in cash for deposit.

The U-Haul van pulled up alongside the courier and White, wearing a mask and a camouflaged vest, exited the van and pointed a firearm at the courier before zip-tying the courier’s hands behind his back. Madison exited the U-Haul van and quickly loaded the cash into the vehicle. After trying to disarm the courier, the two men forced the courier into the back seat of his own car, pepper sprayed him and closed the door.

Surveillance footage showed that the courier managed to remove one hand from the zip-tie restraints while inside his vehicle, draw his firearm and fire four rounds in the direction of the U-Haul van as it fled the scene before calling 911.

After leaving the bank, the men drove the van to a nearby location in Swansea where they met with a third man, Quentin McDonald, driving an SUV. The men then transferred the stolen cash into the getaway SUV and fled.

Following a search of White’s residence in Raynham, zip-ties, a black mask similar to that worn by one of the robbers, a firearm, ammunition and cocaine were recovered. White has prior state convictions for larceny and receiving stolen property.

In June 2025 , Madison pleaded guilty to one count of robbery; one count of conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act robbery; one count of brandishing a firearm in relation to a crime of violence; one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition; and one count of possession with intent to distribute cocaine. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Nov. 9, 2026. In May 2026 , McDonald pleaded guilty to one count of robbery and one count of conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act robbery. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 3, 2026.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Thomas A. Greco, Special Agent in Charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Massachusetts State Police, Bristol County District Attorney’s Office, and the Bridgewater, Brockton, Raynham and Swansea Police Departments. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Philip Cheng, Allegra Flamm and John J. Reynolds III prosecuted the case.
title: Raynham Man Sentenced to Over 12 Years in Prison for Armed Robbery of Cash Courier

NASA will preview two upcoming spacewalks to complete solar array installation and power augmentation of the International Space Station during a news conference at 2 p.m. EDT, Tuesday, Oct. 20, from NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.
NASA will stream the event through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online:
NASA participants in the news conference include:
- Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager, Low Earth Orbit Program
- Garrett Hehn, spacewalk flight director, Flight Operations Directorate
United States-based media interested in attending in person must contact the Johnson newsroom no later than 3 p.m., Monday, Oct. 19, at: jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov. Thursday, Oct. 29
During U.S. spacewalk 100, NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk will exit the station’s Quest airlock to install and deploy an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the 2A electrical power channel. FAA Safety Initiative Expands Air Traffic Controller Training Through Hands-On Flight Deck Experience
WASHINGTON — The Federal Aviation Administration today announced the reinstatement of its Flight Deck Training program, giving air traffic controllers opportunities to gain firsthand experience aboard commercial, general aviation and military aircraft.
This program allows controllers to apply for jumpseat access on eligible flights to gain firsthand experience with flight deck operations, including pilot workload, cockpit procedures and how air traffic control instructions impact flight crews. The FAA worked closely with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) to reinstate this program, which was paused at the start of the pandemic.
“After listening to our frontline controllers, we’re excited to bring back the Flight Deck Training program. Our controllers are the backbone of the National Airspace System and giving them opportunities to build their knowledge and gain firsthand experience makes them better at what they do,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “Communication is key and this program will give controllers and pilots an up-close view of each other’s responsibilities and challenges.”
“NATCA is pleased to see this vital component of air traffic controller training reinstated,” said National Air Traffic Controllers Association President Nick Daniels. “There is no substitute for firsthand experience in the cockpit. The Flight Deck Training program gives participants a unique perspective on the challenges pilots face and how their decisions and actions interact with the air traffic control system, ultimately strengthening their understanding of the National Airspace System.”
Additional information
How it works
Controllers will apply electronically to fly on specific flights, including identifying a training objective. Once approved internally, the FAA will transmit the request to the airlines. Controllers will go through multiple steps of vetting at the airport and when they reach the airplane. After the flight, controllers will submit a report explaining what they learned.
Flight allowances
Controllers can fly on two commercial/general aviation flights and one military flight per year. A controller’s air traffic manager will consider the facility’s available staffing and needs in evaluating a request.
Airline participation
All major U.S. airlines have agreed to participate in the program.
Early testing and insights
The FAA has been testing the program and has already identified benefits, including helping controllers understand when they should refrain from issuing complex instructions and the impact that instructions such as changes in the landing runway can have on pilot workload.
Launch timeline
The FAA expects to start the formal Flight Deck Training program after Thanksgiving.
title: FAA Safety Initiative Expands Air Traffic Controller Training Through Hands-On Flight Deck Experience

Texas Tax Preparer Sentenced to Prison as Part of False Tax Return Scheme
A Texas tax return preparer was sentenced on October 7, 2026, to 14 months in prison for her role in conspiring to file false tax returns on behalf of clients.
According to court documents and statements made in court, from approximately February 2020 to October 2022, Sivagami Chidambaram conspired with a tax return preparation business owner and several of his employees to defraud the United States by filing tax returns for clients that contained false business expenses. These false expenses artificially reduced the taxes the clients owed to the IRS, which enabled them to receive refunds to which they were not entitled. Sometimes, Chidambaram added false business expenses on client returns by asking the client about work-from-home expenses, even though Chidambaram knew such expenses could not be claimed on their returns. In some instances, Chidambaram included false business expenses on clients’ tax returns before speaking with the client. In other instances, Chidambaram added false items to appease clients who demanded higher tax refunds. Chidambaram admitted to causing a tax loss to the United States exceeding $250,000 but less than $550,000.
Three other tax return preparers – including a tax return preparation business owner and two of his employees – were sentenced to prison in July in relation to the same scheme. One tax return preparer who admitted to filing false tax returns for clients was sentenced to home confinement.
Tax preparation business owner Mathews Chacko was previously sentenced to 50 months in prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy to defraud the IRS as part of the same scheme. Chacko admitted to causing a tax loss to the United States exceeding $3.5 million but less than $9.5 million. Tax preparers Anish Pillai, Subhala Suresh, and Mou Kundu were previously sentenced to 26 months’ imprisonment, 18 months’ imprisonment, and 18 months’ home confinement, respectively, after pleading guilty to aiding and assisting the filing of a false tax return as part of the same scheme.
Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons of the Western District of Texas made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case.
Acting Assistant Deputy Chief Marissa R. Brodney and Trial Attorney Michael L. Jones of the Criminal Division’s Tax Section prosecuted the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Texas Tax Preparer Sentenced to Prison as Part of False Tax Return Scheme

ST. PAUL – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that Christopher Erik Septon, of Plymouth, Minnesota, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud and embezzlement of more than $1 million from his former employer.

Septon pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Laura M. Provinzino on October 14, 2026. Sentencing will be set at a later date, and the defendant faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

According to court documents, from on or about 2019 until about 2024, Septon devised and executed a scheme to defraud and embezzle from his former employer, Ellis Properties, a small family-run business in Minneapolis that specializes in commercial real estate. Septon worked for Ellis Properties and was trusted to use company funds to pay vendors, contractors, and other third parties.

Septon abused his position to improperly charge more than $800,000 on the company credit card, directing the payments to his own payment-processing accounts. He wrote false statements in the transaction memo lines, misrepresenting to the company that the transactions were business-related and with third parties, when in fact they were transfers to his own accounts. He then transferred the fraud proceeds to bank accounts he controlled.

The defendant additionally created fake invoices, emails, and lies to induce Ellis Properties personnel to issue him reimbursement checks for expenses he did not actually incur.

To fraudulently induce payments, the defendant also falsely represented that various payments pertained to work with various third parties, including government agencies, such as the City of Minneapolis, the Metropolitan Council, the Minnesota Department of Agriculture, and the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency.

“The defendant impersonated state and local government agencies to embezzle from a family-run business. Today’s guilty plea is one step closer to holding him accountable for defrauding hardworking people,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen.

“Christopher Septon was given the keys to a family’s business, and instead of protecting it, he picked its pockets,” said Marta C. Grijalva, Acting Special Agent in Charge, IRS Criminal Investigation, Chicago Field Office. “He stole more than $1 million from the people who trusted him, then hid behind other people’s identities to cover his tracks. There’s a special kind of dishonesty in stealing from the very people who gave you an opportunity to earn an honest living. Septon mistook trust for weakness, and that mistake has caught up with him.”

This case is the result of an investigation conducted by IRS Criminal Investigation, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and the Minneapolis Police Department.

Assistant United States Attorney Matthew D. Forbes is prosecuting the case.

Note: Previous press release on the indictment here .
title: Plymouth Man Pleads Guilty to Defrauding Small Family-Run Business Out of More Than $1 Million

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Eugene Vindman (Va.-07) today introduced legislation to protect hardworking Virginia families and small businesses from being forced to shoulder the rising electricity costs associated with the growing electricity demands of data centers.
The Make Data Centers Pay Act would amend the Federal Power Act to require large and medium-sized data centers to pay the full incremental costs associated with their electricity use, preventing those expenses from being passed on to residential customers and small businesses.
“Families in Virginia and across the country should not have to pay higher electricity bills to subsidize some of the largest and most energy-intensive data centers and computing facilities in the world,” said Vindman. “As data centers and artificial intelligence drive growing demand for electricity, we need to make sure the companies benefiting from that growth pay their fair share. My bill puts ratepayers first and protects hardworking Virginians from being stuck with higher utility bills to subsidize billion-dollar corporations.”
Under the legislation, covered data centers and high-density computing facilities with electricity demands of at least 20 megawatts would be required to cover the incremental costs of serving their electricity needs. This would help ensure that the costs of infrastructure and electricity service needed to support these facilities are borne by the companies driving that demand, rather than shifted onto everyday ratepayers.
BACKGROUND
Vindman has been a champion for holding data centers and electric utilities accountable.
In August 2026, he introduced the Smart Data Center Policy Act to prevent data center development near neighborhoods, schools, and parks.
Vindman also introduced the Home Energy Affordability Act to limit how often utilities can change residential utility rates and change prices for everyday Virginians, as well as the Utility Hikes Transparency Act, which would create the first comprehensive, machine-readable federal database of retail utility rate changes in the United States.
He has also fought against corruption in the energy sector by championing the Energy Utility Lobbying Ban Act, which would bar former government officials from lobbying on behalf of the companies they used to regulate.
What’s more, Vindman was the first member of Virginia’s congressional delegation to publicly oppose the proposed merger between NextEra and Dominion Energy, raising concerns about its potential impact on electricity rates and Virginia consumers.
Most recently, he delivered remarks at a Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) public hearing on the proposed merger, urging regulators to reject the proposal and put the interests of ratepayers ahead of corporate profits.
###
title: Vindman Introduces ‘Make Data Centers Pay Act’ to Protect Virginians from Rising Electricity Costs

Justice Department Opens Investigation of Pennsauken, New Jersey’s Allegedly Unconstitutional Permit Delays
Today, the Justice Department opened an investigation to determine whether Pennsauken, New Jersey deprives citizens of their right to bear arms through egregious and unjust delays in issuing firearm licenses. The Second Amendment protects the right to keep and bear firearms — including the right to carry firearms. The investigation focuses on the Pennsauken Township Police’s permitting system; the investigation does not support any armed obstruction of federal or local law enforcement.
“I have directed the Civil Rights Division, through our Second Amendment Section, to defend law-abiding citizens from local authorities who infringe on the right to safely carry legal firearms,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “Our investigation aims to discover if allegations of unconstitutional delays in firearm permitting are true, and if so, to fix it.”
It is a violation of the Second Amendment for government officials to delay issuing permits to purchase or carry firearms. In 2022, the Supreme Court held in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen that a state’s permitting process is put towards “abusive ends” when “lengthy wait times in processing license applications or exorbitant fees deny ordinary citizens their right to public carry.” Here, it is alleged that Pennsauken, through the Pennsauken Township Police Department, uses just such “abusive ends” to improperly limit Second Amendment rights.
The Civil Rights Division’s Second Amendment Section enforces the Second Amendment. If you believe your right to keep and bear arms is being infringed, please submit a complaint through www.justice.gov/crt/second-amendment-section.
title: Justice Department Opens Investigation of Pennsauken, New Jersey’s Allegedly Unconstitutional Permit Delays

FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development
WASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 14, 2026—The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a division within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), today announced the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to reimagine the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. As outlined in a new white paper, the Initiative will develop an optimized, fit-for-purpose framework that reflects the realities of rare disease drug development by considering the nuances of each disease, patient needs, product type and the evidence that can be realistically generated in small patient populations.
To solicit feedback on the Rare Disease Framework Initiative from patients and disease advocates, industry, and others, the FDA will host an October 28 meeting at the FDA’s White Oak campus. The meeting will be facilitated by the Reagan-Udall Foundation for the FDA.
“Americans with rare diseases cannot afford a regulatory system that treats every condition the same,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump, FDA is rethinking rare disease drug development by putting patients at the center and matching regulatory requirements to the realities of small patient populations. We will remove unnecessary barriers, embrace cutting-edge science, and accelerate promising treatments while upholding FDA’s rigorous standards.”
“Patients and families living with rare diseases have few or no approved treatment options, and the burden of uncertainty can extend across every part of their lives,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “As we learn more about rare diseases and better understand the breadth of suffering they cause, we must ensure that America’s regulatory system remains at the forefront — prepared to respond to emerging science, anticipate the needs of patients and families, and help bring safe and effective therapies to those who need them. The FDA will fight hard for patients by building a more consistent, predictable, and innovative approach to rare disease drug development while maintaining the rigorous standards Americans expect from the FDA.”
The FDA has long used regulatory flexibility and developed targeted programs to support innovation in the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. These efforts have led to meaningful advances for patients and families. Nevertheless, with only 5% or so of rare conditions having an FDA-approved treatment, the FDA agrees with patients, drug developers, and providers that more must be done to speed the development of safe and effective treatments for rare diseases. In developing the framework, the FDA is committed to the following:
- Providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance and transparent communication.
- Embedding the patient’s voice both early, and at clearly defined milestones, in the drug development and review process.
- Further leveraging external expertise to support customization of regulatory review.
- Building shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review.
- Applying risk-based approaches, particularly to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections.
- Championing the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and innovative statistical approaches in rare disease drug development.
The Initiative is led by the FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, partnering with the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.
“Patients with rare diseases and their families deserve a regulatory process that addresses the uniqueness of each of their conditions while maintaining the FDA’s rigorous standards,” said the Hub’s Director, Amy Comstock Rick, J.D. “A bold vision to reimagine the regulatory framework for rare disease drug development that builds on key learnings and milestones is necessary to meet this moment. This new framework will enhance consistency and predictability for both sponsors and for patients.”
Further opportunities to provide input will follow the public meeting, including sector-specific roundtables, Requests for Information, and internal FDA feedback sessions. This feedback will inform the detailed development of a new framework, which might include potential new or revised guidance, revisions to regulations, staff training, and organizational changes.

text:
For over 250 years, American sailors have defended our Nation upon the seas, forging the most lethal Navy in the history of the world. Today, on the birthday of the United States Navy, Icelebrate this incredible milestone with our active duty and reserve sailors, past and present, whose unparalleled expertise and extraordinary devotion to duty in times of war and peace have carried our Navy to these unrivaled heights.
On October 13, 1775, our Navy was formally established when the Second Continental Congress authorized a pair of armed vessels to sail against the mighty British Empire, intercept enemy supply lines, and defend the cause of American liberty at sea during the Revolutionary War. Since its humble beginnings, the Navy has grown into the most formidable seafaring force the world has ever known.
Today’s sailors are part of a storied legacy of maritime supremacy that has safeguarded our sovereignty in every major conflict since. Our warships are unmistakable symbols of American military might, but the most sophisticated, state-of-the-art fleet is nothing without the elite men and women who carry out every mission at home and abroad with unwavering resolve and professionalism. In home ports and on carrier decks, submarine patrols, and distant oceans, our sailor stand watch around the clock, deterring aggression, keeping the world’s great sea lanes open and free, and carrying American strength to every corner of the globe. Their skill and sacrifice keep our Republic safe and secure in the blessings of liberty, earning the everlasting gratitude of the American People.
As President, I am rebuilding our incredible Navy and restoring the mighty American shipbuilding industry that sustains it, ensuring our fleet is prepared to meet every challenge of our age. Since returning to office, my Administration has secured over $150 billion in investments to usher in the Golden Age of American shipbuilding. In August, I was proud to sign a National Security Presidential Memorandum that directs the Department of War to pursue more direct investments in the American shipbuilding industrial base, expanding our capacity to build warships and creating good-paying jobs for American workers. The Memorandum further directs the Secretary of War to establish a fifth Naval shipyard, the first in more than eight decades, to increase our Nation’s submarine and aircraft carrier repair capacity. Just last week we saw the fruit of those actions as construction began on the largest new shipyard in the United States since World War II, which will build the next generation of American submarines. Under my leadership, our Navy will be bigger, better, and stronger than ever before.
Since the dawn of our glorious Republic, generation after generation of valiant sailors have answered the Navy’s stern call for “faith, courage, service true, with honor over all.” Today, the First Lady joins me in saluting over two and a half centuries of American dominance upon the seas and honor the heroes who secure the freedom and safety of the American People.
title: Presidential Message on the Birthday of the United States Navy

ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock woman has been charged with second degree murder for allegedly shooting and killing a man outside her residence.

According to court documents, on October 4, 2026, Letisha Begay , 39, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, allegedly shot a man following an encounter outside her residence in Shiprock, New Mexico. According to investigators, Begay told responding officers that the man had been drinking throughout the day and returned to her residence looking for his motorcycle. Begay said she returned home after receiving a phone call from her distressed daughter and found the man taking the keys to her truck.

A nearby witness reported hearing a loud bang before seeing a pickup truck backing toward another vehicle. The truck struck the vehicle, and witnesses found the man unconscious behind the wheel with a gunshot wound to his chest. Begay approached the truck and initially told a witness that the man had shot himself. She attempted to stop the bleeding while witnesses called for help. Responding officers attempted lifesaving measures, but the man died at the scene.

While speaking with officers, Begay allegedly admitted shooting the man but said she had not intended to do so. She directed officers to a pistol inside her residence and confirmed that it was the firearm involved in the shooting. Investigators also observed a shattered driver's side window with a small hole in the glass.

Begay is charged with second degree murder and discharging a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence. She will remain on condition of release pending trial, which has not been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Begay faces a mandatory minimum of 10 years in prison and maximum of life imprisonment.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Nation Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua Ray Slatton is prosecuting the case.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Shiprock Woman Charged in Fatal Shooting

HHS Declares Public Health Emergencies for Florida, Alabama following Hurricane Isaias
WASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 14, 2026—U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. yesterday determined that public health emergencies exist in Florida and Alabama as a result of Hurricane Isaias. The determinations follow President Trump’s October 9 emergency declarations for both states (Florida, Alabama). The President’s declarations and the Secretary’s determination allow HHS to authorize temporary waivers and modifications of certain requirements. These flexibilities help the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) support healthcare providers and suppliers serving people enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) in the covered emergency areas.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is giving healthcare providers in Florida and Alabama the flexibility to keep caring for patients in the wake of Hurricane Isaias,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “We are helping them maintain essential services, respond quickly as needs change, and keep care available throughout the response and recovery.”
“When a storm disrupts someone’s ability to get care, the need is immediate and personal,” said Sean Kaufman, HHS Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR). “I want the people affected by Hurricane Isaias to know that we are here to help. Our federal teams worked alongside state and local partners to understand what communities needed and to support the healthcare services they depend on.”
Prior to landfall, ASPR pre-positioned regional staff in areas at risk from the storm to monitor the impacts on public health and healthcare systems and provide technical assistance in anticipation of state requests. Healthcare System Assessment Teams also deployed to evaluate the storm’s impact on healthcare facilities.
In addition, ASPR shared HHS emPOWER datasets with states in the storm’s path. These data can help responders identify, by geographic area, the number of Medicare beneficiaries relying on electricity-dependent medical equipment or certain essential healthcare services, including facility-based dialysis and home healthcare.
Individuals experiencing emotional distress related to Hurricane Isaias can contact the Disaster Distress Helpline by calling or texting 1-800-985-5990. Managed by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), this toll-free, multilingual, crisis support service is available 24/7 to all residents in the U.S. and its territories who are experiencing emotional distress related to natural or human-caused disasters. Callers can be connected with counselors in more than 100 languages via third-party interpretation services by indicating their preferred language to the responding counselor.
In declaring the public health emergency and authorizing flexibilities for CMS providers, suppliers, and beneficiaries, Secretary Kennedy acted within his authority under the Public Health Service Act and Social Security Act. These actions and flexibilities are retroactive to October 6, 2026, in the state of Florida and October 7, 2026, in the state of Alabama.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection announces the extension of the compliance date for new informal entry procedures for international mail from Oct. 22, 2026, to Jan. 20, 2027. The 90-day extension provides importers, brokers, and logistics providers additional time to update their processes while helping avoid disruptions to certain international postal shipments destined for the United States.
As previously announced in the June 24, Interim Final Rule, “Indefinite Suspension of the De Minimis Exemption for Mail Shipments and New Postal Informal Entry Process” and the Federal Register Notice, “Test of the New Electronic Entry Process for Mail,” all international postal shipments that are subject to Section 201, 232, or 301 duty or are the jurisdiction of a Partner Government Agency will be required to be filed electronically in the Automated Commercial Environment through the new Entry Type 13 process for purposes of informal entry (otherwise, formal entry is required).
To allow more time for filers to adjust to the new electronic requirements for informal entry, CBP extends the timeline for mandatory use of Entry Type 13 for these shipments to Jan. 20, 2027. There are no changes to international mail entry procedures before Jan. 20, 2027. Beginning on that date, CBP requires the use of the new Entry Type 13 process for the informal entry of international postal shipments subject to Section 201, 232 or 301 duties or the jurisdiction of a PGA.
“CBP is focused on securing our borders and using advance data to identify threats in international mail before they reach American communities,” said CBP Office of Trade Executive Assistant Commissioner Susan S. Thomas. “These requirements will close gaps that have been exploited by criminals to smuggle contraband sent through international mail.”
CBP has proposed requiring the new entry and data requirements for the informal entry of all international mail packages, except for letters and flats, in the Oct. 8 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking “Low-Value Shipments.” The agency is committed to bringing international mail entry procedures into parity with informal entry procedures across all other cargo modes while setting a global standard for modern customs controls in the international mail environment.
“These requirements will help create a more secure international mail stream, strengthening both our economic and national security,” said Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane J. Sabatino of CBP’s Office of Field Operations. “Advance electronic data will help CBP identify and stop illegal and unsafe shipments before they enter the United States.”
While the mandatory implementation date is being extended, CBP encourages filers to begin using the optional Entry Type 13 process for the informal entry of international mail shipments during this transition period to ensure readiness in advance of the new mandatory deadline. CBP will continue providing guidance, resources, and direct support to help the trade community prepare for and comply with the new international mail entry requirements. Additional information is available on CBP’s e-Commerce page.
Follow the CBP Office of Trade on X@CBPTradeGov, Instagram@cbpofficeoftrade and Linkedin@cbpofficeoftrade, and CBP's Office of Field Operations (Office of Cargo and Conveyance Security) on Instagram@cbptradesecure for breaking news and current events.
title: International Mail Entry Type 13 mandatory implementation date extended to Jan. 20, 2027

text:
This year’s Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank provide an important opportunity to engage on current global economic challenges as well as our work with partners and the international financial institutions to support a pro-growth agenda, macroeconomic and financial stability, and poverty reduction. We thank Thailand for hosting us for the Annual Meetings.
In the United States, President Trump’s America First Investment Policy is promoting robust economic growth and prosperity, fiscal prudence, energy abundance, and regulatory modernization. Internationally, we are getting back to basics by forging a broad consensus on the need to promote growth as the key condition on which durable prosperity depends. As G20 President, the United States is focused on promoting strong economic growth, and has prioritized increasing productivity, addressing global imbalances, engaging with the private sector, advancing financial literacy, improving the sovereign debt architecture, and promoting financial sector innovation and regulatory modernization. When focused on their core missions, the IMF and World Bank are well-placed to help advance these important objectives.
The IMF is making progress at getting back to basics. Through recent policy reviews, the IMF is upgrading its policy toolkit for surveillance and lending and restoring its focus on its core responsibilities. This includes the external sector issues at the heart of the IMF’s mandate, strengthening surveillance of debt vulnerabilities in low-income countries, and making the financial sector surveillance more risk-based. Moreover, the IMF has rightly focused on strengthening program design to enhance the effectiveness of IMF-supported reform programs to durably address balance of payments challenges and restore external viability.
One area where this refocus must go further is in the IMF’s work on global imbalances. This especially includes strengthening its analysis and engagement on the role non-market policies and practices and exchange rates play in driving external imbalances. Policymakers around the world are having difficult discussions about how to sustain market-based systems amid distortionary policies from some economies that skew competition and hurt employment. The IMF was founded to prevent these kinds of distortive policies and negative spillovers, and must exercise its voice on this critical issue or risk being sidelined.
With recent major policy reviews complete, the hard work of implementation begins. The United States will hold the IMF accountable for translating these reforms into stronger surveillance, more effective lending, and more robust assessment of debt sustainability. Successfully delivering on the IMF’s core mandate will require commitment from IMF management to be an unflinching truth-teller through surveillance and to hold borrowers accountable in IMF-supported programs. That same commitment is required of the authorities undertaking painful but necessary macroeconomic adjustments and structural reforms.
The IMF must continue to prioritize its work and focus its resources on its core mandate. New and emerging issues warrant IMF engagement only where they are clearly macrocritical and within the Fund’s mandate, and adding new priorities should require reducing lower-value work, rather than continually expanding the Fund’s agenda such as financing provided through the Resilience and Sustainability Trust that lacks a clear linkage to balance of payments pressures and veers into development-policy lending.
The IMF has sufficient resources to accomplish its mission. The United States remains committed to a strong, quota-based, and adequately resourced IMF, and we continue to work to secure congressional approval for the 16th General Review of Quotas. Future quota reviews should be based on resource adequacy needs, as reflected in the recently approved Diriyah Guiding Principles on IMF Quota and Governance Reforms. Any future quota realignment should reflect members’ relative position in the world economy and be based on a new quota formula.
After years of mission creep, the World Bank is beginning to refocus on its core mission of reducing poverty and raising economic growth. Over the last year, the Bank has strengthened its development agenda by further implementing its jobs initiative, removing inefficient and distortionary climate finance targets, beginning to phase out lending to certain advanced client countries that have not needed Bank support for years, taking steps to better implement its graduation policy, and devising a strategy for supporting a more diversified minerals value chain.
These are necessary steps in returning the Bank to its core mission, but significantly more is needed. The Bank must promote country self-reliance by deploying resources where they are most needed and impactful, graduating more advanced countries from Bank support, delivering better access to reliable, affordable, and abundant energy, and increasing competition and quality in Bank-financed procurement to improve development outcomes. And, in doing these things, the Bank must be more efficient and selective, pursuing operations with the greatest development impact, rather than simply pushing as much money as possible out the door.
We expect the Bank to phase out sovereign lending to countries that have long since met the graduation policy criteria so that the Bank can refocus its resources where they are most needed and impactful. Despite being long overdue, the planned phase outs of lending to China and Poland represent an important milestone for both countries. As the Bank continues to implement the graduation policy, we expect to see Graduation Progress Notes that meaningfully assess where graduation-eligible countries fall short of meeting the graduation criteria, and associated Country Partnership Frameworks focusing Bank programming on addressing those shortcomings. As the Bank enters the longest period in its history without a country graduating from lending eligibility, World Bank Management should take concrete steps to ensure that graduations resume.
Similarly, the International Development Association (IDA) must facilitate graduation so that it can focus its resources on the poorest countries where its investments in foundational infrastructure, as well as in reforms that promote debt sustainability and transparency, enhanced domestic resource mobilization, and strong public financial management, help countries develop and stand up to coercive and opaque lending terms from some creditors. As we discuss IDA’s resources over the next 15 months, IDA must clearly identify its accomplishments in boosting growth, and reducing poverty. We also support extending the deadline for low-income countries to subscribe to the shares allocated under the 2018 capital increases, helping them preserve and strengthen their representation and voice in the institution.
Contributing to country self-reliance also requires the Bank to focus more on the sectors most critical to development and industrialization, chief among them reliable and affordable energy. Energy abundance sparks economic abundance. We continue to support the World Bank and African Development Bank goal to extend energy access to 300 million more people in Africa. Achieving this goal will require the Bank to take a technology-neutral approach rather than restricting borrower choice, including by removing constraints on its support for natural gas and positively responding to borrower demand for gas projects. Accordingly, the World Bank Group should formally retire its prohibition on financing upstream gas and oil. The Bank cannot credibly invoke country ownership while categorically excluding upstream projects before their development merits are even assessed.
We welcome the recent approval of an IDA project to secure near-term gas supply, prepare mid-and downstream investments, and develop gas strategies in West Africa. Ultimately, success must be measured by whether countries gain the energy access needed to drive growth, create jobs, and reduce poverty. We therefore welcome the move to focus on outcomes rather than on arbitrary targets. To further support energy abundance, the United States is also making an initial contribution to the Nuclear Energy Assistance Trust Fund, which will help countries lay the groundwork for future nuclear energy investments.
Critical minerals are foundational inputs to growth and economic security. We welcome the Bank’s recently approved Metals and Minerals Implementation Plan. The Bank has an important role to play through policy and regulatory reform, investing in enabling infrastructure and local processing capacity, project finance and de-risking, and strengthening natural resource management. This includes deep-sea mining, where the Bank can play a catalytic role by providing knowledge and guidance in a nascent sector.
Directing resources to countries most in need is not enough; the Bank must position those resources to deliver value. Procurement policies that reward distortive industrial policies, encourage subsidies, and incentivize corruption and collusion ultimately undermine development, stifle the private sector, and result in higher long-term costs. The Bank must pursue procurement reforms that result in greater competition and quality. We recognize recent efforts to expand the use of quality-based procurement approaches, boost the use of local labor, and improve industry outreach, but much of this was necessary just to move closer to the value-for-money objective embodied in the Procurement Framework adopted over a decade ago. The Bank needs to assess where its current procurement framework, policies, and implementation are still not delivering competition and quality needed for long-term development and adopt further reforms and capacity-building measures to address those shortcomings. The Bank’s peer institutions are implementing a robust procurement reform agenda. We expect the World Bank to lead on these efforts rather than fall behind.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC) can play an important role in mobilizing private capital to support economic growth and private sector development. But higher mobilization levels are not a substitute for the harder work of creating markets and crowding in truly private investment in poorer, less creditworthy countries. We call on the IFC to redouble efforts to meet its 2018 capital increase pledge to make 40 percent of new commitments in the poorest and most fragile countries. The IFC’s rate of progress towards this commitment has fallen unacceptably short, underscoring the need to align the institution more closely with its core mission.
Finally, the IMF and World Bank are ultimately taxpayer-funded public institutions whose budgets should reflect the narrower set of operations that comes with refocusing on their core missions. We appreciate the flat real administrative budget growth being pursued at both institutions this fiscal year, and expect to see this same approach in future years. Both institutions and their Governors can and should go further, including by indefinitely freezing – and even reducing – Executive Board budgets and salaries, which now have a combined annual cost over $200 million. The reduction in the IMF Board’s core budget this year is an important first step in this direction. The Boards are significantly more expensive, both in overall and per-capita terms, than at other international financial institutions. Every unnecessary dollar spent on the Boards is a dollar that cannot be used to reduce poverty, promote macroeconomic stability, or foster growth. The Bank, Fund, and their members must do more to restrain these inexcusably bloated budgets. We also call on the IMF to divest from the Bretton Woods Recreation Center and the Concordia Hotel.
Streamlining policy priorities will allow both the World Bank and IMF to focus limited public resources on effectively fulfilling their core mandates while responding to crises. We look forward to working with Management, staff, and other shareholders, to accomplish this task.
###
title: Statement from U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent for the World Bank Development Committee and IMF International Monetary and Financial Committee

Louisville, KY – On August 19, 2026, a federal grand jury in Louisville returned a second superseding indictment charging 13 men and women with drug trafficking and money laundering offenses. Two of the defendants were previously charged with conspiracy to possess with the intent to distribute over 500 grams of methamphetamine.

United States Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner stated, “A seizure of over 250 pounds of methamphetamine is enormous for Louisville, Kentucky. Methamphetamine is an incredibly addictive drug that has ruined countless lives. I’m very proud of the important work being done by Louisville’s Homeland Security Task Force.”

U.S. Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner of the Western District of Kentucky, Special Agent in Charge Olivia Olson of the FBI Louisville Field Office, acting Special Agent in Charge Dennis M. Fetting of the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Nashville, acting Special Agent in Charge Todd Strom of the IRS Criminal Investigation Detroit Field Office, Special Agent in Charge Robert J. Scott of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), U.S. Postal Inspector in Charge Lesley Allison of the Pittsburgh Division, Special Agent in Charge John Nokes of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) Louisville Field Division, U.S. Marshal Gary B. Burman of the of the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) for the Western District of Kentucky, and Commissioner Phillip Burnett, Jr. of the Kentucky State Police (KSP) made the announcement.

According to the second superseding indictment, Zelos Rashon Fields , 55, of California, Chauncey Lavelle Ransom , 62, of California, Charles Taylor , 53, of California, and Austin Redd , 29, of Louisville, were all charged with one count of conspiring together and with others to possess with the intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine from May 2025 through March 13, 2026, in Jefferson County, Kentucky, and elsewhere.

Additionally, Redd was charged with three counts of distributing methamphetamine, one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, and one count of money laundering conspiracy. Fields was charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and having a prior serious violent felony conviction, and one count of money laundering conspiracy. Ransom was charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and having a prior serious drug felony conviction, and three counts of money laundering conspiracy.

Meshaun Swan , 26, of Louisville, was charged with one count of distribution of methamphetamine. Charles Taylor , Demond Jackson , 54, of California, Dariecea Brock , 28, of Louisville, Iecia Taylor , 28, of Louisville, Raeshonda Presley , 33, of Louisville, Ebony Manson , 44, of California, Laquisha Beals , 32, of Louisville, Lajean Guess , 56, of California, and Kimberly Sowells , 45, of California, are all charged with money laundering conspiracy.

This indictment supersedes an indictment returned April 8, 2026, charging Fields with one count of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute over 500 grams of methamphetamine, and a superseding indictment returned on May 20, 2026, charging Fields and Ransom with one count of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute over 500 grams of methamphetamine.

Prior to the indictments, criminal complaints were issued for Fields and Ransom . The complaints alleged that in March 2026, law enforcement identified Ransom , along with Fields , as two individuals involved in the transport of methamphetamine to Louisville for distribution. On March 13, 2026, law enforcement executed search warrants pertaining to this investigation and recovered approximately 257 pounds of methamphetamine, which had been sent to Louisville by Ransom and Fields for distribution.

Fields and Ransom previously appeared before a U.S. Magistrate Judges of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Kentucky on the underlying drug trafficking charges and were ordered detained.

If convicted of the offenses alleged in the second superseding indictment, Fields and Ransom face a potential minimum penalty of 15 years in prison. Charles Taylor , Redd , and Swan all face a potential minimum penalty of 10 years in prison. Jackson , Brock , Iecia Taylor , Presley , Manson , Beals , Guess , and Sowells all face a potential maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

There is no parole in the federal system.

This case is being investigated by the FBI, HSI, IRS-CI, DEA, ATF, USPIS, USMS and KSP, with assistance from the St. Matthews Police Department, Los Angeles Police Department, Joint Regional Intelligence Center, Shively Police Department, and the Floyd County Sheriff’s Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alicia P. Gomez and Corinne Keel are prosecuting the case with assistance from paralegal Adela Alec.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Louisville comprises agents and officers from FBI, HSI, DEA, ATF, and IRS-CI, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Kentucky.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

New Jersey Brothers Plead Guilty to Stealing More Than $2.6 Million, Collectively, in Tax Refunds
Two New Jersey brothers pleaded guilty in September to stealing more than $978,126 and $1,643,172, respectively, in tax refunds.
According to court documents and statements made in court, in early 2023, Ronald Chrichlow, of Somerset, and Gordon Chrichlow, formerly of Carteret, each filed a false 2022 Form 1041, U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts, on behalf of their trusts. These Forms 1041 falsely reported that the trusts made tax payments to the IRS when they had not and claimed refunds of $978,126 and $1,643,172, respectively. Pursuant to these false filings, in March 2023, the IRS issued Ronald Chrichlow a U.S. Treasury check for $978,126 and Gordon Chrichlow a U.S. Treasury check for $1,643,172. With his proceeds, Gordon Chrichlow purchased a Porsche Taycan for approximately $117,364 and bought a house for approximately $686,258.
In August 2023, the IRS assigned a revenue officer to collect the fraudulently obtained refunds. In response to IRS collection efforts, the Chrichlow brothers mailed to the IRS amended 2022 Forms 1041 for their trusts that removed the originally claimed tax payments. They also mailed 2022 Forms 1040-NR, U.S. Nonresident Alien Income Tax Return, on which they falsely claimed not to be residents of the United States and falsely claimed that their 2022 income was tax exempt pursuant to a tax treaty.
The Chrichlow brothers also willfully failed to file their personal income tax returns in some years, despite earning income. Ronald Chrichlow earned $960,000 in income between 2021 and 2024, but did not file income tax returns between 2022 and 2024. For 2021, he filed a false tax return falsely reporting tax payments he did not make in order to claim a tax refund of $93,228 to which he was not entitled. Gordon Chrichlow willfully failed to file his 2021 through 2024 tax returns, despite earning more than $1.4 million in gross income in those years.
The Chrichlow brothers also filed false COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loan applications on behalf of their business entities in 2020 that reported false numbers of employees and false gross receipts, in order to receive loans and grants to which they were not entitled.
Ronald and Gordon Chrichlow each pleaded guilty to one count of theft of government funds. Ronald Chrichlow is scheduled to be sentenced on January 12, 2027, and Gordon Chrichlow is scheduled to be sentenced on January 27, 2027. They each face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the cases.
Trial Attorneys Melissa Siskind and Likhitha Butchireddygari of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section are prosecuting the cases.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: New Jersey Brothers Plead Guilty to Stealing More Than $2.6 Million, Collectively, in Tax Refunds

EPA Administrator Zeldin Announces American Farmer First Policy During Three-Day Swing in Iowa and Wisconsin
WASHINGTON – Earlier this week, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin traveled across Iowa and into Wisconsin for a number of meetings and engagements with farmers, industry leaders, veterans, and local officials where he highlighted the Trump EPA’s efforts to support American farmers, advance right-to-repair efforts, strengthen domestic energy production, and improve water infrastructure.
During his swing through Iowa, Administrator Zeldin announced EPA’s proposal to reallocate 100% of additional 2025 small refinery exemption volumes under the Renewable Fuel Standard at the Dubuque County Farm Bureau in Iowa. The proposal keeps the agency’s promise to propose 100% reallocation by the end of October and furthers the Trump Administration’s commitment to open stable markets for American farmers to sell their crops. If finalized as proposed, the 100% reallocation will ensure that farmers in Iowa and across the country do not lose the demand for their crops, while also unleashing American energy.
The announcement came on the heels of Administrator Zeldin and U.S. Representative Ashley Hinson’s (R-IA-02) tour of Big River United Energy ethanol facility in Dyersville, Iowa. The visit highlighted the role of American biofuels, which will benefit from EPA’s proposal if finalized, in supporting farmers, rural economies, and domestic energy production.
On Sunday, October 11, Administrator Zeldin visited Summit Products, a member of the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA), in Altoona, Iowa. While there he discussed EPA’s implementation of its February Right to Repair guidance and President Trump’s Freedom to Fix memo. The President’s memo directed EPA to deliver two things: ensure every American has the Freedom to Fix their vehicle and reduce the reliance on California’s emission certification process for aftermarket vehicle products. He highlighted EPA’s work to ensure farmers and equipment operators have the right to repair their own equipment instead of being forced to take it to a dealer, which is often more expensive. Administrator Zeldin touted EPA’s July decision to recognize SEMA as a certification authority for aftermarket vehicle parts.
To celebrate National Farmer’s Day on Monday, October 12, Administrator Zeldin participated in a farmers’ roundtable at Savor the Barn in Monticello, Iowa. Administrator Zeldin met with representatives from the Iowa Farm Bureau, Iowa Soybean Association, Iowa Corn Growers Association, and local agricultural producers to discuss EPA actions to grow the agriculture economy while maintaining strong environmental protections including EPA’s work on to end deratements caused by Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) system failures, the agency’s E15 waivers, EPA’s Waters of the United States (WOTUS) proposal, and more.
Later in the day, Administrator Zeldin and Representative Hinson spent time with local veterans at the Veterans Freedom Center in Dubuque, Iowa. During the visit they heard powerful stories about veterans helping veterans as they transition back home. The pair ended the day by touring Dubuque’s Water & Resource Recovery Center, where a $2 million federally funded project is planned to support upgrades to the facility’s capacity to treat high-strength waste. The improvements are intended to help the facility better serve local residents and businesses.
Administrator Zeldin ended his 3-day Midwest swing by meeting up with Representative Derrick Van Orden (R-WI-03) in Cuba City, Wisconsin where they toured the sixth generation Tranel Family Farms. The Trump EPA’s work reversing DEF deratements, restoring the Right to Repair, and applying common sense to environmental regulations were major topics throughout the visit.
title: EPA Administrator Zeldin Announces American Farmer First Policy During Three-Day Swing in Iowa and Wisconsin
