text:
Crow Presses Pentagon Over Civilian Casualties during Trump’s Iran War
AURORA — Congressman Jason Crow (D-CO), a former paratrooper and Army Ranger who serves on the House Armed Services Committee and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, is demanding answers on a strike that resulted in civilian casualties at a wedding in Iran, reported to have been carried out by the U.S. military during Trump’s war of choice.
According to The New York Times, at least five people were killed, including two children, and nearly 70 more were injured while attending a wedding due to a military strike in the town of Kuhestak, Iran. Additional reporting indicates a high likelihood that the bomb used was launched by American forces as they carried out intense attacks in southern Iran.
Joining Crow in his letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth are Congresswomen Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) and Sara Jacobs (D-CA). The group previously led their Democratic colleagues pressing the Administration for answers on a U.S. strike on an Iranian girls’ elementary school where at least 175 civilians, many of them children, were killed. The Pentagon has yet to provide a sufficient update on the incident.
“We demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran,” Crow and his colleagues wrote. “The consequences of this American strike have been devastating: 5 civilians were killed as a result of the strike in Kuhestak, including a 4-year-old boy and a 16-year-old boy, and dozens of civilians were injured.”
They continued, “We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from U.S. operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department. Acknowledging such incidents, accepting responsibility, and learning from them makes our forces stronger, more effective, and an example to the world. When we fail to do so, it has the exact opposite effect.”
Crow, Co-Chair of the Protection of Civilians in Conflict Caucus, has demanded answers on Secretary Hegseth’s attempts to dismantle civilian protections at the Pentagon.
Crow’s service as a combat veteran in Iraq and Afghanistan informs much of his work in Congress aimed at increasing civilian protection in combat. He helped pass legislation codifying the creation of the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, and has passed major portions of his Protection of Civilians in Military Operations Act and Department of Defense Civilian Harm Transparency Act.
A PDF of the letter can be found here, with full text appearing below:
Dear Secretary Hegseth,
We are once again writing with grave concern regarding the conduct of the administration’s war in Iran. Specifically, there are devastating reports of civilian casualties at a wedding in the town of Kuhestak, Iran, on September 1, 2026. This is the latest in an alarming pattern of civilian casualty incidents in strikes carried out by the United States in Iran since the war began on February 28, 2026. While the Department has not publicly acknowledged responsibility for this incident, the Washington Post recently reported that there is a “high likelihood” that the U.S. was responsible for the incident, citing an official familiar with the operations. Furthermore, analysis from U.S. weapons experts has suggested that the explosion was caused by a U.S. glide bomb.
The Post reported that six U.S. Navy aircraft-launched weapons targeted a communications complex near the home where the wedding was taking place and that one weapon missed its intended target. Accordingly, we demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran. The consequences of this American strike have been devastating: 5 civilians were killed as a result of the strike in Kuhestak, including a 4-year-old boy and a 16-year-old boy, and dozens of civilians were injured.
This incident is regrettably among the latest in a string of civilian casualty incidents arising from the U.S.-led war in Iran. This includes a strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war that killed a reported 175 civilians, including 120 children. While it has been reported that a preliminary investigation by the Department found that the U.S. military was responsible for the strike, over six months later the Department has still not publicly acknowledged responsibility for the strike nor released the findings of its investigation. Similarly, reporting and independent analysis indicate that U.S. forces were responsible for a strike at a youth sports hall in Lamerd, Iran, that killed 21 civilians, including 7 children, on February 28. While the Department has denied responsibility, analysis by weapons experts found that the damage pattern is consistent with that of an American Precision Strike Missile (PrSM).
We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from U.S. operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department. Acknowledging such incidents, accepting responsibility, and learning from them makes our forces stronger, more effective, and an example to the world. When we fail to do so, it has the exact opposite effect.
This is why it is all the more alarming that amid these devastating incidents, the Department has also severely degraded the civilian harm mitigation and response (CHMR) programs and personnel designed to prevent, respond to, and learn from civilian harm. Understanding the civilian environment – including the location of civilian objects and critical infrastructure such as schools and gymnasiums, and patterns of life including large gatherings such as weddings – was intended to be a key aspect of this program. Yet CHMR staff at CENTCOM have reportedly dwindled from over 10 to just one full-time staff. The Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, which was mandated by Congress and designed to support combatant commands in this life saving work, has been cut from over thirty down to just seven.
On March 12, 2026, 121 Members of the U.S. House of Representatives wrote to you demanding answers regarding civilian casualties caused by Operation Epic Fury and the Department's civilian protection efforts. The Department refused to provide any answers, simply stating “The United States Central Command (USCENTCOM) has initiated an investigation of this incident and appointed an investigating officer from outside the USCENTCOM chain of command. USCENTCOM will share the results of this investigation with Congress once it is completed.” Nearly seven months into the war, Congress and the American public still lack basic information about the findings of that investigation and the measures the Department has taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring again.
The strike in Kuhestak makes that failure all the more troubling. In response to the reports regarding U.S. responsibility for the strike in Kuhestak, a spokesperson for the U.S. Central Command stated “The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC.” Similarly, Vice President Vance said at a press briefing recently that he was “skeptical” of reports that the U.S. was responsible for the bombing, while acknowledging that the incident was under investigation.We are concerned this lack of transparency from this Administration is becoming a pattern, given the Department also initially denied responsibility for the Minab strike and has yet to release the investigation related to that incident.
The American people deserve answers on not just this strike, but the Department’s pattern of civilian harm resulting from U.S. military operations in Iran. To that end, we insist on answers to the following questions no later than October 26, 2026.
- Did U.S. forces carry out the September 1, 2026 strike in Kuhestak, Iran, that killed 5 civilians and injured dozens? If so, what was the target and why was the decision taken to execute the strikes? What was the assessed civilian harm risk of the strikes, and what steps were considered or taken to prevent civilian harm?
- Has the Department formally initiated an investigation into the September 1 strike in Kuhestak? If so, please provide the date on which the investigation began, the office responsible for conducting it, whether the investigating officer is independent of the operational chain of command, and the expected timeline for completion.
- What is the status of the USCENTCOM investigation into the February 28 strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab? On what date will the Department provide Congress with the full findings of that investigation, including its conclusions regarding U.S. responsibility and the circumstances that led to the reported civilian casualties? On what date will the unclassified version of these findings be made available to the public?
- Did the Department conduct an initial review of whether it is possible the U.S. was involved in the Lamerd strike on February 28, 2026? What were the results of that initial review? Was additional information provided after the fact, and did this alter the initial review results at all?
  - Did the Department conduct a civilian harm assessment of whether it is more likely than not that civilian harm occurred as a result of this strike? What were the results of this assessment? Was additional information provided after the fact, and did this alter the initial review results at all?
  - Has the Department conducted an administrative investigation, such as an AR 15-6, into the strike? If so, when was the investigation initiated, when are the findings due to the commander, and when will its findings be provided to Congress and released publicly?
- What steps, if any, has the Department taken to prevent civilian harm in targeting practices since the apparent U.S strikes in Minab on February 28, 2026? Please detail any specific policies that have been implemented.
- How many U.S. investigations, initial reviews, and civilian harm assessments into civilian casualties arising from operations in Iran have been initiated since February 28, 2026 and how many have been completed? Please provide details of all ongoing and completed investigations.

title: Crow Presses Pentagon Over Civilian Casualties during Trump’s Iran War

Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season to make landfall in the conterminous United States. It made landfall in the Florida Panhandle as a Category 2 hurricane the night of Friday, October 9, 2026, and brought high wind, significant rainfall, flooding, and power outages to many areas across the Southeast.
On October 9, President Trump issued several emergency declarations for certain counties in Florida, Alabama, and Georgia. These emergency declarations authorized federal assistance to save lives, protect property, and other measures that may prevent the incident from becoming a major disaster. Such measures include evacuations, emergency food and shelter, and the pre-positioning of rescue equipment. The situation remains dynamic; additional declaration requests or amendments to existing requests (i.e., addition of counties) may be forthcoming as states such as Florida are still assessing hurricane-related damage.
Presidential declarations of emergency or major disaster made pursuant to the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (the Stafford Act, P.L. 93-288, as amended; 42 U.S.C. §§5121 et seq.) may authorize FEMA to provide assistance through a suite of disaster programs:
Emergency declarations may authorize more limited forms of assistance than major disaster declarations.
The authorized forms of assistance may vary by designated area, per the declaration (subject to amendment). The President can also amend emergency and major disaster declarations to reduce the affected state's cost-share requirements for PA.
Information about state and county disaster assistance authorizations is published in FEMA's declaration database. Additional releases may be posted to FEMA Blog.
Hurricane damage can be caused by wind, water, or both, but these hazards are insured separately. A Stafford Act declaration is not required for policyholders to make insurance claims.
Wind is generally included as a covered peril in standard homeowners insurance policies. Homeowners insurance policies are sold by private insurance companies, which are regulated at the state level. Because hurricanes can cause significant damage, many states require a separate deductible for hurricane damage. To some degree, depending on the state, insurance companies determine the level of this hurricane deductible and when it should apply; however, the Florida hurricane deductible is set by statute and all insurance companies in Florida are generally required to offer hurricane deductible options.
Homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; homeowners must purchase separate coverage for flood losses. The NFIP is the primary source of flood insurance coverage for residential properties. The NFIP is operated by FEMA and is currently authorized until December 11, 2026. Homeowners and tenants with NFIP flood insurance can make flood damage claims using the normal NFIP claims process. FEMA may institute a claims process specific to Hurricane Isaias at a later date.
FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund (DRF) is the primary funding source for federal government response and recovery activities. As a result, its level of unobligated funds is often used as a proxy for the overall federal resources available for response and recovery.
As of the end of FY2026, roughly $8.3 billion was available in the DRF to pay the costs associated with major disaster declarations. Under the terms of the continuing resolution (P.L. 119-103, Division A) providing interim funding for federal government operations during the first months of FY2027, an additional $26.4 billion is also available until the continuing resolution expires or is replaced by an enacted annual appropriations measure covering FEMA.
The United States takes a "bottom-up" approach to emergency management, and when a state's capacity to manage incident response has been exceeded, it may request assistance from the federal government. Some Members of Congress may be concerned about both state and federal capacity for emergency management.
Regarding federal capacity, congressional concerns may center on whether FEMA is sufficiently staffed, as the Government Accountability Office recently identified staffing gaps within FEMA's disaster workforce. Additional concerns may relate to whether the current Administration is approving declarations in line with historic trends, and whether FEMA's disaster and mitigation programs are operating as they have historically (e.g., no new funding has been approved or obligated for any HMA programs since March 2025).
Regarding state capacity, the Trump Administration has suggested states should take on additional responsibilities related to disaster preparedness, response, and recovery. Further, the FEMA Review Council provided recommendations to this effect, including recommending changes to FEMA's criteria for evaluating whether the President should declare a major disaster authorizing PA and IA (e.g., increasing the PA per capita indicator to account for historic inflation). While implementation would require changes to FEMA's regulations, in the interim, the FEMA Review Council's final report states, "the President could direct through executive action that generally only requests above higher thresholds may be considered." The Administration has also been unusually late to issue notices of funding opportunities and has changed certain policies, including related to the Emergency Management Performance Grant program, which can fund emergency management staff, resulting in some states experiencing uncertainty about funding availability. (FEMA was later directed to amend certain award terms and conditions and disperse allowable costs.)
Regarding insurance, Congress may take interest in the solvency, reform, and reauthorization of the NFIP as well as the state of insurance markets, which have seen insurers raising premiums or withdrawing from certain markets due to elevated risks.
For more information, see CRS Report R46408, Hurricane Events: CRS Experts, and CRS Report WMR10001, CRS Guide to Federal Emergency Management.
title: Hurricane Isaias: Brief Overview of FEMA Programs, Resources, and Selected Issues

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressmen Rob Menendez (NJ-08) and Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08) sent a letter to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. calling on HHS to update federal research and guidance on high-caffeine energy drinks and conduct a comprehensive assessment of their consumption and health effects among school-aged children.
“Kids are consuming more caffeine than ever, and Sarah Katz’s tragic death exposed how dangerous poor labeling and hidden caffeine levels can be,” said Congressman Menendez. “We are calling on HHS to update federal caffeine guidelines, protect our children, and ensure parents and teachers have the information they need to keep children safe.”
“Energy drink use among kids is at record levels, while caffeine-related emergency room visits among middle and high school students have roughly doubled,” said Congressman Krishnamoorthi. “These products can pose serious health risks to children, yet the federal government is still relying on outdated research and guidance. Our government needs to catch up and give parents, schools, and health care providers the information they need to keep kids safe.”
In 2022, 21-year-old Jersey City native Sarah Katz died after drinking an energy drink that was improperly labeled. Congressman Menendez reintroduced the bipartisan Sarah Katz Caffeine Safety Act last year to increase transparency of caffeine in food and beverages. The bill would also require the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) to conduct a safety review for caffeine and support a study to examine how caffeine impacts vulnerable populations, including children.
Today, nearly one in four high school seniors consume energy drinks daily, up from one in six in 2022. From 2017 to 2023, caffeine-related emergency department visits among middle and high school students roughly doubled. Despite this uptick, official CDC guidance still relies in part on a 2013 SAMHSA report using emergency department visit data from 2007 to 2011. 
The lawmakers also raised concerns about a lack of federal oversight and caffeine labeling requirements for energy drinks. FDA guidance is over ten years old, nonbinding, and provides no recommended caffeine limit for children or adolescents.
Menendez and Krishnamoorthi requested that HHS conduct a comprehensive assessment of energy drink consumption and its health effects among school-aged children and provide answers to the following questions:
The lawmakers called on HHS to make the assessment publicly available so parents, schools, and healthcare providers can understand the risks these products pose and the steps being taken to address them.
To read the full letter, please click here.
Congressman Menendez currently serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Subcommittees on Energy, the Environment, and Communications and Technology. Since coming to Congress, he has advocated for transparency in caffeine labeling and reintroduced the Sarah Katz Caffeine Safety Act during the 119th Congress.
title: Menendez and Krishnamoorthi Push for Stronger Energy Drink Safety Rules to Protect Kids

Representative April McClain Delaney Joined 99 Democratic Lawmakers in Slamming Department of Education for Failure to Enforce Title IX and Protect Student Survivors
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Democratic Women’s Caucus (DWC) member Maxine Dexter (OR-03), DWC member Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), DWC Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03) and Rep. Mark Takano (CA-41) led a letter to the Office of the Inspector General at the Department of Education. The letter urges the Acting Inspector General to open an investigation into the Department’s gutting of the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and Title IX rollbacks and its impact on the Department’s ability to enforce Title IX protections for student survivors of sexual assault and harassment. 99 House Democrats joined the effort.
The call for the investigation comes after Jane Doe’s story from Cornell University and Kendall Francis’ story from Louisiana State University (LSU) sparked a national outcry about the high rate of sexual violence on college campuses. Additionally the survivors’ stories have renewed scrutiny of how colleges and universities respond, and how the Department of Education enforces Title IX protections for survivors.
One in four undergraduate women experience sexual assault or rape while in college. Sexual violence against women on college campuses is a public health crisis, yet significant barriers remain that block accountability and protections for students. Changes in staffing, resources, case-processing, and enforcement priorities under the Trump administration have only made that worse and have undermined the Department’s ability to properly investigate complaints and enforce Title IX protections.
As of January 2025, OCR reportedly faced a backlog of nearly 12,000 civil rights cases, while the administration reduced OCR’s workforce by nearly half. The Department has closed zero college sexual harassment or sexual violence cases. The Department also formalized weaker protections and processes for student survivors: narrowing the definition of sexual harassment, reducing school liability, and implementing intimidating investigative and hearing procedures that are retraumatizing to survivors.
Without proper federal enforcement and institutional accountability, Title IX protections become just words on a page. The Department of Education is failing student survivors. Protections for survivors are not partisan and should always be a priority, however the Department’s rollback of vital protections creates additional barriers for survivors and is leaving them to fend for themselves in their most vulnerable moments.
In their letter, the members explained how the Department’s changes will leave student survivors vulnerable and why an investigation is necessary:
“We urge the Office of Inspector General to immediately open an investigation into the Department’s failure to adequately enforce Title IX protections for survivors of sexual harassment and assault, including whether changes in staffing, resources, case-processing, and enforcement priorities have undermined the Department’s ability to protect students, investigate complaints in a timely manner, and hold institutions accountable.”
The members outlined the Department’s policies that have weakened protections for student survivors:
“At the same time that OCR’s staff and regional capacity were substantially reduced, the Department announced and pursued Title IX enforcement priorities concerning transgender students’ participation in athletics and access to sex-separated facilities, and also dismantling Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) programs. These reprioritizations do nothing to address the backlog of sexual violence cases.”
The letter also explains how reprioritizations and restructuring by the Department have decreased OCR’s capacity to investigate cases of sexual violence on campus:
“This restructuring threatens to further delay investigations, erode OCR’s institutional expertise, and create additional barriers for survivors seeking accountability. These reprioritizations, staff reductions, and the interagency agreement raise significant questions about whether OCR has sufficient capacity to investigate Title IX complaints, communicate with complainants, and fulfill its civil rights enforcement responsibilities in a timely and effective manner.”
The members also outlined what they are urging the Inspector General to investigate:
- Examining whether the Department has fulfilled its legal and administrative responsibilities to investigate and resolve Title IX complaints in a timely and effective manner.
- The causes and consequences of the absence of resolution agreements involving college sexual harassment and assault complaints since January 2025.
- Whether reductions in OCR staffing, the closure of regional offices, or changes in enforcement priorities have contributed to delays, backlogs, or failures to resolve these complaints.
- Examining whether OCR has sufficient staffing, resources, policies, and procedures to effectively enforce Title IX and protect students from sex discrimination, including sexual harassment and violence.
- Identifying how survivors have been harmed by these changes.
Lastly, the members asked the Inspector General to answer the following questions:
- How many Title IX sexual harassment and sexual violence complaints are currently pending before OCR, and how long have they been pending?
- How have processing times, case closures, investigations, and resolution agreements changed since January 2025?
- Have staffing reductions or office closures affected OCR’s ability to investigate complaints or communicate with survivors?
- Have Department officials directed, formally or informally, OCR personnel to deprioritize certain categories of Title IX complaints?
- What safeguards are currently in place to ensure Title IX complaints involving sexual violence receive timely and appropriate review?
- What corrective actions are necessary to ensure the Department is meeting its obligations to protect students under Title IX?
Read the full letter here.
The letter was signed by: Amo, Gabe; Ansari, Yassamin; Balint, Becca; Barragán, Nanette; Beatty, Joyce; Beyer, Donald; Bonamici, Suzanne; Brownley, Julia; Brown, Shontel; Bynum, Janelle; Carter, Troy; Castor, Kathy; Chu, Judy; Clarke, Yvette; Craig, Angie; Crockett, Jasmine; Davids, Sharice; Dean, Madeleine; DeGette, Diana; DeSaulnier, Mark; Dexter, Maxine; Dingell, Debbie; Elfreth, Sarah; Escobar, Veronica; Espaillat, Adriano; Evans, Dwight; Fletcher, Lizzie; Foster, Bill; Foushee, Valerie; Frankel, Lois; Frost, Maxwell; Garamendi, John; Garcia, Sylvia; Goldman, Daniel; Goodlander, Maggie; Grijalva, Adelita; Houlahan, Chrissy; Hoyle, Val; Ivey, Glenn; Jackson, Jonathan; Jayapal, Pramila; Johnson, Julie; Kamlager-Dove, Sydney; Kelly, Robin; Kennedy, Timothy; Khanna, Ro; Landsman, Greg; Latimer, George; Lee, Summer; Leger Fernandez, Teresa; Lynch, Stephen; Magaziner, Seth; Matsui, Doris; McBride, Sarah; McClain Delaney, April; McClellan, Jennifer; McIver, LaMonica; Mejia, Analilia; Menefee, Christian; Meng, Grace; Mfume, Kweisi; Morelle, Joseph; Mullin, Kevin; Nadler, Jerrold; Norton, Eleanor; Omar, Ilhan; Pelosi, Nancy; Pettersen, Brittany; Pingree, Chellie; Quigley, Mike; Ramirez, Delia; Randall, Emily; Raskin, Jamie; Ross, Deborah; Salinas, Andrea; Scanlon, Mary Gay; Schakowsky, Janice; Scholten, Hillary; Sewell, Terri; Simon, Lateefah; Stansbury, Melanie; Stanton, Greg; Stevens, Haley; Strickland, Marilyn; Subramanyam, Suhas; Sykes, Emilia; Takano, Mark; Thompson, Bennie; Thompson, Mike; Titus, Dina; Tlaib, Rashida; Tokuda, Jill; Tonko, Paul; Trahan, Lori; Velázquez, Nydia; Walkinshaw, James; Watson Coleman, Bonnie; Williams, Nikema; Wilson, Frederica.

MONROE – On September 30, 2026, a federal jury found Sirkeameo Vandrell Johnson, 32, of Monroe, guilty of Conspiracy to Possess with Intent to Distribute Methamphetamine, Distribution of Methamphetamine, Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon, Possession with Intent to Distribute Methamphetamine, and Possession of a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Offense, following a two day trial, announced United States Attorney Zachary A. Keller. Johnson faces a mandatory minimum sentence of at least fifteen years in federal prison and up to life imprisonment. Sentencing is scheduled for January 6, 2027, before United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty.

According to evidence presented at trial, a confidential informant conducted multiple controlled purchases of methamphetamine and firearms from Johnson and a co conspirator. Wearing audio and video monitoring devices, the informant made several visits to Johnson to conduct the controlled buys, which were corroborated through law enforcement surveillance. In addition to the drug charges, Johnson is prohibited from possessing firearms due to a prior felony conviction. This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Drug Enforcement Administration, Metro Narcotics of Ouachita Parish, Monroe Police Department, Ouachita Parish Sheriff’s Office, and West Monroe Police Department. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys William Gaskins and Alexandra Porubsky, with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Stephanie Stewart.

This case was prosecuted as part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Learn more at www.justice.gov/psn.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer. The case number for this matter is 3:25-cr-00341-TAD-KDM.

Trump Administration Announces New Funding to Support Rural Healthcare Workers and Expand Maternal Care Across Missouri
Federal investment will expand childcare support for rural healthcare workers and launch nurse midwife training to help address maternal care gaps across Missouri
Today, the Trump Administration announced more than $2.3 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to strengthen Missouri’s rural healthcare workforce and expand access to maternal care. This investment supports two targeted workforce initiatives in Missouri: expanding affordable, dependable childcare for rural healthcare professionals and delivering funding to establish a certified nurse midwife training program.
This transformational funding will deliver $1.46 million to tackle healthcare recruitment and retention challenges across rural Missouri. The funding will expand a cost-sharing childcare program that brings the state, rural health employers, and families together to make dependable childcare more affordable for healthcare workers, providing peace of mind that their loved ones are cared for while they care for their patients. In addition, $879,000 will support initial work to establish Missouri’s first certified nurse midwife training program, with rural clinical rotations designed to build a pipeline of maternal care providers for underserved communities.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is expanding access to quality healthcare, regardless of a patient’s zip code, and equipping rural health systems with the workforce and infrastructure needed to deliver timely care. This funding will make critical investments to strengthen rural healthcare, expand access to lifesaving services, and bring modern technology to communities across Missouri.
“President Trump understands that every American deserves high-quality healthcare, no matter where they live,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “We are putting resources directly into rural communities to strengthen the health workforce, modernize infrastructure, expand access, and bring care closer to home. We are giving states the flexibility to build solutions around the people they serve, while demanding accountability for results. That is how we strengthen rural health, improve the lives of patients and families, and Make America Healthy Again.”
“Every state knows best what its rural communities need, and thanks to President Trump’s Rural Health Transformation Program, they now have the resources to meet those needs,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “As states put these resources to work, we’re focused on turning these investments into meaningful, sustainable improvements for the health systems that serve rural Missourians.”
Today’s investment was made possible through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act — passed by Republicans in Congress and unanimously opposed by Democrats — delivering a historic $50 billion investment to help states transform the way healthcare is delivered in America.
“As Missouri’s Rural Health Transformation Program continues to make strides in strengthening rural healthcare access with community-driven solutions, this funding brings much-needed childcare support for rural healthcare workers and expands access to critical maternal care across our state,” said Gov. Mike Kehoe. “We appreciate the Trump Administration’s continued focus and partnership in working to create stronger, healthier rural communities.”
"Rural hospitals across Missouri have been struggling for decades. Thanks to the Trump Administration, this $2.3 million award will expand access to maternal care and childcare support for rural healthcare workers. This investment will not only support our healthcare workers but also help ensure families in rural Missouri can access the quality care they deserve. I’m proud to have supported this program through the Working Families Tax Cut Act, and I’ll continue fighting to ensure rural Missourians get the care they need," said Sen. Eric Schmitt.
“Supporting rural healthcare workers and the community that relies on them is incredibly important. This funding will directly strengthen and expand access to maternal health care here in Missouri so moms and children have access to the care they need and deserve, and I was proud to vote for this funding in the Working Families Tax Cut legislation. I will always work to support families in Missouri and across the country, and I thank the Administration for joining me in prioritizing parents and their children,” said Rep. Ann Wagner.
“This Administration has demonstrated a strong commitment to strengthening rural healthcare across Missouri, and this additional investment will build on those efforts to address critical workforce shortages and expand access to maternal care in our rural communities,” said Rep. Bob Onder. “As a physician, I know how important it is for patients to have access to quality care when they need it most. This funding will help ensure Missouri families can receive the care they need and that qualified healthcare professionals are there to provide it.”
“Rural Missouri families deserve quality care close to home, and that starts with the people who deliver it. This Rural Health Transformation Program funding is part of the largest ever single investment in rural health care through Republicans’ Working Families Tax Cuts. It will expand access to childcare for rural healthcare workers and stand up a certified nurse midwife training program so we can recruit and keep more caregivers in our communities. That’s real help for mothers and for the workforce that keeps rural hospitals and clinics open. I’m grateful the Trump Administration is putting these dollars to work in Missouri,” said Rep. Mark Alford.
"The future of rural healthcare depends on having a trained workforce," said Rep. Sam Graves. "This funding from the Working Families Tax Cuts law will help recruit and retain healthcare professionals, while expanding the availability of maternal care, which is critically needed in North Missouri. These types of investments are why we created the Rural Health Transformation Program, and I’m pleased to see the Trump Administration continue to direct this money to Missouri.”
“A rural mom shouldn’t have to drive an hour or more to find someone to deliver her baby. That’s exactly why I authored and fought for the Rural Health Transformation Program in the One, Big, Beautiful Bill. This funding will help Missouri recruit and retain the nurses and healthcare workers our rural communities depend on, and it will bring maternal care closer to home for families across southeast Missouri and the entire state. I’ll keep fighting to make sure rural Missouri is a place where moms can raise a family and get the care they need right where they live,” said Rep. Jason Smith.
Today’s announcement is one part of the larger overall funding amount awarded to Missouri for fiscal year 2026.
Key initiatives the overall RHTP funding will focus on include:
- Building the rural healthcare workforce: Supporting recruitment, training, and retention strategies to strengthen the pipeline of healthcare professionals serving rural communities.
- Strengthening rural facilities and access: Supporting partnerships, operational improvements, and care-delivery changes that help rural providers maintain essential services and improve access.
- Advancing innovative care and payment models: Supporting new approaches to delivery and financing designed to improve quality, strengthen primary care, and support sustainable rural healthcare.
- Expanding community-based and preventive care: Investing in school-based care, mobile services, and other community strategies that improve prevention, address chronic disease, and expand access to care.
- Modernizing rural healthcare technology: Expanding remote care and data-driven tools to improve coordination and extend healthcare services to rural communities.
The Trump Administration is delivering on its commitment to strengthen rural America by investing in solutions that modernize technology to promote health and well-being for rural communities. Led by CMS, the RHTP is moving beyond the failed one-size-fits-all approach and giving rural communities the tools to build stronger, more innovative, and more sustainable health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes for the Americans they serve.
For more information about the RHTP, visit: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health.

text:
U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran since February 2026 and subsequent Iranian military actions throughout the Persian Gulf have disrupted global commercial markets.1 Oil is among the commodities affected.2 According to AAA, on September 23, 2026, in nominal dollars, the average price of a gallon of gasoline for U.S. consumers was more than $1.30 higher than it had been a year before.3 President Trump and multiple Members of Congress have proposed suspending the federal excise tax on gasoline (federal gas tax) as a way to partially offset this price increase.4
The federal gas tax is the primary source of revenue for the federal Highway Trust Fund. Congress established the federal gas tax rate in statute.5 While some Members of Congress have previously proposed suspending the federal gas tax, no such law has ever been enacted. This report provides information about the federal gas tax and the Highway Trust Fund. It also discusses considerations related to a potential suspension of the federal gas tax.
In the past, some Members of Congress have proposed suspending the federal diesel tax as well as the federal gas tax. On October 5, 2026, President Trump issued an executive order seeking to "defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations and to provide penalty relief to the extent permitted by law."6 This report focuses solely on suspension of the federal gas tax.
The federal gas tax is one of several federal transportation-related excise taxes that provide revenue for the Highway Trust Fund (see "Highway Trust Fund Insolvency," below). Other such federal taxes include the diesel fuel tax, alternative fuel taxes, taxes on certain heavy truck and trailer sales, taxes on heavy truck tires, and a weight-based annual heavy vehicle use tax, as reflected in Table 1. Between FY2015 and FY2024, the most recent 10-year period for which data are available, fuel taxes accounted for 82% of Highway Trust Fund revenue. The federal gas tax alone accounted for 58% of Highway Trust Fund revenue.7
The rates for the taxes that provide revenue for the Highway Trust Fund are set by law. Congress last raised the federal gas tax in 1993, when it set the rate at 18.4 cents per gallon.8 Of this amount, 0.1 cent is directed to the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund, often referred to as the LUST Trust Fund.9 The remaining 18.3 cents are directed to the Highway Trust Fund.10 The Highway Trust Fund has two accounts, the highway account and the mass transit account. The highway account receives an allocation equivalent to 15.44 cents per gallon of the gasoline tax, and the mass transit account receives 2.86 cents per gallon.
The federal gas tax is not collected at the point of sale to the consumer (i.e., at the pump) as a retail sales tax might be. Instead, the federal government collects revenue from roughly 850 registered suppliers, distributers, refiners, and blenders of fuel.11 This simplifies tax administration, as the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has to monitor compliance of these entities; therefore, the group of 850 represents a smaller number when compared with the number of gas stations across the country.12 Some economists assert that all or nearly all of the federal excise taxes levied on motor fuels are passed on to the final consumer in the form of higher prices.13
Table 1. Federal Transportation-Related Excise Taxes Deposited into the Highway Trust Fund as of FY2026
Sources: In addition to the statutes cited above, see 26 U.S.C. §9503(b) and Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), "Chapter 7: The Highway Trust Fund," in Funding Federal-aid Highways, FHWA-PL-17-011, January 2017, https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policy/olsp/fundingfederalaid/07.cfm.
Notes: N/A = not applicable. Some of the taxes have expiration dates or dates on which the amount of the tax is set to decrease. In previous surface transportation reauthorization acts, Congress has extended these expiration/reduction dates.
a. Some of the taxes deposited into the Highway Trust Fund are set to expire or reduce on certain dates. These dates are established in the relevant statutes.
b. Gasohol is a blend of gasoline and ethyl alcohol, commonly 90% gasoline and 10% ethanol or 85% gasoline and 15% ethanol.
c. 26 U.S.C. §4081(a)(2)(B) imposes an additional 0.01 cent-per-gallon tax on gasoline for the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund, bringing the total federal gas tax to 18.4 cents per gallon.
d. Biasply tires are constructed of layers of material positioned at an angle (a bias) as opposed to standard radial tires in which the layers of material run perpendicular to the road. Biasply tires tend to be more durable than radial tires. A super single tire is one large tire able to take the place of a pair of standard tires.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) makes periodic estimates of the components of the retail price of gasoline. In May 2026, 52% of the retail price of regular gasoline was attributable to the price of crude oil, 22% to refining, and 15% to distribution and marketing. Federal, state, and local taxes comprised 12% of the total average price.14 When retail prices are higher, the price of crude oil and refining tend to comprise a higher share of the retail price, whereas marketing and taxes form lower shares. For example, in May 2022 (when gas prices averaged $4.44 per gallon), 59% was attributable to crude oil, 26% to refining, 5% to distribution and marketing, and 11% to taxes. The share of the retail price attributable to taxes varies across the country, as state and local gas tax rates vary. Total state taxes added 51.7 cents to the price of a gallon of gasoline, on average, compared with the federal excise tax of 18.4 cents.15 At current price levels, the federal tax comprises about 4% of the retail price, on average.
The Highway Trust Fund is a federal accounting mechanism that provides a dedicated source of funding for certain federal surface transportation programs.16 Congress established the Highway Trust Fund in 1956 to support construction of the Interstate Highway System and certain other roads.17 Today, Highway Trust Fund dollars are used to meet obligations authorized under surface transportation reauthorization legislation,18 such as the provisions contained in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; P.L. 117-58) enacted in 2021.19
The Highway Trust Fund has two accounts: the highway account and the mass transit account.20 The majority of funds flow through the highway account. The highway account provides funding primarily for the federal-aid highway program and highway and vehicle safety programs, as well as for highway research.21 Congress established the mass transit account as part of the Surface Transportation Assistance Act of 1982 (P.L. 97-424, §531). The mass transit account provides funding for "making capital or capital related expenditures" on public transportation projects.22 Because the highway account and the mass transit account fund separate programs with separate spending levels, the balance of one account may deplete more quickly than the other.
For many years, Highway Trust Fund revenue exceeded or was roughly equal to expenditures.23 Expenditures first exceeded revenue in FY2001 and have exceeded revenue since FY2008 consistently. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects that if current revenue and expenditure trends continue, the balance in the mass transit account will approach zero in FY2027 and that the balance in the highway account will approach zero in FY2028.24
The Highway Trust Fund cannot incur a negative balance. As the account balances approach zero, the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) and Federal Transit Administration may slow reimbursements to states and local governments for the federal portion of transportation project costs.25 FHWA could also reduce annual highway apportionments to the states.26
The federal gas tax has not been suspended since the establishment of the Highway Trust Fund in 1956. Some Members of Congress have proposed such suspensions, which are sometimes referred to as "gas tax holidays." Some Members of Congress have previously proposed temporarily suspending the federal gas tax in response to various factors, such as rising gas prices, economic conditions, or world events. For example, multiple Members of Congress proposed suspending the federal gas tax in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and inflation in FY2021 and FY2022.27 In FY2008 and FY2009, during the "Great Recession," multiple Members introduced similar legislation to suspend the federal gas tax.28 Proposals have included suspending the federal gas tax for a set period, as well as those that would suspend or reduce the federal gas tax whenever gas prices exceed a certain level.29
During the 119th Congress, multiple Members have introduced bills to suspend the federal gas tax, including H.R. 3768; H.R. 7919; H.R. 8572; H.R. 8600; H.R. 8753; H.R. 8795; H.R. 10392; H.R. 10589; H.R. 10668; S. 4032; S. 4485; S. 5458; and S. 5530.30 As Congress deliberates suspending the federal gas tax, considerations may include the possible effects on gas prices, the Highway Trust Fund, and the LUST Fund.
The September 2026 price of gasoline is at a level above that of early February 2026. Reducing the price of gas by 18.4 cents per gallon by suspending the federal gas tax and passing this amount through to consumers could provide some price relief. However, even with an 18.4-cent reduction, gas prices would still have risen more than a dollar between September 2025 and September 2026.
Suspension of the federal gas tax may not reduce consumer prices by exactly 18.4 cents per gallon or may not reduce consumer prices at all. Gasoline suppliers, distributers, refiners, and blenders could choose to reduce prices by more or less than 18.4 cents per gallon or, in theory, not reduce prices at all. Some Members of Congress have introduced legislation to address alleged "price gouging" in the context of gasoline prices.31
In the 119th Congress, several bills express the intent that "consumers immediately receive the benefit of the reduction in taxes" and that suppliers "take such actions as necessary to reduce [prices] to reflect such reduction." These bills encourage the Secretary of the Treasury to "use all applicable authorities to ensure the benefit of the reduction in taxes ... is received by consumers." Such a provision may be difficult for the federal government to enforce, as it may require estimating what the price of gasoline in each locality would have been in the absence of a federal gasoline tax suspension. Over an extended period, other factors, such as changes in the price of crude oil and other inputs, would likely affect the hypothetical price of gasoline without a federal gasoline tax suspension, potentially complicating implementation.
Although the federal government has never suspended its federal gas tax, states have suspended their state gas taxes. Economic studies of these state gas tax suspensions found that less than the full amount of the suspended tax typically is passed on to consumers in lower prices. For example, one economic study of cross-state price variation following a state gas tax suspension found that about 70% of the savings was passed on to consumers through lower prices.32 Subsequent studies of other state gas tax suspensions generally have found that tax savings were not fully passed on to consumers through lower prices.33
Suspension of the federal gas tax would reduce the revenue provided to the Highway Trust Fund. The Bipartisan Policy Center calculated that suspending the federal gas tax from May 2026 through September 2026 would reduce revenue to the Highway Trust Fund by $17 billion.34 Some of the bills proposed in the 119th Congress would not compensate the Highway Trust Fund for revenue lost during a given suspension. Other bills would compensate that fund, such as by transferring funds from the Treasury's General Fund (general fund) to the Highway Trust Fund. With such a general fund transfer, a gas tax suspension would not affect the health of the Highway Trust Fund, but it would increase the federal budget deficit.
If the reduction in revenue were not coupled with a general fund transfer, the balances in the highway account and the mass transit account would likely approach insolvency months sooner than CBO has predicted. As the account balances approach zero, state and local governments may receive slower reimbursements for work on federally funded highway and public transportation projects. State and local governments also may receive less federal funding through the highway formula programs at the beginning of the fiscal year. This could delay planned highway projects or lead to fewer highway projects overall.
In the past, Congress has prevented Highway Trust Fund insolvency through general fund transfers, raising the possibility of a general fund transfer subsequent to a federal gas tax suspension that could include the amount of money not collected during a federal gas tax suspension. For a discussion of other options for preventing Highway Trust Fund insolvency, see CRS Report R48472, The Highway Trust Fund's Highway Account, by Ali E. Lohman, and CRS Report R47573, Funding and Financing Highways and Public Transportation Under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), by William J. Mallett.
In 1986, in the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (P.L. 99-499), Congress established the LUST Trust Fund to help the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and states cover costs of responding to leaking underground petroleum storage tanks in cases where the owner or operator does not clean up a site, among other prevention and detection activities. In the United States, these leaking tanks have been a leading source of groundwater contamination and a threat to public drinking water. The federal gas tax is the primary source of monies for the LUST Trust Fund, and EPA typically has allocated approximately 90% of the annual trust fund appropriation to states to perform cleanups, conduct inspections, and carry out other activities to prevent petroleum releases into the environment.35 If the LUST Trust Fund were to not receive funding from the federal gas tax or be compensated with transfers from the general fund, the fund would receive little or no new funds, and the remaining balance would be depleted over time. EPA would be required to rely on annual appropriations for LUST activities, and states may have limited access to federal funding to conduct petroleum tank cleanups and other activities to protect groundwater.36
CRS Senior Research Librarians Lena A. Maman and Lynn J. Cunningham conducted research for this report. CRS Analyst in Public Finance Anthony Cilluffo and CRS Specialist in Environmental Policy Angela Jones contributed language to this report.
title: Suspension of the Federal Gas Tax: In Brief

LAS VEGAS – A Las Vegas man was sentenced today by United States District Judge Gloria M. Navarro to 420 months in prison, followed by 35 years of supervised release for sexual exploitation of children, coercion and enticement, and possession of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The government recommended a sentence of 420 months in prison, followed by a lifetime term of supervised release.

“Predators who target our most vulnerable will find no safe haven and no mercy in our justice system,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “This sentence sends an unmistakable warning to anyone engaging in these abhorrent crimes: we will hunt you down, dismantle your network, and ensure you spend your years behind bars.”

“Protecting children and holding those who harm them fully accountable remains one of the FBI’s highest priorities,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher S. Delzotto for the FBI Las Vegas Field Office. “The FBI and our law enforcement partners will pursue anyone who preys on a child with unwavering determination. And when these offenders are convicted in federal court, they face consequences that include justice without the possibility of parole.”

According to court documents, between April 27, 2025, and April 28, 2025, Daniel Hennigh used social media applications to communicate with another individual about sexually abusing children. During that time, he distributed a CSAM video he produced of a child in his care.

Hennigh pleaded guilty to one count of sexual exploitation of children; one count of coercion and enticement; one count of distribution of child pornography; and one count of possession of child pornography.

In addition to the term of imprisonment, under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act, Hennigh will be required to register as a sex offender and keep the registration current.

This case is part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

The public is urged to remain vigilant and report suspected exploitation of a child through the FBI’s tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI (225-5324), tips.fbi.gov , or by calling your local FBI field office.

CONCORD – Former New Hampshire physician Steven Powell, 56, was sentenced to 12 months and a day in federal prison on one count of health care fraud, in connection with a scheme to defraud Medicare by prescribing medical equipment without ever seeing, speaking to, or otherwise examining patients.

Powell, who now lives in Georgia, was sentenced today by U.S. District Court Judge Paul Barbadoro. According to court documents and statements made in court, Powell, a licensed psychiatrist, signed hundreds of medically unnecessary orders for durable medical equipment (DME), including knee, wrist, back, and shoulder braces. He did not examine, speak with, or meaningfully evaluate the Medicare beneficiaries for whom he purported to prescribe these devices. Instead, he approved large volumes of pre‑populated brace orders within minutes, making meaningful medical review impossible. These orders enabled DME suppliers to submit approximately 1,400 fraudulent claims to Medicare totaling more than $1.9 million in claims, of which Medicare paid $761,202.75.

Between December 2018 and March 2019, Powell signed brace orders for more than 500 Medicare beneficiaries, often approving multiple braces per patient. In one instance, he completed more than 100 pages requiring 75 signatures in just over a minute, further demonstrating the absence of any legitimate medical assessment.

In addition to the prison sentence, Powell was ordered to pay $761,202.75 in restitution to the Medicare program.

“This defendant abused his position and his medical license in order to defraud taxpayers with nearly $2 million in bogus medical bills, and will now spend time behind bars,” said Erin Creegan, U.S. Attorney for the District of New Hampshire. “The U.S. Attorney’s office will continue to pursue accountability for those who commit fraud and steal from the taxpayers, and strict penalties for those siphon precious healthcare resources meant to help elderly and low-income patients.”

“Dr. Steven Powell abandoned all pretense of professional ethics when he caused nearly $2 million in false Medicare bills from bogus prescriptions for medical equipment,” said Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI’s Boston Division. “By looting these funds, this physician not only strained the system, but cheated the taxpayers who fund it. Know that your FBI is committed to fighting health care fraud, one case at a time, because every dollar lost to bogus billing is a dollar less to use for legitimate treatments and services.”

“Powell used his medical license as a tool to facilitate fraud, signing orders for medically unnecessary equipment without examining patients and helping to fuel a scheme that sought to defraud Medicare of millions of dollars,” said Special Agent in Charge Roberto Coviello of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. “Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of that conduct and reinforces our commitment to protecting the integrity of federal health care programs and the taxpayers who fund them.”

The Federal Bureau of Investigation and U.S Department of Health and Human Services – Office of the Inspector General led the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney John Kennedy prosecuted the case.
title: Former New Hampshire Doctor Sentenced to Year in Prison for Role in $1.9 Million Medicare Fraud Scheme

ICYMI: “Maintaining A Strong Community Is a Shared Responsibility:” Congresswoman Lee Discusses Her Life and Service in Southern Nevada
LAS VEGAS, NV – Congresswoman Susie Lee (NV-03) was featured in the October issue of the Desert Foothills Living Magazine. She discussed her years of nonprofit experience before coming to Congress, her upbringing, and life with her family.
Read more below:
Desert Foothills Living: A Life Rooted in Family, Service & Community
October 2026 | Brandilyn Hallcroft
For Susie Lee, home has always been about more than a house or a neighborhood. It is about opening the door, bringing people together, helping others feel welcome, and doing her part to strengthen the community around her.
Susie raised her two children, Nevada “Nevie” Lee, 26, and Cody Lee, 21, in Eagle Hills. The family moved to the neighborhood when Nevie was in third grade, and Summerlin became the backdrop for countless family traditions, outdoor adventures, celebrations, and everyday moments.
“I love living in Southern Nevada, and especially Summerlin,” Susie shared. “It’s been a great place to raise my children.”
Susie’s commitment to family, hard work, and community service began long before she arrived in Nevada. Born and raised in a working-class family of 10 in Canton, Ohio, she grew up as one of eight children. Her father was a military veteran who worked in a steel plant, while her mother stayed home to care for their large family.
Susie’s first job was delivering newspapers, not simply to earn spending money, but to help her parents make ends meet. After graduating from public schools, she attended Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, paying for her education through scholarships, loans, and part-time jobs. Mindful of the financial burden, she completed a five-year program that allowed her to accomplish six years of college-level work in less time.
Following graduation, Susie worked for an environmental economics consulting firm in Boston. In 1993, she moved to Las Vegas, arriving during the intense heat of August and wondering what she was doing in the middle of the desert. She soon found her purpose here.
When Jan Jones Blackhurst launched her campaign to become Nevada’s first female governor, Susie jumped at the opportunity to get involved. Although the campaign was unsuccessful, it led to another important chapter when Jones Blackhurst established the MASH Center, a one-stop resource center serving people experiencing homelessness, and asked Susie to run it.
Susie had never worked specifically in the homelessness field, but she understood nonprofit leadership. More importantly, she felt increasingly drawn to work that could create lasting opportunities for children and families.
Several years later, the late Elaine Wynn recruited Susie to establish the Inner-City Games, now known as After-School All-Stars. Susie later served as president of Communities In Schools of Nevada, helping it grow into the state’s largest dropout prevention program. Her years of nonprofit leadership ultimately helped shape her approach to public service and her work in Congress.
Throughout her career, Susie was fortunate to learn from pioneering women who served as mentors and demonstrated the difference strong leadership can make. Those lessons, combined with the values she learned from her parents, continue to guide her today.
While Susie’s professional life has centered on service, her personal life has always revolved around her children, her community, and plenty of time outdoors.
Sports were an important part of Susie’s childhood. She and her siblings participated primarily in swimming and basketball, and Susie became both a synchronized and competitive swimmer. She continued competing throughout high school and at Carnegie Mellon University.
That love of athletics was passed down to Nevie and Cody. When they were young, Susie encouraged them to try different activities until they discovered sports they genuinely enjoyed. Between the two children, those experiments included soccer, fencing, competitive swimming, and basketball. Cody eventually found his place playing lacrosse with Rough Riders Lacrosse, while Nevie participated in synchronized swimming with the Nevada Desert Mermaids. Drawing on her own experience as a collegiate swimmer, Susie even stepped in to help coach the Desert Mermaids.
Nevie was also a Girl Scout, Cody was a Boy Scout, and both children took piano lessons with Miss Maya in Summerlin. Sundays often began with a family hike in Red Rock Canyon, a tradition Susie credits with helping her children develop their own appreciation for nature.
Today, the family continues to enjoy hiking, biking, skiing, and climbing at Red Rock. Susie is an avid hiker and cyclist and can often be found on the trails at Red Rock Canyon before her workday begins. She also enjoys supporting Southern Nevada’s small businesses and restaurants and connecting with residents at local community events.
At home, Susie is joined by her two dogs, Bridger, a Labradoodle, and Teton, a Sheepadoodle. The dogs fit naturally into a family that has never needed much of an excuse to celebrate. Susie once organized a neighborhood dog birthday party, complete with a birthday cake made from dog food. She also hosted an 11/11/11 party and always made sure Nevie and Cody’s birthdays felt special.
Hosting has long been one of Susie’s favorite ways to bring people together. Thanksgiving and Easter were major occasions in the Lee household, and Susie made a point of inviting anyone who might not have somewhere else to go. At least one evening each week, friends or family could be found gathered in her backyard for a barbecue.
Her enthusiasm for creating community extended throughout Eagle Hills. When her children were younger, Susie organized neighborhood scavenger hunts that sent local kids door-to-door collecting items from houses along the block. Halloween remains her favorite holiday, and she especially loves greeting generations of trick-or-treaters at her home.
Travel is another important part of the family’s story. Whether in summer or winter, Susie, Nevie, and Cody enjoy taking an outdoor-focused trip each year. The specific destination may change, but mountains, nature, and time together remain the common thread.
After more than three decades in Las Vegas, Susie continues to appreciate the people and places that make Southern Nevada feel like home. She believes maintaining a strong
community is a shared responsibility that requires residents to participate, speak up, and remain engaged.
“Southern Nevada is an incredible place to live, work, and raise your kids, and it’s because of all the incredible residents who call it home,” Susie said. “It takes all of us to continue to keep this a great place to raise our families. We all need to pitch in, get involved, speak up, and especially, vote.”
For Susie, that message is not simply about public service. It reflects the way she has lived throughout her life: working hard, welcoming others, showing up for her neighbors, and never missing an opportunity to bring people together.

Sioux Falls - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier has sentenced a Sioux Falls, SD, man convicted of Possession of a Firearm by a Prohibited Person. The sentencing took place on October 5, 2026.

Jorge Ramos, 37, was sentenced to two years and nine months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Ramos was indicted for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person by a federal grand jury in April 2026. He pleaded guilty on June 22, 2026.

In January of this year, Ramos, wearing a black facemask, was driving a car with dealer plates and had attempted to evade law enforcement numerous times, speeding away when detectives activated their lights and attempted to initiate a traffic stop. Ramos ultimately fled from the vehicle and threw a semi-automatic pistol to the ground where it was discovered by law enforcement. The gun had previously been stolen from a parked car in Sioux Falls. Ramos, who was found in possession of fentanyl, pills, and drug paraphernalia, admitted not only to possessing the stolen semi-automatic pistol but to having traded methamphetamine to acquire the gun earlier that day. Ramos was prohibited from possessing the gun because of a felony conviction for Identity Theft in 2024, in Minnehaha County. He has been convicted of several other offenses.

“This habitual offender was up to no good,” said U.S. Attorney Parsons. “A stolen gun, methamphetamine, fentanyl, and fleeing from police. The good news is that he will be off the streets of Sioux Falls for a while.”

“This habitual offender was up to no good,” said U.S. Attorney Parsons. “A stolen gun, methamphetamine, fentanyl, and fleeing from police. The good news is that he will be off the streets of Sioux Falls for a while.”

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan McFall prosecuted the case.

Ramos was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

Hours Long Stand Off in Cleveland Ends After Multiple Shots Fired by Suspect
For immediate release
Anne Murphy, Public Affairs Officer
CLEVELAND – Early this morning, members of the U.S. Marshals led Northern Ohio Violent Fugitive Task Force (NOVFTF) attempted to arrest Ke’Yon Sanchez Moore, 20. Moore was wanted by Cleveland Division of Police for aggravated robbery. *
At approximately 8:00am, officers arrived at the home in the 3500 block of East 120th St. They were able to confirm that Moore was in the home in the second and third stories of the residence. Over a period of more than four hours, officers deployed chemicals into the home along with robots and drones. At two separate times, Moore fired multiple rounds at the police robots and towards officers. Negotiators attempted to gain a surrender from Moore throughout the incident. The Cuyahoga County SWAT Team deployed to the area to assist as well. At approximately 1:00pm, another gun shot was heard from inside the home. Officers were able to confirm that Moore had shot himself and died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. Medical personnel on scene immediately confirmed this information. No officers or civilians were injured during this incident.
Anyone with information concerning a wanted fugitive can contact the Northern Ohio Violent Fugitive Task Force at 1-866-4WANTED (1-866-492-6833), or submit a tip by emailing usmstips@usdoj.gov. Reward money is available, and tipsters may remain anonymous. Follow the U.S. Marshals on Twitter @USMSCleveland.
The Northern Ohio Violent Fugitive Task Force – Cleveland Division is composed of the following federal, state and local agencies: U.S. Marshals Service, Cleveland Police Department, Cuyahoga County Sheriff’s Office, Cuyahoga Metropolitan Housing Authority Police Department, Euclid Police Department, Ohio Adult Parole Authority, Ohio State Highway Patrol, Independence Police Department, Parma Police Department, Aurora Police Department, Solon Police Department, Cleveland RTA Police Department, Westlake Police Department, Bedford Police Department, Middleburg Heights Police Department, Newburgh Heights Police Department and the Metrohealth Police Department.
*While the NOVFTF was searching the home for Ke’Yon Moore an additional warrant, for murder, was issued for Moore. The warrant was issued by the Cleveland Division of Police. If there are any questions regarding that investigation, please contact the Cleveland Division of Police Public Affairs Officer at (216) 623-5033.
