CVS Pharmacy Inc., a Rhode Island-based pharmacy chain, and its related corporate entities (collectively, CVS) have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve allegations that, from October 17, 2013 through December 2, 2025, CVS illegally filled prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances in violation of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) , and then sought payment for many of those invalid prescriptions from Medicare and other federal healthcare programs in violation of the False Claims Act (FCA).

“Not only does this settlement hold bad actors accountable for their fraudulent activities, but Americans are safer because of it,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances.”

“Today’s settlement requires CVS to implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “The remedial measures in this agreement — including proactive monitoring of opioid prescribing patterns — will provide critical protections for patients and federal healthcare programs. The Department of Justice will continue to take steps to prevent the unlawful dispensing of opioids.”

“The opioid epidemic has affected families and communities across Rhode Island and throughout the nation,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles C. Calenda for the District of Rhode Island. “Pharmacies that dispense controlled substances must maintain effective compliance systems to identify and respond to warning signs that prescriptions may be unlawful or medically unnecessary. This settlement demonstrates the importance of those obligations and the consequences of failing to implement safeguards designed to prevent the improper dispensing of controlled substances.”

The settlement resolves allegations in the government’s complaint, which the United States filed on Dec. 13, 2024, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island, that CVS knowingly filled prescriptions for controlled substances that lacked a legitimate medical purpose, were not valid, and/or were not issued in the usual course of professional practice. The United States alleged that CVS dispensed prescriptions for dangerous and excessive quantities of opioids, opioid prescriptions filled too early, and “trinity” prescriptions, a dangerous and abused combination of an opioid, a benzodiazepine, and a muscle relaxant. CVS also allegedly filled prescriptions for controlled substances from “pill mill” prescribers who issued large numbers of controlled substance prescriptions without any medical purpose. Further, the United States alleged that CVS pharmacists filled these prescriptions despite clear red flags indicating that there was a high likelihood that the prescriptions lacked a legitimate medical purpose, were not valid, or were not issued in the course of professional practice. Many of these prescriptions were ultimately billed to and reimbursed by federal healthcare programs.

The complaint further alleged that CVS’s violations stemmed from corporate-imposed performance metrics, incentive compensation, and staffing policies that prioritized corporate profits over patient safety. CVS failed to employ enough pharmacists to serve patients, comply with CVS’s legal obligations, and meet corporate performance metrics. In addition, CVS’s policies allegedly prevented pharmacists from warning one another about certain problematic prescribers.

In addition to the monetary payment announced today, CVS has entered into a memorandum of agreement with DEA to address its future obligations in dispensing controlled substances. This agreement requires CVS to establish a hotline for both employees and the public to report suspected illegal dispensing of controlled substances, proactively monitor the dispensing patterns of its pharmacies to identify and address potentially illegal dispensing, and establish a process to evaluate prescribers suspected of illegal prescribing.

“This settlement agreement highlights DEA’s commitment to protecting the health and safety of Americans while holding CVS accountable for dispensing unlawful prescriptions and endangering the public,” said DEA Assistant Administrator Cheri Oz. “DEA is unwavering in its commitment to protect public health and ensuring pharmacies adhere to the highest standards of responsible dispensing. We will continue to work closely with law enforcement, regulatory agencies, and the healthcare community to prevent the misuse of controlled substances, and we will hold those who jeopardize the safety of our citizens accountable.”

“Behind every unlawful prescription is a patient who could be put in harm’s way,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Scott J. Lampert of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS‑OIG). “The allegations in this case point to warning signs that should never be overlooked. HHS‑OIG will not tolerate conduct that jeopardizes lives, and we will continue to pursue those who betray the trust placed in them.”

The civil settlement resolves a civil lawsuit filed by Hillary Estright, a former CVS employee, under the whistleblower provision of the FCA, which authorizes private parties to sue on behalf of the United States and receive a share of any recovery. It also permits the United States to intervene and take over such lawsuits, as it did here. The amount to be recovered by the private whistleblower has not yet been determined. The qui tam case is captioned United States ex rel. Hillary Estright v. CVS Health Corporation, et al ., No. 22-cv-00222 (D.R.I.).

This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for the American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division.

The resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Civil Division’s Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section, and the Enforcement & Affirmative Litigation Branch, along with the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Rhode Island, Eastern District of Virginia, Eastern District of Texas, and District of Hawaii. The DEA’s Office of Diversion Control, Los Angeles Field Division, Richmond District Office, and Office of Chief Counsel led this case with substantial assistance from Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, Defense Criminal Investigative Service, Defense Health Agency (DHA), Office of Personnel Management (OPM), Department of Labor (DOL) Office of Inspector General, and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

The investigation and resolution of this matter illustrate the government’s emphasis on combating healthcare fraud. One of the most powerful tools in this effort is the False Claims Act. Tips and complaints from all sources about potential fraud, waste, abuse, and mismanagement, can be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services at 800-HHS-TIPS (800-447-8477).

The United States is represented in this matter by attorneys from the Justice Department’s Civil Division Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section (Assistant Director Natalie Waites and Trial Attorneys Claire Norsetter and Megan Engel) and Enforcement & Affirmative Litigation Branch (Deputy Director Lisa Hsiao and Trial Attorneys Kathleen Brunson and Katherine Ho), as well as from the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Rhode Island (Assistant U.S. Attorney Rachna Vyas), Eastern District of Virginia (Assistant U.S. Attorney John Beerbower), Eastern District of Texas (Assistant U.S. Attorney James Gillingham), and District of Hawaii (Assistant U.S. Attorney Tracy J. Weinstein).

The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability.

WASHINGTON -- Ashley Gause, 33, of the District of Columbia, was sentenced today to 140 months in federal prison for her role as a co-leader of a violent multi-state robbery crew that targeted more than a dozen pharmacies and cellphone stores in the District, Maryland, Virginia, and New Jersey, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“Ashley Gause and her co-conspirators participated in an extended campaign of violence that caused terror without any regard for their victims,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “They treated these pharmacies and cellphone stores as their own personal cash machines, garnering $300,000 in ill-gotten proceeds and prescription drugs, and leaving the store employees scarred for life.”

“Ashley Gause and her co-conspirators participated in an extended campaign of violence that caused terror without any regard for their victims,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “They treated these pharmacies and cellphone stores as their own personal cash machines, garnering $300,000 in ill-gotten proceeds and prescription drugs, and leaving the store employees scarred for life.”

Gause, aka “Cray,” was found guilty by a federal jury on Oct. 28, 2025, after a six-week trial, of conspiracy to interfere with interstate commerce by robbery (Hobbs Act Robbery), conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances from the pharmacy robberies, and eight individual counts of Hobbs Act Robbery.

In addition to the 140-month prison term, Judge Amy Berman Jackson ordered Gause to serve three years of supervised release. Federal prosecutors had requested a 235-month prison sentence.

Joining in the announcement were FBI Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the Washington Field Office, and Interim Chief Jeffery Carroll of the Metropolitan Police Department (MPD). According to court documents, from May 9, 2020, through May 26, 2021, Gause and her co-conspirators targeted pharmacies and cellular retail stores in the mid-Atlantic region, seeking to rob the businesses of prescription drugs and cellphones that they could then resell in the District.

Many of these offenses involved crew members brandishing and pointing a firearm at the victims. Gause was convicted of five such offenses.

Multiple co-defendants have been sentenced, or are awaiting trial, for their roles in a number of the robberies.

D’Marrell Mitchell, 36, of the District, was sentenced to 192 months in prison after he was found guilty of conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act Robbery, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances, and nine individual counts of Hobbs Act Robbery.

Floyd Neal, 32, of the District, was sentenced to 157 months in prison after pleading guilty to multiple counts of interstate commerce by robbery and possessing a firearm during a drug trafficking offense.

Ashawntea Henderson, 33, of the District, was sentenced to 57 months in prison after pleading guilty to interference with commerce by robbery and aiding and abetting.

Glenn Dolford, 32, of the District, who pleaded guilty to one count of interference with interstate commerce by robbery, was sentenced to 38 months to be served concurrent with a 42-month sentence out of DC Superior Court Case for an aggregate term of 80 months. Dolford is also serving a 22-year sentence for murder.

Terrance Barnham, 36, of the District, was sentenced to 78 months in prison after being found guilty of conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act Robbery, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances, one count of Hobbs Act Robbery, and one count of carrying a firearm during a crime of violence.

Police Department, and Prince George’s County Police Department.

RALEIGH, N.C. - On Monday, October 5, 2026, the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of NC held its 5 th annual Economic Crimes Summit in Raleigh, North Carolina.

This year’s summit had the privilege of Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (NFED) headlining as the keynote speaker. AAG McDonald and Boyle focused on national and local efforts to concentrate attention on the previously ignored massive fraud schemes across the country. As international governments and gangs, local and national criminal groups, and individual offenders continue to exploit government programs, financial systems, and vulnerable people, Americans face rising financial losses. As fraud grows in size and complexity, it causes headaches, ruins families, and can significantly disrupt small businesses.

“Our fraud mission is national in scope but local in execution,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “The strength of our enforcement efforts depends on the collaborative efforts of the partners found at this summit. I commend the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina for organizing this event and for fostering a community of dedicated individuals united in service to our country.” “Fraud harms everyone. I’m a taxpayer. You’re a taxpayer. They are stealing our money, and the citizens we could help are feeling the pinch,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle. “They steal taxpayer dollars, undermine trust in public programs, and target some of our most vulnerable citizens in Eastern North Carolina. Our office is committed to holding these vultures and hyenas accountable and working with partners nationwide to protect the public. Know this: if you steal taxpayer dollars in the EDNC, we will find you, we will prosecute you, and a cold concrete federal prison box awaits you. Cheaters. Never. Win.”

“Our fraud mission is national in scope but local in execution,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “The strength of our enforcement efforts depends on the collaborative efforts of the partners found at this summit. I commend the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina for organizing this event and for fostering a community of dedicated individuals united in service to our country.”

“Fraud harms everyone. I’m a taxpayer. You’re a taxpayer. They are stealing our money, and the citizens we could help are feeling the pinch,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle. “They steal taxpayer dollars, undermine trust in public programs, and target some of our most vulnerable citizens in Eastern North Carolina. Our office is committed to holding these vultures and hyenas accountable and working with partners nationwide to protect the public. Know this: if you steal taxpayer dollars in the EDNC, we will find you, we will prosecute you, and a cold concrete federal prison box awaits you. Cheaters. Never. Win.”

To combat the ever-growing fraud epidemic, the Economic Crimes Summit brought together over 175 primary agency partners such as the FBI, IRS-CI, HSI, HHS, VA-OIG, SBI, SHP, USDA, Department of Insurance, along with many other state and local partners to network, learn from specific training, receive guidance on priorities, and support the ongoing implementation of the NFED. A wide range of state and federal agencies collaborate and cooperate to investigate economic crimes, and fraudsters against federal programs in the EDNC.

The Summit highlighted the contributions to the work of the NFED. DOJ created NFED in early 2026 as a centralized unit to investigate and prosecute fraud against taxpayer dollars, federal programs, and other government-funded initiatives. President Donald J. Trump announced the creation of the NFED in January 2026, commissioning it with a broad mandate to enforce federal criminal and civil laws against fraud targeting federal programs, federally funded benefits, businesses, nonprofits, and private citizens. The NFED’s mission includes investigating and prosecuting fraud against taxpayer funds and programs, coordinating with agencies administering benefit programs, partnering with federal, tribal, state, territorial, and local law enforcement, developing systems and processes for efficient fraud detection, and providing prosecutors and law enforcement with advanced tools and resources.

For too long, fraudster piggies fed at the trough of federal programs without any oversight. No more. Federal agencies across the country have renewed their robust authority to strengthen oversight, pursue investigations, improve coordination, and provide training to law enforcement and prosecutors so they can detect and stop fraudulent activity more quickly. However, law enforcement alone cannot solve this problem. American citizens play a crucial role in preventing fraud by staying alert and reporting suspicious activity. Simple steps—guard personal information, verify the identity of anyone requesting sensitive details, and regularly checking financial and medical statements—can stop scams before they explode. Communities also strengthen fraud prevention when they talk openly about common schemes, especially those targeting older adults. When people recognize red flags early and quickly report concerns to the proper authorities, they help protect public programs, safeguard taxpayer dollars, and prevent others from falling victim.

The EDNC U.S. Attorney’s Office will continue prioritizing cases that safeguard taxpayers, support victims, and reinforce integrity across federal programs. The EDNC thanks AAG McDonald for his attention to this matter and will pull out all stops to achieve the NFED mission. One diverted penny is too much. Ellis Boyle, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of North Carolina, made the announcement

A copy of this press release is located on our website .
title: Fraud Enforcement Assistant Attorney General McDonald and U.S. Attorney Boyle Host Summit on Fighting Fraud in the EDNC

Tampa, Florida – Stanley Richardson Joseph (28, Brooklyn, NY), Kallie Nicole Valerie Halliday (26, Brooklyn, NY), and Kristy Marie Bochecchio (47, Tampa) have been charged in a federal indictment with conspiracy, theft of government money or property, and aggravated identity theft. If convicted on all counts, each faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in federal prison. The indictment also notifies the defendants that the United States intends to forfeit the proceeds traceable to the offenses. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to the indictment, Joseph, Halliday, and Bochecchio intercepted U.S. Treasury checks, which had been placed in the mail to be delivered to the victims. Once the defendants obtained the checks, they created counterfeit driver licenses to match the names and identities of the victims. They then used these counterfeit licenses to open new accounts at various financial institutions and deposited the stolen Treasury checks.

An indictment is merely a formal charge that a defendant has committed one or more violations of federal criminal law, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless, and until, proven guilty.

This case was investigated by the U.S. Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration and the Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation, with assistance from the U.S. Postal Inspection Service and Homeland Security Investigations, New York. It will be prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Merrilyn Hoenemeyer.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The core mission of the Fraud Division is to zealously investigate and prosecute those who steal or fraudulently misuse taxpayer dollars. Department of Justice efforts to combat fraud support President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Three Individuals Arrested for Attempting to Steal More Than $2 Million in Treasury Checks

SPRINGFIELD, Mo. – A Carthage, Mo., man pleaded guilty in federal court today for his illegal possession of a firearm.

Skylar Wyrick, 36, pleaded guilty before U.S. Chief Magistrate Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr., to one count of being a felon illegally in possession of a firearm. This defendant was charged as a part of Operation Spring Cleaning, that was coordinated by the United States Attorney’s Office and law enforcement across Southwest Missouri.

Wyrick pleaded guilty to the sole count of the indictment that charged him with illegal possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. On Oct. 3, 2025, Wyrick was contacted by law enforcement during a traffic stop for failing to display a front license plate. During that contact, Carthage Police Officers found that Wyrick had drug paraphernalia, a gun magazine and ammunition on his person. Officers then conducted a probable cause search of the vehicle. During that search, officers found additional drug paraphernalia, substances that were recognized as illegal narcotics, and a KelTec, P-32, .32 auto caliber firearm. Wyrick has prior felony convictions for robbery in the 2 nd degree and tampering with a motor vehicle in the 1 st degree. Both convictions carried with them sentences that exceeded one year of imprisonment, making Wyrick a person who was prohibited from possessing a firearm.

Under federal statutes, Wyrick is subject to sentences of up to 15 years in federal prison without parole and a maximum fine of $250,000 for count one, felon in possession of a firearm. The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as the sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled after the completion of a presentence investigation by the United States Probation Office.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Patrick Carney. It was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Springfield Missouri Police Department, and the Carthage, Missouri Police Department.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), a program bringing together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce violent crime and gun violence, and to make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. On May 26, 2021, the Department launched a violent crime reduction strategy strengthening PSN based on these core principles: fostering trust and legitimacy in our communities, supporting community-based organizations that help prevent violence from occurring in the first place, setting focused and strategic enforcement priorities, and measuring the results.
title: Carthage, Missouri Man Pleads Guilty to Being a Felon in Possession of a Firearm

WASHINGTON – Representatives Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Sara Jacobs (CA-51), and Jason Crow (CO-06) led 74 House Democrats in demanding answers from Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on a September 1 strike at a wedding in Kuhestak, Iran, that reportedly killed five civilians, including two children, and injured dozens. The lawmakers demand a full account of the strike and answers about the broader pattern of civilian harm resulting from Trump’s U.S. military operations in Iran, including whether U.S. forces were responsible and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties.
In their letter, the lawmakers write, “We are once again writing with grave concern regarding the conduct of the Administration’s war in Iran. Specifically, there are devastating reports of civilian casualties at a wedding in the town of Kuhestak, Iran, on September 1, 2026. This is the latest in an alarming pattern of civilian casualty incidents in strikes carried out by the United States in Iran since the war began on February 28, 2026.”
They further state, “The Post reported that six U.S. Navy aircraft-launched weapons targeted a communications complex near the home where the wedding was taking place and that one weapon missed its intended target. Accordingly, we demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran.”
Ansari’s letter is co-signed by Representatives Gabe Amo (RI-01), Jake Auchincloss (MA-04), Becca Balint (VT-AL), Ami Bera (CA-03), Donald Beyer (VA-08), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Yvette Clarke (NY-09), Jim Costa (CA-21), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Jason Crow (CO-06), Madeleine Dean (PA-04), Rosa DeLauro (CT-03), Christopher Deluzio (PA-17), Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Sarah Elfreth (MD-03), Veronica Escobar (TX-16), Dwight Evans (PA-03), Bill Foster (IL-11), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), John Garamendi (CA-08), Jesús García (IL-04), Maggie Goodlander (NH-02), Al Green (TX-09), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Chrissy Houlahan (PA-06), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Sara Jacobs (CA-51), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Henry Johnson (GA-04), Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), William Keating (MA-09), Robin Kelly (IL-02), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), James McGovern (MA-02), Gregory Meeks (NY-05), Analilia Mejia (NJ-10), Christian Menefee (TX-18), Grace Meng (NY-06), Kweisi Mfume (MD-07), Dave Min (CA-47), Gwen Moore (WI-04), Seth Moulton (MA-06), Kevin Mullin (CA-15), Jerrold Nadler (NY-12), Joe Neguse (CO-02), Eleanor Norton (DC-AL), Ilhan Omar (MN-05), Brittany Pettersen (CO-07), Chellie Pingree (ME-01), Mark Pocan (WI-02), Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), Emily Randall (WA-06), Jamie Raskin (MD-08), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Mary Gay Scanlon (PA-05), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Adam Smith (WA-09), Eric Sorensen (IL-17), Melanie Stansbury (NM-01), Greg Stanton (AZ-04), Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10), Dina Titus (NV-01), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Jill Tokuda (HI-02), Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), James Walkinshaw (VA-11), and Maxine Waters (CA-43).
Read the letter below.
Dear Secretary Hegseth,
We are once again writing with grave concern regarding the conduct of the Administration’s war in Iran. Specifically, there are devastating reports of civilian casualties at a wedding in the town of Kuhestak, Iran, on September 1, 2026. This is the latest in an alarming pattern of civilian casualty incidents in strikes carried out by the United States in Iran since the war began on February 28, 2026. While the Department has not publicly acknowledged responsibility for this incident, the Washington Post recently reported that there is a “high likelihood” that the U.S. was responsible for the incident, citing an official familiar with the operations. Furthermore, analysis from U.S. weapons experts has suggested that the explosion was caused by a U.S. glide bomb.
The Post reported that six U.S. Navy aircraft-launched weapons targeted a communications complex near the home where the wedding was taking place and that one weapon missed its intended target. Accordingly, we demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran. The consequences of this American strike have been devastating: 5 civilians were killed as a result of the strike in Kuhestak, including a 4-year-old boy and a 16-year-old boy, and dozens of civilians were injured.
This incident is regrettably among the latest in a string of civilian casualty incidents arising from the U.S.-led war in Iran. This includes a strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war that killed a reported 175 civilians, including 120 children. While it has been reported that a preliminary investigation by the Department found that the U.S. military was responsible for the strike, over six months later the Department has still not publicly acknowledged responsibility for the strike nor released the findings of its investigation. Similarly, reporting and independent analysis indicate that U.S. forces were responsible for a strike at a youth sports hall in Lamerd, Iran, that killed 21 civilians, including 7 children, on February 28. While the Department has denied responsibility, analysis by weapons experts found that the damage pattern is consistent with that of an American Precision Strike Missile (PrSM).
We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from U.S. operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department. Acknowledging such incidents, accepting responsibility, and learning from them makes our forces stronger, more effective, and an example to the world. When we fail to do so, it has the exact opposite effect.
This is why it is all the more alarming that amid these devastating incidents, the Department has also severely degraded the civilian harm mitigation and response (CHMR) programs and personnel designed to prevent, respond to, and learn from civilian harm. Understanding the civilian environment – including the location of civilian objects and critical infrastructure such as schools and gymnasiums, and patterns of life including large gatherings such as weddings – was intended to be a key aspect of this program. Yet CHMR staff at CENTCOM have reportedly dwindled from over 10 to just one full-time staff. The Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, which was mandated by Congress and designed to support combatant commands in this lifesaving work, has been cut from over thirty down to just seven.
On March 12, 2026, 121 Members of the U.S. House of Representatives wrote to you demanding answers regarding civilian casualties caused by Operation Epic Fury and the Department’s civilian protection efforts. The Department refused to provide any answers, simply stating “The United States Central Command (USCENTCOM) has initiated an investigation of this incident and appointed an investigating officer from outside the USCENTCOM chain of command. USCENTCOM will share the results of this investigation with Congress once it is completed.”
Nearly seven months into the war, Congress and the American public still lack basic information about the findings of that investigation and the measures the Department has taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring again.
The strike in Kuhestak makes that failure all the more troubling. In response to the reports regarding U.S. responsibility for the strike in Kuhestak, a spokesperson for the U.S. Central Command stated “The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC.” Similarly, Vice President Vance said at a press briefing recently that he was “skeptical” of reports that the U.S. was responsible for the bombing, while acknowledging that the incident was under investigation. We are concerned this lack of transparency from this Administration is becoming a pattern, given the Department also initially denied responsibility for the Minab strike and has yet to release the investigation related to that incident.
The American people deserve answers on not just this strike, but the Department’s pattern of civilian harm resulting from U.S. military operations in Iran. To that end, we insist on answers to the following questions no later than October 26, 2026.
- Did U.S. forces carry out the September 1, 2026 strike in Kuhestak, Iran, that killed 5 civilians and injured dozens? If so, what was the target and why was the decision taken to execute the strikes? What was the assessed civilian harm risk of the strikes, and what steps were considered or taken to prevent civilian harm?
- Has the Department formally initiated an investigation into the September 1 strike in Kuhestak? If so, please provide the date on which the investigation began, the office responsible for conducting it, whether the investigating officer is independent of the operational chain of command, and the expected timeline for completion.
- What is the status of the USCENTCOM investigation into the February 28 strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab? On what date will the Department provide Congress with the full findings of that investigation, including its conclusions regarding U.S. responsibility and the circumstances that led to the reported civilian casualties? On what date will the unclassified version of these findings be made available to the public?
- Did the Department conduct an initial review of whether it is possible the U.S. was involved in the Lamerd strike on February 28, 2026? What were the results of that initial review? Was additional information provided after the fact, and did this alter the initial review results at all? 
  - Did the Department conduct a civilian harm assessment of whether it is more likely than not that civilian harm occurred as a result of this strike? What were the results of this assessment? Was additional information provided after the fact, and did this alter the initial review results at all?
  - Has the Department conducted an administrative investigation, such as an AR 15-6, into the strike? If so, when was the investigation initiated, when are the findings due to the commander, and when will its findings be provided to Congress and released publicly?
- What steps, if any, has the Department taken to prevent civilian harm in targeting practices since the apparent U.S strikes in Minab on February 28, 2026? Please detail any specific policies that have been implemented.
- How many U.S. investigations, initial reviews, and civilian harm assessments into civilian casualties arising from operations in Iran have been initiated since February 28, 2026 and how many have been completed? Please provide details of all ongoing and completed investigations.
Sincerely,
Yassamin Ansari
Member of Congress
Follow @RepYassAnsari on all social media platforms and visit Ansari.House.gov to learn more.

title: Ansari Leads 74 House Democrats in Demanding Answers on Civilian Deaths in Iran

Windsor Locks, CT – Amtrak Vice President of Infrastructure and Project Delivery Warren LeBeau joined Gov. Ned Lamont, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Connecticut Transportation Commissioner Garrett Eucalitto, and state and local leadership to announce the opening of a newly constructed Windsor Locks Train Station. The station will serve Amtrak’s Hartford Line, Northeast Regional, Valley Flyer and Vermonter routes, as well as CTrail trains starting Oct. 18.
“Congratulations to the Town of Windsor Locks, our partners at CTDOT, and everyone who will benefit from this station for years to come,” Amtrak Vice President Infrastructure Delivery Warren LeBeau said. “Together, we’ve created a new, modern, and accessible station for customers, built improved infrastructure that strengthens the railroad, and providing better connections for residents, commuters, visitors all while supporting future growth in Windsor Locks and throughout the region.”
In fiscal year 2025, Windsor Locks Train Station served 35,576 riders. The new station features a relocated passenger rail and bus service from the south of the town’s downtown area to a central location near Main Street and track and signal enhancements to improve operational flexibility, reliability and capacity along the Northeast Corridor.
Thanks to support from our partners at the Federal Railroad Administration, Amtrak is also embarking on a new era of rail, including additional investments in Connecticut.
For example, Amtrak is replacing the 119-year-old Connecticut River Bridge, one of the most significant rail infrastructure projects in the Northeast. And in Norwalk, CT, Amtrak has contributed a portion of the funding for Connecticut DOT’s replacement of Walk Bridge.
title: Amtrak Joins Gov. Lamont, Connecticut DOT for Windsor Locks Train Station Ribbon Cutting

NASA’s SpaceX 35th commercial resupply mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT Tuesday aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, carrying more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and hardware, bound for the International Space Station. Following its successful launch, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft will carry new scientific experiments, cargo, and the final pair of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays to the orbiting laboratory.
Dragon is scheduled to autonomously dock at 11 a.m., Thursday, Oct. 15, to the space-facing port of the space station’s Harmony module. NASA will stream rendezvous and docking coverage beginning at 9:15 a.m., through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online:
The final pair of solar arrays will complete the space station’s power system augmentation, boosting available electricity for research, operations, and the station’s safe, controlled deorbit. Astronauts will install the arrays during a series of spacewalks planned for later this fall.
Dragon also is delivering several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity that could help restore vision for patients on Earth and 3D heart tissue models to advance large-scale drug testing on future space missions. Dragon also will carry materials to study how a new type of glass is formed in microgravity, and brain organoids that could uncover potential treatment targets for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.
These are just a sample of the hundreds of investigations conducted aboard the orbiting laboratory in the areas of biology and biotechnology, physical sciences, and Earth and space science. Research and technology investigations taking place aboard the space station benefit people on Earth and lay the groundwork for other agency deep space missions. As part of NASA’s Artemis program, the agency will send astronauts to the Moon to prepare for future human exploration of Mars, inspiring the world through discovery in a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration.
The Dragon spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the space station until mid-November when it will depart and return to Earth with time-critical research and cargo, splashing down off the coast of California.

POCATELLO – On October 7, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho filed charges in federal court alleging two Canadian citizens residing in eastern Idaho unlawfully voted in the 2022 general election, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis announced today.

According to court records, Taralynn Kathleen Bosco, 48, who was residing in Rexburg, is alleged to have voted in the 2022 general election even though she was not a United States citizen.

In a separate case, Stanley Richard Walton, 82, currently residing in Chubbuck, is alleged to have voted in the 2022 general election, even though he was not a United States citizen.

Bosco and Walton are scheduled for initial court appearances on October 26, 2026, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Debora K. Grasham of the U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho.

If convicted of the charges of illegal voting by aliens, Bosco and Walton face a fine up to $100,000, and up to one year in prison.

U.S. Attorney Davis commended the work of the Idaho State Police and Homeland Security Investigations which led to the charges.

Charges are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

SAN ANTONIO – A San Antonio man was sentenced in federal court today to 115 months in prison for being a felon in possession of a firearm, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents, Jovan Antwone Flemings, 37, was arrested in May 2024 due to multiple outstanding state warrants. At the time of his arrest, Flemings possessed a 9mm handgun with an extended 20-round magazine and a round in the chamber. The firearm was located inside a bag along with a black ski mask, a black long-sleeved shirt, and a pair of black sweatpants.

Being a convicted felon, Flemings was charged with one count of felon in possession of a firearm. His criminal record at the time of arrest included four convictions for aggravated assault, along with convictions for making terroristic threats, robbery, drug possession, and a prior state conviction for the being a felon in possession of a firearm.

Flemings pleaded guilty on May 6, 2025.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the U.S. Marshals Service, the San Antonio Police Department, and the Texas Department of Public Safety investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys John Fedock and Sarah Wannarka prosecuted the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

Rep. Min and Sen. Welch Lead Probe into Role of Trump Cabinet Members in Obtaining Pardons of Convicted Felons
Sen. Blumenthal and Rep. Scanlon also join investigation
Washington, DC. — This week, U.S. Representative Dave Min (D-CA-47), Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ Anti-Corruption Task Force, alongside U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on The Constitution, was joined by U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, and U.S. Representative Mary Gay Scanlon (D-PA-05), Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Constitution and Limited Government, in raising questions about the role of cabinet members in securing presidential pardons, as part of their ongoing investigation into executive clemency actions since January 20, 2025.
The bicameral group of lawmakers are looking into whether U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin used their access to inappropriately influence President Trump’s decision to grant full presidential pardons to convicted felons Trevor Milton and Troy Lake.
“Public reports of high-profile individuals—including yourself—appealing directly to the President on behalf of pardon recipients risk subversion of the established pardon review processes by financial influence and political access,” write the lawmakers. “Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution authorizes the President to ‘grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offenses against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.’ The U.S. Supreme Court has characterized executive clemency as ‘an act of grace’ exercised for the ‘public welfare.’ President Trump’s use of this authority appears to deviate from this traditional purpose.”
The lawmakers conclude: “Congress has a compelling interest in ensuring that the constitutional pardon power is exercised with fairness and transparency. Given these circumstances, we are seeking additional information to better understand the extent to which influence and access have overridden the standard pardon review process.”
In their letter to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., the lawmakers request answers about Secretary Kennedy’s reported role in President Trump’s decision to pardon convicted fraudster Trevor Milton, who defrauded and misled investors regarding technology and products related to his company, Nikola Corporation. The victims of Mr. Milton’s fraud include individuals who lost their retirement savings and others who had never invested in the stock market before. President Trump’s pardon eliminated Milton’s obligation to potentially pay $660 million in court-ordered restitution to his victims. Milton did not serve any of his four-year prison sentence.
“According to public reporting, you personally appealed to the President to grant Mr. Milton a pardon, arguing that he had been unfairly prosecuted by the previous administration’s Justice Department. Days before granting Mr. Milton’s pardon request, President Trump reportedly told him to call you and thank you for convincing the President to grant him a pardon,” write the lawmakers. “Your reported involvement in this matter is particularly troubling, given that Mr. Milton reportedly donated $750,000 to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Political Action Committee (PAC), which was launched in late 2024 by senior members of your presidential campaign to unite your supporters behind President Trump. Public reporting also indicates that Mr. Milton and his wife donated approximately $1,800,000 to President Trump’s 2024 reelection campaign a month before the election.”
In their letter to EPA Administrator Zeldin, the lawmakers demand answers about the administrator’s reported role in President Trump’s decision to grant a full presidential pardon to Troy Lake, and a subsequent corporate pardon to Lake’s company, Elite Diesel Service Inc. Lake’s conviction arose from allegations that he and his company disabled the monitoring components of emissions control systems on hundreds of heavy-duty commercial
trucks.
The lawmakers write: “According to public reporting, two friends of Mr. Lake petitioned you in an August 2025 email, urging you to reach out to the President to request a pardon. Mr. Lake’s wife publicly attributed progress on her husband’s pardon efforts to your subsequent intervention. Such progress included a phone call with Sean Hayes, a White House attorney who works closely on pardons.”
The lawmakers’ letters seek information from HHS Secretary Kennedy and EPA Administrator Zeldin regarding:
- The nature of their relationships with the pardoned felons;
- The process by which clemency requests were initiated and considered;
- Whether intermediaries, lobbyists, or advocates were involved;
- Any contacts with Trump Administration officials or associates;
- Their role in any other clemency decisions made by the Trump Administration;
- Whether financial contributions or payments were made in connection with clemency efforts; and
- The extent of third-party advocacy supporting the requests.
Read and download the lawmakers’ full letters to HHS Secretary Kennedy and EPA Administrator Zeldin.
In May, Senator Welch and Rep. Min sent letters to 17 individuals who received pardons or commutations under circumstances that warrant further congressional scrutiny, including several individuals connected to major fraud schemes, financial crimes, and high-profile political or financial relationships tied to President Trump and his associates. The earlier letters sought information regarding the clemency process, including whether financial contributions, lobbyists, intermediaries, or personal connections played a role in securing presidential clemency.
Among the individuals who received letters are convicted fraudsters, political fundraisers, corporate executives, and wealthy donors, such as Changpeng Zhao, whose cases have generated public reporting suggesting unusual access to Trump’s network of political allies and associates, direct lobbying efforts, large political donations, or other concerning connections surrounding their clemency requests.
The lawmakers continued their investigation in June, sending four additional letters to the Department of Justice’s Office of the Pardon Attorney, the White House Office of Records Management, the White House Pardon Czar, and the United States Secret Service.

text:
KENNETH DENNING, 69, of Holland, Massachusetts, was sentenced today by U.S. District Judge Victor A. Bolden in New Haven to 16 months of imprisonment and three years of supervised release for offenses stemming from his operation of the Electric Blue, a strip club in Tolland, Connecticut, where he and his employees promoted and facilitated prostitution.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Denning owned and oversaw the operation of the Electric Blue, which employed dancers who performed nude dances and lap dances for customers. The Electric Blue was owned by “Denning Enterprises,” a holding company nominally owned by Denning’s wife but controlled by Denning, from the 1990’s until it was sold in January 2025.

Denning and his employees typically required dancers to pay a “house fee” of up to $50 each shift, and dancers were encouraged to engage in commercial sex transactions with customers in private and semi-private rooms, including a “lap dance room,” “VIP rooms” and “Champagne rooms.” Customers, who had paid a cash cover charge to enter the Electric Blue, paid the club a fee, typically in cash, to use one of the private rooms, and then negotiated an additional fee directly with the dancer. The dancers kept these negotiated fees, which often were hundreds of dollars. Club employees collected the cash received by the club, placed the cash in envelopes noting the source of the cash, and then placed the envelopes in a safe in Denning’s office. They referred to this cash as “Kenny’s money,” and used this money to pay business expenses and fund Denning’s personal expenditures, including trips to casinos where Denning spent large sums of money. As an example, on February 23, 2023, Denning deposited approximately $21,700 in cash at the Mohegan Sun Casino for gambling purposes.

Denning and his bookkeeper provided spreadsheets of the Electric Blue’s purported income to the club’s tax return preparer that purposefully omitted “Kenny’s money.” On March 16, 2023, investigators seized $45,421 in cash from a safe inside Denning’s office at the Electric Blue. Documentation found with the cash indicated that approximately $39,751 of the cash represented “Kenny’s money” that was collected between March 2 and March 15, 2023. Based upon an extrapolation analysis of this two-week period, investigators calculated that Denning and employees caused nearly $3 million in material taxable business receipts not to be reported to the IRS for the 2020, 2021, and 2022 tax years.

In March 2020, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (“CARES”) Act provided emergency financial assistance to Americans suffering the economic effects caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. One source of relief provided by the CARES Act was the distribution of Economic Injury Disaster Loans (“EIDLs”), through the U.S. Small Business Administration (“SBA”), which provided working capital to eligible small businesses to meet operating expenses. Denning applied for and received an EIDL loan during the pandemic by falsely certifying that the business did not “present live performances of a prurient sexual nature.” On the EIDL application, Denning characterized the Electric Blue’s business activity as “Eating & Drinking Places.” In July 2020, the Electric Blue received $149,900 in EIDL funding. Denning almost immediately transferred $20,000 of those funds from the Electric Blue’s business bank account into his personal bank account.

Denning was arrested on May 15, 2024. On May 19, 2026, he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to use an interstate facility to promote or facilitate prostitution, one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS, one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering, and two counts of engaging in a monetary transaction in property derived from unlawful activity.

Judge Bolden ordered Denning to pay restitution of $549,999 to the IRS and $150,000 to the SBA. Denning also agreed to forfeit $1,525,842, including the $45,421 seized from the Electric Blue in March 2023, and $1,047 seized from his residence at the time of his arrest.

Denning, who is released on a $250,000 bond, is required to report to prison on November 17.

This matter has been investigated by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation Division, the Connecticut State Police, the Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection – Liquor Control Division, and the Massachusetts State Police, with the assistance of the Willimantic Police Department and the Manchester Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Robert S. Dearington and Alexis L. Beyerlein.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

HOUSTON – Another 260 people face federal charges for immigration and border security-related crimes from Oct. 2-8.

A total of 177 criminal complaints involved felony reentry after prior removal, while another 41 people face charges of illegal entry. Most of those charged have prior felony convictions involving narcotics, violent crimes, and immigration offenses. In addition, 37 people face human smuggling charges, including 13 illegal aliens. The remaining five cases filed this week involve other immigration crimes and firearms charges.

One of those charged with felony reentry is Orlando Rene Flores-Orellana, a Guatemalan national whom law enforcement allegedly discovered unlawfully in the country near Peñitas despite his March 3 removal. According to the criminal complaint, he has a prior conviction for firearm possession.

Law enforcement also discovered Jose Manuel Fernandez-Martinez near Pharr after his removal March 11, 2022. Court records reflect a prior conviction for manufacturing and delivering of cocaine.

Both face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

In addition to the new cases, Honduran national Eliseo Henriquez‑Joya aka Cheyo, received a 72‑month prison sentence for conspiring to transport illegal aliens. Authorities identified him as a leader who coordinated the smuggling of approximately 188 illegal aliens in box trucks, refrigerated trucks, and tractor‑trailers.

During the investigation, authorities stopped vehicles at checkpoints and discovered hidden compartments and false walls that concealed individuals in spaces with little or no ventilation, no air conditioning, and no means of escape.

The cases are referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations, ICE - Enforcement and Removal Operations, Border Patrol, Drug Enforcement Administration, FBI, U.S. Marshals Service, as well as the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives with additional assistance from state and local law enforcement partners.

The cases are part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigrants, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Under current leadership, public safety and a secure border are the top priorities for the Southern District. Enhanced enforcement both at the border and in the interior of the district have yielded aliens engaged in unlawful activity or with serious criminal histories, including convictions for human trafficking, sexual assault, and violence against children.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas remains one of the busiest in the nation. It represents 43 counties and more than 10 million people covering 44,000 square miles. Assistant U.S. Attorneys from all seven divisions including Houston, Galveston, Victoria, Corpus Christi, Brownsville, McAllen, and Laredo work directly with our law enforcement partners on the federal, state, and local levels to prosecute the suspected offenders of these and other federal crimes.

An indictment or criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law.

David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced that RICK MARRO, 45, of Stamford, pleaded guilty today before U.S. District Judge Kari A. Dooley in Bridgeport to a child exploitation offense.

According to court documents and statements made in court, law enforcement began investigating Marro in August 2023 after a 16-year-old male victim reported that he had been sexually exploited by Marro. The victim reported that he met Marro on a dating application, and they then began communicating on Snapchat in April 2023. The victim indicated that they met in person at Marro’s house on multiple occasions and two of the encounters were sexual in nature. The victim reported that Marro gave him “poppers,” that Marro was “into” asphyxiation, and, on one occasion, Marro strangled him and he passed out “for a minute or two.” A law enforcement review of the victim’s Snapchat account showed that Marro sent him videos that Marro had recorded of them engaged in sexual activity. He also sent the victim a video depicting Marro choking him.

Law enforcement subsequently seized and searched Marro’s cell phone. During the examination of Marro’s phone, investigators located the same videos that he recorded and sent the victim showing them engaged in sexual activity. They also located text messages that Marro had sent to another individual in which Marro stated that he “choked [the victim] all the way to unconscious today by accident.”

Marro, who was arrested on a criminal complaint on January 18, 2024, pleaded guilty to receipt and distribution of child pornography, an offense that carries a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of five years and a maximum term of imprisonment of 20 years. Judge Dooley scheduled sentencing for January 6.

Marro has been detained since his arrest.

This matter has been investigated by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Stamford Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Neeraj N. Patel.

This prosecution is part of the U.S. Department of Justice’s Project Safe Childhood Initiative, which is aimed at protecting children from sexual abuse and exploitation. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

To report cases of child exploitation, please visit www.cybertipline.com .

text:
The Federal Trade Commission and seven states today asked a federal judge to hold Martin Shkreli in contempt based on their allegations that he flagrantly and repeatedly violated a 2022 court order that banned him from the pharmaceutical industry.
In a motion and brief filed today, the FTC and its state co-plaintiffs allege that Shkreli, since his release from prison in May 2022, has been violating the court order by publicly trading in pharmaceutical industry stocks and broadcasting his opinions about the business and management of many pharmaceutical industry companies.
“After a full trial, the court found that Martin Shkreli’s conduct drove up prescription drug costs for American patients and blocked the entry of lower-cost generics,” said Daniel Guarnera, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition. “When judgment is entered by a court, whether it’s a settlement or an order following a trial, defendants must fulfill their obligations. Today’s action should serve as notice that the FTC will not hesitate to enforce violations of court orders."
The FTC voted unanimously in January 2020 to initiate the case against Shkreli, another individual executive and the companies they founded, Vyera Pharmaceuticals LLC and Phoenixus AG. In 2022, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled that Shkreli organized an illegal anticompetitive scheme to perpetuate a monopoly for the life-saving drug Daraprim, a treatment for a rare, potentially fatal parasitic infection known as toxoplasmosis.
The court found that the anticompetitive scheme executed by Shkreli and his codefendants prevented generic competition and protected their ability to increase Daraprim’s price from $17.50 per tablet to $750 per tablet. The court further found that “Shkreli’s egregious, deliberate, repetitive, long-running and ultimately dangerous illegal conduct” warranted an industry ban, and the court ordered Shkreli to disgorge over $64 million.
Contempt Filing
The joint motion alleges numerous examples of Shkreli violating the order’s lifetime ban by publicly trading in pharmaceutical industry stocks of at least 60 companies and broadcasting online his opinions about the business and management of many pharmaceutical companies. These activities run afoul of the court’s 2022 permanent injunction, which banned Shkreli “from directly or indirectly participating in any manner in the pharmaceutical industry,” including by “[a]cquiring or holding an Ownership Interest in a Pharmaceutical Company” or “[t]aking any action to directly or indirectly influence or control the management or business of any Pharmaceutical Company,” according to the FTC and states’ joint motion.
Shkreli has publicized his order violations by livestreaming and posting on numerous social media platforms, including YouTube, X, and Reddit. The motion alleges that, while livestreaming his trades in pharmaceutical industry stocks, Shkreli told his viewers “I’m showing you how to trade and invest in biotech.” The motion further alleges that, in another livestream, Shkreli confessed his “magic trick”: “It doesn’t matter what trades I make because I can always find a couple of biotech stocks to smoke.” As alleged in the motion, Shkreli used his livestreams to wage multiple public campaigns to short certain pharmaceutical company stocks based on his prediction that their key clinical trials would fail.
In their contempt filing, the FTC and its co-plaintiff states ask the court for an order to show cause why Shkreli should not be held in civil contempt for violating the lifetime ban imposed by the court and ultimately to issue civil sanctions to force Shkreli to comply with the terms of the court’s 2022 injunction.
Sanctions sought in the contempt filing seek to require Shkreli to:
- Divest any pharmaceutical company stocks he currently owns;
- Pay a fine equal to his profits from any pharmaceutical company stock trading (plus prejudgment interest) without the ability to account for offsetting losses; and
- Face clear and escalating consequences for any future violations, including financial penalties and potential incarceration.
The Commission vote to authorize staff to file a civil contempt action against Martin Shkreli was 1-0. FTC Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson is recused. Commissioner Mark R. Meador issued a statement. The motion was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and to protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. You can learn more about how competition benefits consumers, file an antitrust complaint, or comment on a proposed merger. For the latest news and resources, follow the FTC on social media, subscribe to press releases and read our blog.
title: FTC, States Ask Federal Court to Hold Martin Shkreli in Contempt for Allegedly Violating Lifetime Ban from Pharmaceutical Industry

CHARLESTON, W.Va. – Gary W. Jackson, 42, of Charleston, pleaded guilty today to distribution of 50 grams or more of a substance containing methamphetamine.

According to court documents and statements made in court, on April 23, 2024, Jackson sold approximately 233 grams of a substance containing methamphetamine to a confidential informant in exchange for $1,400. As part of his guilty plea, Jackson admitted that he conducted the transaction and that it occurred at his residence on Charleston’s West Side.

Jackson further admitted to three additional drug transactions. Jackson sold approximately 27.97 grams of a substance containing methamphetamine and approximately 30.12 grams of a substance containing fentanyl in exchange for $1,600 at his residence on August 9, 2023, approximately 110.99 grams of a substance containing methamphetamine in exchange for $800 on a West Side corner on December 6, 2023, and approximately 53.67 grams of a substance containing methamphetamine in exchange for $400 at a West Side intersection on May 15, 2024. Each transaction was with a confidential informant.

Jackson is scheduled to be sentenced on January 28, 2027, and faces a mandatory minimum of five years and up to 40 years in prison, at least four years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $5 million.

United States Attorney Moore Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the Metropolitan Drug Enforcement Network Team (MDENT), which is composed of the Charleston Police Department, the Kanawha County Sheriff’s Office, the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office, the Nitro Police Department, the St. Albans Police Department, and the South Charleston Police Department.

United States District Judge Thomas E. Johnston presided over the hearing. Assistant United States Attorney Jennifer D. Gordon is prosecuting the case.

A copy of this press release is located on the website of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of West Virginia. Related court documents and information can be found on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:25-cr-39.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Lou Correa (D-CA), alongside Congresswoman Laurel Lee (R-FL), introduced the bipartisan Bankruptcy Relief for Innocent Partners Act, which would ensure that people are not stuck with debt from fraud their partner committed alone, and that survivors of domestic and financial abuse are not forced to stay in dangerous relationships for financial reasons.
"If you didn't commit the fraud, you shouldn't carry the debt for the rest of your life," said Correa. "For a survivor of abuse, that debt can be a chain. Abusers use debt to control their partners and keep them from leaving. This bill removes one more chain."
“No one should be left responsible for debt caused by a partner’s fraud they neither knew about nor participated in,” said Laurel Lee. “For victims of domestic or financial abuse, being forced to bear the financial consequences of a partner’s wrongdoing can compound an already devastating situation. The Bankruptcy Relief for Innocent Partners Act is a matter of fundamental fairness. It provides meaningful relief for innocent individuals while ensuring our bankruptcy laws hold those who commit fraud accountable.”
The bill amends the Bankruptcy Code so that only the person who committed fraud is barred from discharging the resulting debt. Innocent partners would get the same fresh start as any other honest filer. The bill also protects survivors of domestic and financial abuse from being forced to stay in a relationship for financial reasons.
"NACBA strongly endorses this legislation because a person can be held legally responsible for someone else’s fraud without having committed fraud themselves. Bartenwerfer blurred that critical distinction in bankruptcy, allowing an innocent debtor to be saddled for life with a debt arising from misconduct they neither knew about nor could prevent. This bill would restore a simple rule: the extraordinary consequence of nondischargeability for fraud should follow the person who committed the fraud. It does not excuse wrongdoing or eliminate anyone’s underlying liability—it ensures that an honest debtor is not denied a fresh start because of someone else’s misconduct. We're grateful to Representative Correa and his colleagues on both sides of the aisle for taking it up," said Richard Nemeth, President, National Association of Consumer Bankruptcy Attorneys (NACBA).
“Ninety-nine percent of domestic violence survivors experience economic abuse and half experience coerced debt. Beyond the hard costs, coerced debt creates an economic ripple effect by damaging credit, and preventing a survivor from accessing housing, employment and the basic resources needed to be safe. The Bankruptcy Relief for Innocent Partners Act would provide critical relief to domestic violence survivors who are burdened with debt through no fault of their own. By naming the fraud, this legislation will remove a substantial barrier to bankruptcy relief, offering a pathway to economic security and safety for domestic violence survivors across the nation,” said Erika Sussman, Founder & Executive Director, Center for Survivor Agency and Justice.
Background
In Bartenwerfer v. Buckley, a couple ran a house-flipping business together, and one partner committed fraud without the other's knowledge. After the couple filed for bankruptcy, the Supreme Court ruled that current law did not allow the innocent partner to discharge the fraud-related debt.
The issue is especially serious in abusive relationships. Half of domestic abuse survivors report experiencing "coerced debt," where abusers use debt to maintain control and limit their partners' economic resources.

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Jalen Smith, 30, of Charlotte, North Carolina, was sentenced today to 72 months in prison, three years of supervised release, restitution of approximately $1.1 million, and forfeiture of $75,000 by United States District Judge Nitza I. Quiñones Alejandro, for his role in a bribery and point-shaving scheme to fix National Collegiate Athletic Association (“NCAA”) Division I men’s basketball games, as well as a firearms offense.

The defendant was charged by indictment in January of this year in connection with the bribery and point-shaving scheme. He was subsequently charged by information with possession of a firearm by a felon, arising from a 2025 search of Smith’s Charlotte residence, in which a loaded semi-automatic pistol was recovered.

In March, Smith pleaded guilty to one count each of bribery in sporting contests, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, and possession of a firearm by a felon.

“Jalen Smith played a central role in this point-shaving scheme, which corrupted the integrity of NCAA games and the sport of basketball itself,” said U.S. Attorney Metcalf. “As his prosecution and sentence show, we will not permit the criminal corruption of athletic competition to go unanswered. Those engaged in such behavior may profit in the short term, but they’ll lose much more when our team takes them to court.”

“Today’s sentencing sends a clear message: Those who exploit professional and collegiate athletes for personal gain will be held accountable,” said Wayne A. Jacobs, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Philadelphia. “This conduct does more than harm individual athletes. It undermines the integrity of sports and the trust placed in fair competition. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to pursue those who seek to manipulate that trust for their own financial benefit and ensure they are held responsible for their actions.”

As detailed in court filings, the overall scheme to influence or fix CBA and NCAA men’s basketball games lasted from approximately September 2022 to February 2025. After co-schemers profited on fixed CBA games, they turned their attention to influencing NCAA men’s basketball games.

Jalen Smith was a “fixer” in the scheme, working together with others to recruit and bribe NCAA men’s basketball players to underperform and help ensure their team failed to cover the spread in games during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 NCAA men’s basketball seasons.

Then, through various sportsbooks, Smith helped to arrange for large wagers to be placed on those games, betting against the team whose player or players they had bribed to engage in this point-shaving scheme. Smith had a leadership role in the scheme, particularly in recruiting, managing, and paying players for their roles in the scheme.

Smith and other fixers approached and communicated with the players, in person and through social media, text message communications, and cellular telephone calls, offering the players bribe payments, usually ranging from $10,000 to $30,000 per game.

Smith and other fixers specifically targeted college players for whom the bribe payments would meaningfully supplement, or exceed, the student-athletes’ legitimate opportunities for “Name-Image-Likeness” compensation. The fixers also generally targeted in their scheme players on teams that were underdogs in games and sought to have them fail to cover the spreads in those games. Many of these players accepted the offers and agreed to help fix specific games so that the fixers would win their wagers.

In total, the bribery and point-shaving scheme involved more than 39 players on over 17 different NCAA Division I men’s basketball teams, who fixed and attempted to fix more than 29 NCAA games. The scheme also resulted in more than $3 million in fraudulent wagers placed on these games, and more than $1.1 million in financial losses to sportsbooks throughout the country.

This case was investigated by FBI Philadelphia, with valuable assistance from FBI New York and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Louis D. Lappen and Jerome M. Maiatico.
title: Jalen Smith, a Leader of Bribery and Point-Shaving Scheme to Fix NCAA Men’s Basketball Games, Sentenced to Six Years in Prison

U.S. Congressman Everton Blair Introduces the SUN Act to Transform Highway Corridors into Clean Energy and High-Speed Broadband Hubs
Federal legislation that targets underutilized interstate medians to power local homes, strengthen the electric grid, and close the digital divide across Georgia and the nation.
Media Contact:
Allison Phipps, Allison.Phipps@mail.house.gov Amya Enlow, Amya.Enlow@mail.house.gov
Washington, D.C. – On Friday Oct. 9, 2026 Congressman Everton Blair (GA-13), introduced the Solar Use Network Act (or the SUN Act), legislation designed to turn unused federal highway rights-of-way into productive community assets for clean energy generation, electric vehicle (EV) charging, grid resilience, and high-speed broadband expansion.
The SUN Act amends the U.S. Code to allow interstate highway medians and roadside rights-of-way to be utilized for EV charging stations, renewable energy installations, electric grid infrastructure, and broadband deployment. By tapping into these underutilized public lands, the bill creates strategic opportunities to lower energy costs and expand digital infrastructure, particularly in rural and underserved communities.
“While the people of Georgia’s 13th face rising energy costs and internet coverage gaps, millions of acres of medians on federal highways like I-85 and I-20 sit unused,” said Congressman Blair. "The SUN Act turns this idle roadside land into community assets, powering homes, expanding EV charging networks, and building out broadband to close the digital divide."
The legislation addresses overlapping economic and infrastructure demands at a critical time for American households.
"With electricity costs rising, reliance on the grid at an all-time high, and Americans experiencing the real-time impacts of extreme weather, families are facing growing financial pressure," Congressman Blair added. "We need innovative, but practical solutions that lower costs for working families while building a cleaner, more resilient future. The SUN Act meets this moment."
###

Paulo Jorge Silva (right) during his arrest by HSI Philadelphia
