99 Democratic Lawmakers Slam Department of Education for Failure to Enforce Title IX and Protect Student Survivors
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Democratic Women’s Caucus (DWC) member Maxine Dexter (OR-03), DWC member Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), DWC Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03) and Rep. Mark Takano (CA-41) led a letter to the Office of the Inspector General at the Department of Education. The letter urges the Acting Inspector General to open an investigation into the Department’s gutting of the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and Title IX rollbacks and its impact on the Department’s ability to enforce Title IX protections for student survivors of sexual assault and harassment. 99 House Democrats joined the effort.
The call for the investigation comes after Jane Doe’s story from Cornell University and Kendall Francis’ story from Louisiana State University (LSU) sparked a national outcry about the high rate of sexual violence on college campuses. Additionally the survivors’ stories have renewed scrutiny of how colleges and universities respond, and how the Department of Education enforces Title IX protections for survivors.
One in four undergraduate women experience sexual assault or rape while in college. Sexual violence against women on college campuses is a public health crisis, yet significant barriers remain that block accountability and protections for students. Changes in staffing, resources, case-processing, and enforcement priorities under the Trump administration have only made that worse and have undermined the Department’s ability to properly investigate complaints and enforce Title IX protections.
As of January 2025, OCR reportedly faced a backlog of nearly 12,000 civil rights cases, while the administration reduced OCR’s workforce by nearly half. The Department has closed zero college sexual harassment or sexual violence cases. The Department also formalized weaker protections and processes for student survivors: narrowing the definition of sexual harassment, reducing school liability, and implementing intimidating investigative and hearing procedures that are retraumatizing to survivors.
Without proper federal enforcement and institutional accountability, Title IX protections become just words on a page. The Department of Education is failing student survivors. Protections for survivors are not partisan and should always be a priority, however the Department’s rollback of vital protections creates additional barriers for survivors and is leaving them to fend for themselves in their most vulnerable moments.
In their letter, the members explained how the Department’s changes will leave student survivors vulnerable and why an investigation is necessary:
“We urge the Office of Inspector General to immediately open an investigation into the Department’s failure to adequately enforce Title IX protections for survivors of sexual harassment and assault, including whether changes in staffing, resources, case-processing, and enforcement priorities have undermined the Department’s ability to protect students, investigate complaints in a timely manner, and hold institutions accountable.”
The members outlined the Department’s policies that have weakened protections for student survivors:
“At the same time that OCR’s staff and regional capacity were substantially reduced, the Department announced and pursued Title IX enforcement priorities concerning transgender students’ participation in athletics and access to sex-separated facilities, and also dismantling Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) programs. These reprioritizations do nothing to address the backlog of sexual violence cases.”
The letter also explains how reprioritizations and restructuring by the Department have decreased OCR’s capacity to investigate cases of sexual violence on campus:
“This restructuring threatens to further delay investigations, erode OCR’s institutional expertise, and create additional barriers for survivors seeking accountability. These reprioritizations, staff reductions, and the interagency agreement raise significant questions about whether OCR has sufficient capacity to investigate Title IX complaints, communicate with complainants, and fulfill its civil rights enforcement responsibilities in a timely and effective manner.”
The members also outlined what they are urging the Inspector General to investigate:
- Examining whether the Department has fulfilled its legal and administrative responsibilities to investigate and resolve Title IX complaints in a timely and effective manner.
- The causes and consequences of the absence of resolution agreements involving college sexual harassment and assault complaints since January 2025.
- Whether reductions in OCR staffing, the closure of regional offices, or changes in enforcement priorities have contributed to delays, backlogs, or failures to resolve these complaints.
- Examining whether OCR has sufficient staffing, resources, policies, and procedures to effectively enforce Title IX and protect students from sex discrimination, including sexual harassment and violence.
- Identifying how survivors have been harmed by these changes.
Lastly, the members asked the Inspector General to answer the following questions:
- How many Title IX sexual harassment and sexual violence complaints are currently pending before OCR, and how long have they been pending?
- How have processing times, case closures, investigations, and resolution agreements changed since January 2025?
- Have staffing reductions or office closures affected OCR’s ability to investigate complaints or communicate with survivors?
- Have Department officials directed, formally or informally, OCR personnel to deprioritize certain categories of Title IX complaints?
- What safeguards are currently in place to ensure Title IX complaints involving sexual violence receive timely and appropriate review?
- What corrective actions are necessary to ensure the Department is meeting its obligations to protect students under Title IX?
Read the full letter here.

WASHINGTON – Maurice Spears, 34, of Washington, D.C., was sentenced today to a total of 65 years and 180 days in prison for the sexual abuse of two different women in April and July 2024, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“Two victims. Eight days of violence, threats, and relentless sexual abuse. Today, the court delivered justice,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Maurice Spears will spend more than 65 years in prison — a consequence that reflects the fear he inflicted and the lives he tried to destroy. This sentence ensures he will never again have the chance to prey on another person in our community.”

“Two victims. Eight days of violence, threats, and relentless sexual abuse. Today, the court delivered justice,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Maurice Spears will spend more than 65 years in prison — a consequence that reflects the fear he inflicted and the lives he tried to destroy. This sentence ensures he will never again have the chance to prey on another person in our community.”

Spears was found guilty by a Superior Court jury of six counts of first-degree sexual abuse, two counts of felony threats, and one count of misdemeanor sexual abuse on May 14, 2026. Superior Court Judge Jason Park ordered the prison term to be followed by a lifetime supervised release. The defendant must also register as a sex offender.

According to the governments evidence, on April 15, 2024, Spears went on a single date with the first victim. After the date, they ended up back in the defendant’s storage unit, where he was living. While inside the storage unit, Spears threatened to kill the victim and her children if she left and told her that he planned to force her into prostitution. He also showed her a fake police badge and told her that he had law enforcement in his pocket. The defendant forced the victim to spend the next three days with him and sexually assaulted the victim twice inside his storage unit. He later took her to Virginia and kept her in a motel room. She was eventually rescued by her family and taken to the hospital.

On July 26, 2024, the second victim met Spears when they were both at a services provider for homeless individuals. The defendant promised to help the victim get some shoes. The victim ran into Spears the next day and he started to follow her around and refused to leave her tent when she asked him to. Eventually Spears started threatening her, telling her that he was connected to law enforcement and that he had people who would harm her if he told them to. The defendant spent the next five days repeatedly sexually assaulting her and refused to let her out of his sight. The victim was eventually able to call 911 and escape from the defendant.

Spears was arrested on September 9, 2024, and has been in custody since.

October 09, 2026
Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families
For release at 10:00 a.m. EDT
The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families.
The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.
Key findings from the 2025 survey include:
- Real median family income rose 7 percent between the 2022 to 2025 surveys to $82,200, while real mean family income fell 6 percent to $145,200. Families in the lower ends of the income and net worth distributions saw modest increases in median and mean income, while families in the upper ends saw declines.
- Between 2022 and 2025, real median net worth rose by 2 percent to $215,900, while real mean net worth rose by 7 percent to $1.24 million. Most families across the net worth and income distributions experienced increases in median and mean wealth.
- The homeownership rate was 66 percent in 2025, about unchanged from 2022. For families that owned a home, the median net housing value (the value of a home minus home-secured debt, such as a mortgage) rose to $230,000 in 2025 from $218,900 in 2022.
- Retirement plan participation, which includes account-type plans, individual retirement accounts, or defined benefit plans, was up slightly between 2022 and 2025 at around 65 percent. For families with account-type plans, mean and median balances rose.
- Participation in the stock market, which includes direct stock and indirect holdings, declined slightly from 58 percent in 2022 to 56 percent in 2025. Conditional on holding stock, median stock holdings grew 36 percent from $56,900 in 2022 to $77,400 in 2025.
- The fraction of families with any type of debt remained about stable at 77 percent. Median and mean debt outstanding remained unchanged from 2022.
- The fraction of families with debt payment-to-income ratios greater than 40 percent, which are families with particularly high debt payment obligations relative to their incomes, increased from 6.5 to 8.6 percent, a level last seen in the 2013 survey.
In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here. Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here.
The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families.
For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.
title: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

Release Number 9310-26
CFTC Seeks Public Comment on Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Concerning the Inclusion of Certain Event Contracts in the Definition of Swap
October 09, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that proposes providing additional market clarity by expressly further defining the term “swap” to include event contracts, including those based on sports, politics, cultural, and weather-related events. The proposal notes these contracts are financial instruments that are commonly known to the trade as swaps and proposes to resolve any ambiguity regarding these contracts.
“Americans use event contracts to hedge risks, speculate, and provide the public with information about the outcome of future events,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “These products are commodity derivatives squarely within the CFTC’s regulatory remit under the Commodity Exchange Act and are within the agency’s exclusive jurisdiction.”
Comments to the NPRM must be submitted in writing via Regulations.gov and received within 30 days of the NPRM’s publication in the Federal Register.

text:
Forest Service finalizes rule to accelerate forest management projects
Today, the U.S. Forest Service announced that final revisions to 36 CFR Part 218 will be published in the Federal Register. The regulations govern the project-level pre-decisional administrative review process, commonly referred to as the objection process, and are in effect 30 days from publication in the Federal Register.
The Forest Service updated the regulations to consolidate and streamline processes, increase efficiency and ensure consistency with recent amendments to the National Environmental Policy Act and USDA’s recently revised regulations. These updates modernize environmental review procedures across the department and support the Trump Administration’s Executive Oder 14192 Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
“Updating the rule will help ensure the Forest Service can act swiftly to deliver projects that create healthier, more resilient forests, grasslands, and infrastructure,” said Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz. “The final rule maintains a responsible environmental review process while removing unnecessary delays. This will save time and money while ensuring public input is considered before a final decision is made.”
The objection process applies to project proposals that support implementation of land and resource management plans. These projects include forest and vegetation management, grazing, infrastructure and recreation, wildlife habitat, energy and special-use projects, and projects authorized under the Healthy Forests Restoration Act.
The updated rule shortens objection filing and review periods and restricts review period extensions, reducing the overall objection process timeline by up to 73% for environmental assessments and up to 48% for environmental impact statements. The changes align the process with recent statutory and regulatory updates to the NEPA and help reduce delays in project analysis, environmental review, objection responses and project implementation.
The updated process also includes page limits for objections, additional requirements for focused objection content, and expanded use of technology for receiving comments and objections and distributing objection responses.
The previous objection process regulations were in place since 2013. Since then, Congress enacted statutory changes and USDA updated the NEPA procedures, resulting in inconsistencies with the existing regulations. The final rule addresses those changes, eliminates inconsistencies, and creates a more efficient and streamlined review process.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Jahana Hayes (CT-05), was joined by Congressman Greg Landsman (OH-01) and Congressman Buddy Carter (GA-01) to introduce the Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act, bipartisan legislation to reauthorize $1 billion in funding to help school districts across the country replace traditional school buses with electric bus alternatives. Specifically, the legislation would provide $1 billion for the Clean School Bus program at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
Every day, 20 million children and thousands of bus drivers breathe polluted air during their commute to school, which negatively impacts student health and attendance, particularly for students with asthma and other respiratory conditions. The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act addresses this challenge by providing school districts with grants to invest in bus replacement, charging infrastructure, and workforce development.
“Since I came to Congress in 2019, I have advocated for clean school bus funding. As an educator with over a decade of classroom experience, I know how damaging diesel exhaust can be for student well-being and learning. The consequences of diesel emissions extend to our environment, exacerbating the effects of greenhouse gas emissions. The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act will help to provide cleaner and healthier air for school children in Connecticut and across the country, support clean energy jobs, and protect our environment for decades to come,” said Congresswoman Hayes.
“School buses that run on clean energy have a major impact on the environment, and they save money for our school districts. The Clean School Bus Act is an important investment in our education system that will keep our kids and our communities safe for years to come”, said Congressman Landsman.
“Getting students to and from school safely and reliably is a priority for families and school districts across Georgia. By extending the Clean School Bus Program, this legislation will give schools greater certainty as they plan for the future, replace aging buses, and make transportation decisions that best meet the needs of their communities. I’m proud to co-lead this bipartisan effort to help ensure our schools have the tools they need to keep students moving safely and reliably,’ said Congressman Carter.
The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act builds on efforts led by Congresswoman Hayes since her first time in Congress.
- In 2019, Congresswoman Hayes introduced the Clean School Bus Act to establish a grant program authorized for up to $1 billion over five years for school districts, particularly those with lower-income students, to replace diesel school buses with electric school buses.
- In 2021, Congresswoman Hayes introduced the Clean Commute for Kids Act to invest $25 billion to replace existing diesel buses with electric buses.
- Congresswoman Hayes fought for clean school bus funding in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, signed into law in 2021. This led to the inclusion of over $5 billion for the EPA to administer rebates, grants, and contracts to replace a portion of the nearly 500,000 school buses with more environmentally safe models.
- In 2023, Congresswoman Hayes joined her colleagues to urge President Biden to include at least $300 million in additional funding for clean school buses in his FY24 budget request.
- In June of 2023, The Congresswoman joined Brenda Mallory, Chair of the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) and other officials to announce the award of 25 zero-emission school buses to DATTCO Inc. to provide school transportation services for the Connecticut Technical Education and Career System (CTECS).
- In 2024, the EPA announced 67 recipients for the first Clean School Bus Program Grants Competition. The grants help awardees purchase over 2,700 clean school buses in 281 school districts across 36 states including Connecticut. The Congresswoman released the following statement.
- During Fiscal Year 2027 appropriations, Congresswoman Hayes led over 120 of her colleagues to request $300 million for the Clean School Bus program.
The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act is endorsed by the American School Bus Industry Coalition which includes Blue Bird, First Student, Beacon Mobility, National Express, Highland, Greenpower Motor Company, National School Transportation, Student Transportation of America, and IC Bus. Additional endorsers include the American Bus Association, American Asthma and Allergy Foundation (AAFA), League of Conservation Voters, Moms Clean Air Force, Sierra Club, Union of Concerned Scientists, and World Resources Institute’s (WRI) Electric School Bus Initiative.
“Reauthorizing the Clean School Bus Program is important to American manufacturing, American workers, our nation’s school children and local communities throughout the country. As Americans, we can take pride in the fact that almost all school buses sold in the United States, including electric school buses, are also manufactured in the United States by American workers. The school bus industry has seen great enthusiasm and increased demand for alternative fuel and zero-emissions school buses from parents and school districts, and the Clean School Bus Program has significantly expanded access to these vehicles. On behalf of U.S. school bus manufacturers, and private school bus operators, the American School Bus Industry Coalition commends Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Greg Landsman and Rep. Buddy Carter for the bipartisan introduction of a five-year reauthorization bill that will positively benefit our nation’s kids.” – American School Bus Industry Coalition
Text of the Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act is available here.
title: Hayes, Landsman, Carter Introduce Bipartisan Clean School Bus Legislation

CHICAGO — A California businessman has been sentenced to three and a half years in federal prison for fraudulently obtaining more than $14 million in small business loans under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (“CARES”) Act.

DARREN CARLYLE SADLER participated in a scheme to fraudulently obtain loans pursuant to the Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”), which was created by the CARES Act to provide financial relief for small businesses during the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2020, Sadler submitted and caused the submission of at least 63 PPP loan applications for himself and his clients. The applications falsely represented, among other things, the number of employees and the average monthly payroll of the purported businesses. The false applications resulted in the issuance of more than $14 million in loans to Sadler and his clients, including $1.3 million in loans for Sadler himself. Sadler also received more than $1.9 million in fees from clients for fraudulently obtaining the loans on their behalf.

Sadler used the fraud proceeds to rent a villa for several months during the pandemic and to travel across the country on private jets to meet clients at bank branches to secure fund transfers. He also purchased luxury vehicles, including a Rolls Royce, multiple Mercedes-Benzes, and a Land Rover.

Sadler, 40, of Sacramento, Calif., pleaded guilty last year to a federal wire fraud charge. On Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin sentenced Sadler to 42 months in federal prison and ordered him to pay more than $14,692,762 in restitution. The government also seized a bank account controlled by Sadler worth more than $1.8 million, which was turned over to the government pursuant to court order.

The sentence was announced by Andrew S. Boutros, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois; Ryan Whalen, Special Agent-in-Charge of the Chicago Field Office of the FBI; Nicholas Bucciarelli, Inspector-in-Charge of the Chicago Division of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service; and William W. Kirk, Inspector General of the U.S. Small Business Administration, Office of the Inspector General.

“It is uncontroverted that defendant’s offense conduct was serious and borne of greed,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Kartik K. Raman argued in the government’s sentencing memorandum. “To enrich himself, defendant engaged in an extremely large, complex scheme that defrauded an important pandemic financial assistance program during a time of great uncertainty.”

Consistent with the Administration’s priorities to identify, investigate, and prosecute criminal fraud in the federal government entitlement and benefit programs, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois has been taking a fresh look at Covid-19 fraud.

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: California Businessman Sentenced to Three and a Half Years in Federal Prison for Orchestrating $14 Million Covid-Relief Fraud

Former Medical Doctor Convicted of Naturalization Fraud
Defendant was previously convicted of attempted murder and felonious assault of his then-girlfriend and their unborn child
CLEVELAND – U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services provided critical assistance to the investigation leading to the conviction of a former medical doctor for naturalization fraud. Yousif Abdulraouf Alhallaq, 47, of Canton, Ohio, lied on his Form N-400, Application for Naturalization, and during an in-person interview. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio made the announcement.
According to court documents, Alhallaq was born in Kuwait and entered the United States on an H-1B visa in 2006. He filed an application to become a lawful permanent resident of the United States in 2011 and was approved.
Evidence presented at trial shows that Alhallaq began work as an internal medicine doctor in Northeast Ohio in 2012. In December 2014, he poisoned his girlfriend’s oatmeal with an abortion drug after she became pregnant with his child to terminate the pregnancy without her knowledge. Several years later, the victim learned the truth about the incident and reported him to police. On March 18, 2021, Alhallaq was indicted and charged with one count of attempted murder and two counts of felonious assault for trying to purposely cause the termination of the victim’s pregnancy in 2014 causing serious, physical harm to her and her unborn child. In September 2021, Alhallaq pleaded guilty and was sentenced to four years in prison.
Before Alhallaq was sentenced for those charges in 2021, he submitted a Form N-400 to become a naturalized U.S. citizen. He submitted his application in 2017 and on the application answered “no” to the following questions:
- 14D - Were you ever involved in any way with badly hurting, or trying to hurt a person on purpose?
- 22 - Have you ever committed, assisted in committing, or attempted to commit a crime or offense for which you were not arrested?
Alhallaq was interviewed by an immigration officer in 2018 to review the answers he submitted on his Form N-400. Under oath, Alhallaq verbally confirmed his answers to questions 14D and 22 as “no,” matching those he initially submitted by mail. On May 4, 2018, he became a naturalized U.S. citizen.
Alhallaq knowingly committed acts of attempted murder and felonious assault by attempting to unlawfully terminate his girlfriend’s pregnancy, but he attested to federal officials that the information he provided was true and was subsequently granted U.S. citizenship.
Alhallaq faces a maximum of up to 10 years in prison for naturalization fraud and faces denaturalization because of his conviction.
The investigation was conducted by USCIS’ Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations in Cleveland.

Court records indicate that the defendant was identified by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) as a poly-drug trafficker in the Tallahassee area. text:
Remarks by Director Michael Kratsios at the Science: A New Golden Age Summit
Remarks as prepared for delivery
Oct. 8, 2026
Good morning, and thank you all for being here. It has been so encouraging to see “Science: A New Golden Age” receive such a warm reception, and thrilling to see the enthusiasm with which leaders from across government, industry, philanthropy, and the academy are stepping forward to contribute to remaking the American science enterprise for the 21stCentury.
The American people depend on and deserve a science ecosystem that is bold and ambitious; a science enterprise that seeks to solve grand national challenges; and a science community that is unapologetic in its hope that fundamental discovery will enable new breakthroughs for the improvement of daily life. This summit is an opportunity to share such a vision for the future, and some of the small steps and giant leaps being taken to get there.
“Science: A New Golden Age” was born of a three-fold tasking from President Trump: to maintain and extend American technological leadership; to ensure all Americans enjoy the benefits of rapidly advancing emerging technologies; and to revitalize America’s research enterprise by empowering America’s scientists to do their best work.
The world in which science is conducted today has been radically transformed since Vannevar Bush pointed us toward the Endless Frontier in 1945—in large part by his program’s successes. Now more than eight decades on from Bush’s project, the U.S. research ecosystem stands in need of an update, and the Federal Government can help lead the way.
Today, the private sector and philanthropy play a much larger role in American basic science, and technologies have transformed the way research is done. Over the past two decades the share of private funding dedicated to fundamental research has grown by a factor of five. And while Bush’s program assumed an essentially “linear” model of innovation—in which government-supported university research led sequentially to industrial development and commercialization—the reality of today’s innovation cycle is one of iterative, continuous, and recursive discovery. Meanwhile, the rise of super intelligence now presents a new revolution in the conduct of research across every scientific discipline.
It is out of recognition of a changing landscape and the need to mark new trails that “Science: A New Golden Age” emerged. And since even before its public release in July, my team at the White House has been driving a whole-of-government effort to fulfill the president’s mandate along the lines sketched out in the report. We’ve already accomplished a lot I’m very proud of.
In May, NSF announced $1.5 billion over 10 years for X-Labs, novel research organizations focused on pressing scientific challenges and breakthrough discovery. “Golden Age” emphasizes the need for new institutions of discovery, experimenting with not just how we fund, but what we fund.
Our goal is to empower young scientists to do their best work, and this spring saw NSF’s largest Graduate Research Fellows Program cohort in history, expanding a talent-development program that can claim 50 Nobel laureates as alumni. This funding is portable, giving promising young Americans maximum flexibility as they launch their careers in science.
Ph.D. programs have been designed to train for academia even though 60% of graduates do not pursue careers in the academy. We are tackling this reality, too. In July, NSF announced a $47 million investment for a novel four-year Ph.D. to give more than 250 doctoral students hands-on experience in industry.
Even as we update our organizational and institutional forms for the 21st Century, “Golden Age” upholds the American 20th Century’s defining push to accomplish grand national missions.
Our flagship whole-of-nation effort is The Genesis Mission, America’s super intelligence for science initiative. In July, the White House announced the expansion of the mission from the DOE to a mobilization of more than 15 federal agencies, and committed $5 billion to solving National Science and Technology Challenges.
The President has also set ambitious goals for quantum, including the production of a scientifically relevant, fault tolerant quantum computer by the end of this term.
In space, the Artemis Program will put Americans back on the lunar surface and the first nuclear reactor into orbit in 2028, and will plant the first elements of a moonbase by 2030.
And in energy, our fusion roadmap has set a goal of commercial fusion activity by mid 2030s, and the President’s nuclear EO’s have laid the foundation of a renaissance in advanced reactor development and the buildout of atomic energy infrastructure.
Our ambitions to meet grand challenges extend beyond our borders, and we continue to restore American scientific leadership through joint work with trusted international partners. The Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science, endorsed by 17 countries last week, demonstrates the international enthusiasm for the spirit of the “New Golden Age” report, and makes renewing national science and technology enterprises a shared diplomatic priority.
But from X-Labs to the Kyoto Vision, those initiatives have just been the start of restoring scientific greatness, and barely scratch the surface of our ambitions for America’s science enterprise.
Over the course of this summit today, we are launching the most comprehensive and far-reaching suite of science initiatives by America’s partnership of government, the private sector, and universities since the Second World War bound them together in the first place. It is my privilege to announce some of these initiatives now.
Super intelligence promises to be the greatest accelerant of scientific progress in human history, if we match its capabilities with an ecosystem adapted to keep up with its speed and scale. In the age of super intelligence for science, you can’t do frontier science without access to frontier compute. That’s a scarce resource in even shorter supply in an academic or public laboratory, limiting researchers’ ambitions. So I’m very proud to announce that Genesis Mission industry partners are committing $2.4 billion in compute, frontier SI for science models, and other tools for researchers.
In parallel, the NSF and DOE are launching a $100 million investment in developing the instrumentation needed for autonomous, SI science, and a nationally integrated research system in which anyone can send their experiments to programmable cloud labs. In a world where robotic experimental loops are possible the biggest limit on our ambitions will be good data. To help address this problem, I am proud to announce the DOE will be federating 190 key datasets across 14 federal agencies through its American Science and Security Platform. And yesterday, DOE and NIH announced a $1.8 billion dollar partnership with Biohub to develop the SI-ready data needed to build predictive models for biology and medicine.
In fact, every level of government—federal, state, and local—and every part of the national research ecosystem—the academy, philanthropy, and industry—are coming together to support researcher access to compute and SI for science infrastructure. The U.S. Southeast in particular is stepping up. Today, I am pleased to announce that 14 institutions in 10 states are launching the Southeast Regional AI Computing Consortium; in North Carolina, UNC Chapel Hill, Duke, NC State, Clemson, and the Research Triangle Institute are launching their own compute hub; and Georgia Tech and Emory University are investing $1 billion in frontier compute and frontier SI tools to equip and empower Georgia’s researchers and workforce to thrive in an SI-driven world.
Just as science itself advances with the refinement of methods and the update of old models, so too does the scientific enterprise. As I emphasize in the “Golden Age” report, revitalizing America’s science enterprise requires us to institutionalize continuous improvement.
This means experimenting with how we fund science, how we judge results, how research institutions are formed, and how science is conducted—applying, through metascience, the principles of the scientific method to every part of our work. And this means committing to and enforcing gold-standard scientific conduct—showing the reproducibility, transparency, impartiality, integrity, and humility that the public expects, and which forms the foundation of trust on which the scientific enterprise depends.
To operationalize practical improvements in how NSF funds and supports America’s researchers, the NSF is launching its Office of Metascience with its first two experiments, focused on Golden Tickets and distributed review, to encourage funding more outside-the-box research proposals. NASA, too, is launching a new metascience initiative in its Science Mission Directorate, with its own new double-blind peer review experiment in research-merit review. And today the DOE is launching a Golden Tickets metascience experiment of its own, to encourage support for high-risk, high-reward proposals.
As I said, last week I had the privilege of announcing the Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science in partnership with 17 countries committed to the spirit of this report and summit. Continuing this momentum, I’m pleased to announce the NSF will be partnering with the United Kingdom Research and Innovation’s Metascience Unit, laying the foundation of an international network of metascience units that will share experimental results and best practices.
But even the conduct of metascience is dependent on the reliability of established findings. That is what makes scientific replication so important. The need is particularly clear in biomedical research. As was announced just last week, the NIH is focused on addressing the replication crisis, launching R3PEATS, a $174 million reproducibility initiative, as well as “linked discoveries,” a tool to determine whether or not research has been replicated or invalidated at scale.
As mentioned, the NSF has committed to experimenting with focused research organizations through its X-Labs initiative. Today, I am pleased to announce establishment of the X-Labs Consortium, with $310 million of private contributions to support X-Labs teams focused on physical SI and quantum technologies. We are bringing together the whole national research enterprise to align private money and public priorities.
As a practice, a tradition, and vocation, science depends on a transmission from one generation to the next. “Golden Age” stresses the importance of supporting early carer scientists, and that starts in K-12 STEM education.
We have understood the importance of talent development in the past. From 1986 to 1996, the NSF Young Scholars program provided more than 18,000 of our brightest high school students with advanced STEM enrichment programs. I am thrilled to announce that the NSF is renewing the Young Scholars Program in partnership with National Math Stars and Jane Street, to encourage more of our most talented young people to pursue a vocation in science.
For those students who hear that call, we want to encourage them to begin their serious science studies early and to finish formal training quickly. I’m proud to announce the launch of NSF’s $50 million NextGen Workforce Program, which aims to accelerate formal education for our best STEM talent through an integrated 6-year Bachelor to Ph.D. program, so they don’t have to wait to make a serious contribution to human knowledge.
This is in line with our accelerated, NSF 4-year Ph.D.s launched soon after Golden Age’s publication, which represent an innovative partnership with universities and industry. Today, I’m thrilled to announce DOE is launching its own $100 million 4-year Ph.D. program, the Genesis Mission Fellowships, which will culminate in young scientists spending a year in National Labs and industry.
One of the biggest obstacles to good work for a young scientist is paperwork. It’s hard for people outside the sciences to understand what researchers go through to get funding. As the National Academies have found, researchers spend as much as 45% of their time working on administrative and regulatory tasks instead of in the laboratory. To help address this terrible waste, NSF and NIH are launching an initiative to convert more than half of their conventional funding application forms to a “just in time” approach that only requires the paperwork be submitted as a proposal moves forward in the approval process.
We are also taking steps to better cultivate American talent in biomedicine, where the premier research institution remains the NIH. The NIH offers support for extramural research through grants, and is itself a home for highly prestigious intramural work. But these important research opportunities, both extramural and intramural, are increasingly out of reach for young scientists. We have to free more young scientists to do more ambitious work at the most ambitious point of their life.
In the 1980s, the share of first-time NIH grant recipients who were under the age of 35 was 22. By 2025, that same proportion had dropped to 1.3%. This year, I am pleased to announce NIH is funding its largest cohort of extramural early-career investigators in history. And perhaps more exciting—in light of estimates finding the median age for intramural researchers at NIH is 71 years old—today I am thrilled to announce the launch of NIH’s Generation Discovery, bringing a hundred exceptional early-career scientists into the institutes’ celebrated Intramural Research Program.
In the partnership of government, academia, philanthropy, and industry that forms America’s research enterprise, it is the government’s unique contribution to set clear goals and priorities for the nation. As a people, our proudest technical achievements have been accomplished because political leaders identified national priorities and coordinated the resources required to achieve them.
Today, America’s science enterprise faces a transforming world, increasingly defined by technological change at home and competitors abroad. We must respond by planting the flag and choosing to lead, continuing to labor in whole-of-nation efforts that unite us in the work of discovery. Together, we can unleash a Golden Age of Science in America.
Thank you so much for joining me.
title: Remarks by Director Michael Kratsios at the Science: A New Golden Age Summit

MINNEAPOLIS – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that yesterday a federal jury found Alejandro Rojas Garcia, 65, a Mexican national in the United States illegally, guilty of attempted production of child pornography.

The guilty verdict was returned after a four-day trial starting on October 5, 2026, before U.S. District Judge John R. Tunheim. Sentencing will be set at a later date and Garcia faces a mandatory minimum of 180 months in prison. The defendant is also facing state criminal charges for related conduct.¹

Photo of Alejandro Rojas Garcia

“Garcia is a predator. A verdict cannot undo the evil he brought on two innocent girls, but it is justice,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen.

According to federal court documents, evidence presented during trial, and as alleged in public state court documents, in early April 2024, law enforcement began an investigation into Garcia after receiving information that he had sexually assaulted two sisters, including Minor Victim 1 and Minor Victim 2, both of whom were then under the age of 13.

Garcia was a longtime family friend of the victims’ family, and the family trusted Garcia to care for the children a few days of the week. When Garcia provided childcare for the minor victims, they spent time at Garcia’s apartment. Minor Victim 1 stated that in the spring of 2024, Garcia sexually assaulted her and was violent.

Minor Victim 2 stated that, on multiple instances, Garcia would sexually assault her and that he caused her pain.

On April 5, 2024, Garcia was arrested. Officers conducted a search of Garcia’s apartment pursuant to a search warrant. The officers seized multiple cellphones, cameras, laptop computers, flash drives, other data storage devices, and a massage gun. Garcia had several hidden cameras placed throughout his apartment, including five cameras hidden in the bathroom. Cameras were aimed at the genital area of a person sitting on the toilet and towards the shower and bath area.

Electronic Storage Devices Found in Garcia’s Apartment

Officers searched the various storage devices Garcia had stashed in his apartment and found numerous child sexual abuse material, including that of Minor Victim 1 and of other unknown child victims. While searching Garcia’s apartment, an electronic storage detection dog indicated the presence of evidence in a wooden crucifix hanging on a wall in Garcia’s bedroom. Inside the crucifix, behind a bottle of holy water, was a micro-SD card which contained child sexual abuse material involving Minor Victim 1.

Front of Crucifix

Inside Crucifix Depicting Holy Water and Micro-SD Card

At trial, Garcia testified. Under oath, he claimed that he was unaware of the child sexual abuse material on the various devices in his apartment. Regarding the child sexual abuse material involving Minor Victim 1 found on the micro-SD card inside the crucifix, Garcia acknowledged that he put the material on the micro-SD card but denied producing the material with the intent of gratifying his sexual desire.

This case was the result of an investigation by Homeland Security Investigations and the Stillwater Police Department, with assistance from Washington County Child Protective Services.

Assistant United States Attorneys Dana M. Joseph, Echo D. Fatsis, and William C. Mattessich are prosecuting the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

¹ Garcia has been charged by complaint in Washington County District Court File No. 82-CR-24-1329 on two counts of Criminal Sexual Conduct in the 1st Degree.
title: Illegal Alien Convicted at Trial of Child Pornography Charge

ICYMI in HousingWire | HUD Action Ensures FHA Loans are for Americans Only
Following HUD Action, Homeownership Loans for Illegals and Non-Residents Drop
October 9, 2026
WASHINGTON - New data reveals Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans for non-permanent residents and illegals fell from 6% to nearly zero after the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development revoked their eligibility in May 2025.
“President Trump promised to put Americans first, and HUD delivered,” said Secretary Turner. “We are preventing illegals and non-residents from accessing taxpayer-backed programs at the expense of American homebuyers. Today, that share is zero. Make no mistake — exploit our citizens, and HUD will act.”
Watch Secretary Turner break down what this means for Americans:
Learn more from HousingWire:
Changes to residency requirements for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans have sharply reduced the share of FHA purchase mortgages made to non-permanent residents, according to origination data from Intercontinental Exchange (ICE).
In March 2025, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued Mortgagee Letter 2025-09 and Title I Letter 490, removing the “non-permanent resident” category from FHA’s Single Family Title I and Title II programs, effective May 25, 2025.
Before the policy changes took effect, non-permanent residents accounted for about 5.8% of FHA purchase originations and 5.6% of purchase mortgages across the broader market, according to ICE data shared with HousingWire. After the changes, their share of FHA purchase loans fell to about 0.1%, while their share of purchase mortgages across all loan types declined by 2.2 percentage points to 3.4%, the data shows.
“President Trump promised to put Americans first, and HUD delivered,” Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement. “We are preventing illegals and non-residents from accessing taxpayer-backed programs at the expense of American homebuyers. Today, that share is zero. Make no mistake — exploit our citizens, and HUD will act.”
Market-specific impacts
The changes have had a larger impact in some markets where non-permanent residents had previously represented a relatively significant share of FHA purchase activity.
ICE evaluated markets with the highest non-permanent resident alien share of purchase originations prior to the FHA policy change (measured from second-quarter 2024 through first-quarter 2025) and filtered to the 100 largest U.S. markets and 33 markets along the U.S. borders with Mexico and Canada.
Utah markets recorded some of the largest declines. In Salt Lake City, non-permanent residents accounted for 26% of FHA purchase originations before the changes, compared with 0.15% afterward (Q4 2025 to the present). In Provo, the share fell from 20% to less than 0.5%.
Florida markets also saw declines. In Orlando, the pre-policy share went from 16.1% to a post-policy share of 0.2%. Lakeland went from 13.6% to 0.16%, and both Cape Coral and Miami went from 10% to less than 1%.
Other markets also recorded significant declines. Raleigh‘s share fell from 11.1% to 0.8%, while San Jose’s fell from about 10% to 0%.
The data suggests that conventional lending has not fully offset the decline in FHA lending to non-permanent residents. ICE data shows that non-permanent resident volume across conventional prime conforming loans remained relatively stable rather than increasing by a comparable amount.
“This new policy has definitely had an impact on families that would have qualified before May 2025,” said Michael Brown, a Tennessee-based home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage. “Many of these borrowers are doing conventional loans now because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac permit lawful non-permanent residents to obtain financing.”
Brown said that non-QM loans are another option for non-permanent residents, but that the new policy limits affordable financing options. “Some of these non-permanent residents will end up having to put more money down, work on improving their credit scores to qualify, or simply will need to wait until they obtain permanent-resident status,” he said.
Isaac Schultz, a Michigan-based home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, echoed that the only options for non-permanent residents are conventional financing or “some flavor of non-qualified mortgage financing.”
“I am currently working on a loan in one such scenario, and it does make it far more difficult for the borrower to qualify. For better or for worse, that was the main desired result of the policy change,” Schultz said.
Home price declines
It is unclear whether the declines have affected affordability, but most markets in the ICE dataset recorded lower prices after the policy changes took effect, according to HousingWire Data.
In Salt Lake City, the median list price for a single-family home ranged from $619,900 to $795,000 from Q2 2024 through Q1 2025. From Q4 2025 to the present, prices ranged from $620,000 to $742,450.
In Provo, the median list price ranged from $630,000 to $877,400 from Q2 2024 through Q1 2025, compared with $589,900 to $699,950 from Q4 2025 to the present.
Prices also shifted in Florida markets. In Orlando, the median list price ranged from $490,000 to $544,950 before the policy change, then dropped to a range of $489,000 to $525,000 afterward.
The change appeared to have no impact on prices in Lakeland, where they ranged from $350,000 to $374,999 before the change, and from $357,000 to $375,000 afterward. In Cape Coral, however, prices ranged from $475,000 to $510,000 before the policy changes, compared with $420,000 to $467,450 afterward.
In Raleigh, the median list price for a single-family home ranged from $579,900 to $699,000 before the change, but later dropped to $522,000 to $624,900.
San Jose, one of the nation’s most expensive markets, saw a smaller shift. The median list price for a single-family home there ranged from $1.56 million to $1.70 million from Q2 2024 through Q1 2025. From Q4 2025 to the present, prices ranged from $1.498 million to $1.70 million.

Hoyer Statement on Trump Administration Decision to Lift Sanctions on Russian Diesel
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) released the following statement after President Donald Trump announced a 180-day suspension of sanctions on Russian diesel and indicated that the U.S. may purchase large quantities of the fuel:
"It is outrageous for the President of the United States to purchase tons of diesel from Russia in direct contravention of legislation he signed three weeks ago imposing the toughest sanctions on Russia’s oil and gas. Doing so would fuel the very war of aggression in Ukraine that our sanctions are meant to stop. It is a sudden and mendacious shift in policy from the pressure of our sanctions to actively aiding and abetting the war effort of Russia against Ukraine - and an infusion of economic assistance to Russia. Both of these are the exact opposite of Congress’s intent and the President’s statement in enacting and signing the Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act three weeks ago. This action bails out both Putin and Trump - for Putin, his faltering war effort and economy; for Trump, the consequences of a war of choice in Iran: exorbitant fuel costs for Americans.
"President Trump’s action of helping Russia while at the same time asking our allies to shoulder more of the burden of support for Ukraine is clearly duplicitous.
“Congress must take action, drawing on the strong bipartisan support behind the sanctions law, to prevent a penny of American funds from being used to purchase Russian petroleum products, on which Putin relies to fund his war.”
title: Hoyer Statement on Trump Administration Decision to Lift Sanctions on Russian Diesel

SAN DIEGO – Isaac Jimenez, a U.S. citizen residing in Tijuana, was sentenced in federal court today to 12 years in prison for his role in a human smuggling conspiracy whose members kidnapped migrants and extorted their families for ransom.

Two victims in unrelated kidnappings—a father of four U.S. citizen children and a 21-year-old woman from Tijuana—were never heard from again. The woman was found dead in Tijuana; the man is believed to have been killed in Mexico by Jimenez’s coconspirators.

Jimenez crossing the border to pick up ransom money from victim's wife

U.S. District Judge Janis L. Sammartino also ordered Jimenez to pay $24,500 in restitution to family members of the victims for funeral and related expenses and for a portion of the ransom payments made during the conspiracy.

Judge Sammartino imposed the sentence after the government detailed Jimenez’s extensive history of alien smuggling and his knowing participation in the Tijuana-based organization that used kidnapping, threats and violence against migrants who had paid to be smuggled into the United States.

“There’s a fantasy of human smugglers as being on the side of the vulnerable. Then there’s the truth: They are liars, blackmailers and killers. You want proof, keep reading,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon.

“Today’s sentencing holds the defendant accountable for knowingly supporting a human smuggling organization that exploited vulnerable people through kidnapping, extortion, threats, and violence,” said Kevin Murphy, Special Agent in Charge of HSI San Diego. “Human smuggling networks profit from human suffering and show a callous disregard for the lives they endanger. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement partners on both sides of the border to identify, investigate, and dismantle those responsible for these crimes.”

At today’s hearing, Judge Sammartino described the case events as “the most deliberate and unnecessary loss of life I’ve seen in a very long time.” Addressing Mr. Jimenez, she said, “You preyed upon the most vulnerable people.”

Jimenez, who previously lived in Escondido before moving to Tijuana, had been involved in alien smuggling for years before joining the organization in 2024. He was convicted of alien-smuggling offenses in 2015 and 2017 and was arrested again in 2022 in connection with another smuggling investigation. In early 2024, after being released from custody in Mexico, Jimenez began working for members of a Tijuana-based organization, transporting migrants from the border area to locations in the United States for payment.

As Jimenez became more involved, he learned that the organization was holding migrants against their will and demanding additional payments from them and their families as a condition of their release. He also received photographs and videos depicting kidnappings and murders involving members of the organization. Despite this knowledge, Jimenez continued to participate in the conspiracy.

In September 2024, the organization agreed to smuggle C.G.C., a father of four U.S. citizen children who had previously resided in Southern California, into the United States from Mexico. Instead of being smuggled into the United States, C.G.C. was held captive in Mexico while his kidnappers demanded $30,000 from his family and threatened to kill him.

At the direction of his coconspirators, Jimenez collected $15,000 in ransom payments from C.G.C.’s wife, transported the money to Tijuana and delivered it to the kidnappers. Additional ransom demands followed, including demands for money and vehicles. When the family could no longer pay, the kidnappers threatened to provide the location of C.G.C.’s body. Communications eventually ceased. C.G.C. remains missing and, according to court documents, is presumed to have been killed in Mexico by Jimenez’s coconspirators.

Three months later, Jimenez agreed to coordinate the smuggling of V.A.E., a 21-year-old Mexican woman, for $7,000. Jimenez was to earn a $1,000 commission. Instead, his coconspirators took V.A.E. to a safe house and held her captive, demanding $30,000 from her family for her release. The kidnappers sent videos showing V.A.E. being threatened with firearms and beaten; they threatened to kill her if the ransom was not paid.

V.A.E.’s family eventually paid approximately $10,000, but she was never released. Her skeletal remains were discovered in the Tijuana area in November 2025 and were identified through DNA testing. According to court documents, V.A.E. was likely killed in Mexico by Jimenez’s coconspirators.

At today’s hearing, Judge Sammartino described the case events as “the most deliberate and unnecessary loss of life I’ve seen in a very long time.” Addressing Mr. Jimenez, she said, “You preyed upon the most vulnerable people.”

Even after the two victims disappeared, Jimenez continued working with the organization and coordinating smuggling operations. Investigators recovered messages from his phone reflecting his continued involvement and awareness of the organization’s use of threats and violence. In one exchange, Jimenez discussed an unidentified woman who was not cooperating and suggested taking her to an office. Other communications among members of the organization referred to making people disappear and torture. Investigators also recovered a video showing a man with his wrists bound as though he had been detained or kidnapped.

As part of his guilty plea, Jimenez admitted coordinating alien-smuggling events and collecting ransom payments from family members of migrants who were instead held captive by his coconspirators.

The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Escondido Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert J. Miller and former Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alex Biggs and Samson Schatz prosecuted the case.

DEFENDANT Case Number 25cr2648-JLS

Isaac Jimenez Age: 30 San Diego, CA

SUMMARY OF CHARGES

Conspiracy to Bring in Certain Aliens – Title 18, U.S.C., Section 371, and Title 8, U.S.C., Section 1324(a)(2)(B)(ii)

Maximum penalty: Five years in prison and $250,000 fine

Bringing in Aliens for Financial Gain – Title 8, U.S.C., Section 1324(a)(2)(B)(ii)

Maximum penalty: Ten years in prison (and a mandatory minimum three years) and $250,000 fine

INVESTIGATING AGENCY

Homeland Security Investigations

This investigation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF San Diego comprises agents and officers from FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, DEA, ATF, U.S. Marshals, Department of Defense, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Naval Criminal Investigative Service, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Coast Guard, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Interpol, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California.
title: Man Sentenced for Role in Smuggling Organization that Kidnapped Migrants and Extorted Their Families; One Dead, Another Missing After Families Paid Ransoms in Vain

Scott, DeSaulnier Demand Answers from Trump Administration on Ability to Protect 155 Million Workers’ Benefits
WASHINGTON – House Committee on Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee Ranking Member Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10) demanded the Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) Assistant Secretary Daniel Aronowitz share a detailed accounting of the agency’s staffing, the damage done by the Trump-Musk federal workforce cuts, and its actions to effectively enforce the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA).
ERISA governs 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 retirement plans, and 521,000 other employee benefit plans that cumulatively cover 155 million Americans. However, under the Trump Administration, EBSA has experienced chronic underfunding, reduced staff, and weakened enforcement capacity, allowing bad actors to evade accountability for harming workers’ hard-earned benefits.
“The chaotic nature of the Trump Administration’s campaign to slash the federal workforce has also obscured the exact scope and severity of the damage imposed on the Agency’s workforce. Over the last 20 months, we have had to rely on media reports and top-line figures in annual budget requests to ascertain EBSA’s capacity, which are often vague or outdated. Moreover, your responses to the Committee’s questions for the record after your appearance failed to provide any substantive information on staffing. In order for the Committee to evaluate EBSA’s ability to effectively carry out its mission, as well as to advocate for more resources, it is imperative we have a robust and up-to-date picture of the Agency’s workforce changes and composition,” wrote Ranking Members Scott and DeSaulnier.
The Ranking Members requested the agency turn over documents and information related to this request no later than October 22, 2026.
Background:
On November 18, 2025, the Ranking Members urged the Trump Administration to adequately staff EBSA to ensure it can fulfill its enormous mission and called on Secretary Aronowitz to tackle wrongful claim denials by group health plans and insurance companies and secure coverage for working people under ERISA.
To read the full letter to Assistant Secretary Aronowitz, click here.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – Dominican authorities extradited Patricia Joanna Almonte-Frías and her partner Rineldys Feliciano Díaz-Cuevas to the United States to face cyberstalking and sextortion conspiracy charges filed in the District of Puerto Rico, announced Héctor Ramírez-Carbó, Acting United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico. The defendants were arrested in the Dominican Republic on August 19, 2026, at the request of the United States, and extradited to Puerto Rico on September 30, 2026.

According to court documents, Patricia Joanna Almonte-Frías and Rineldys Feliciano Díaz-Cuevas operated an international, financially motivated “sextortion” scheme that conspired to engage in, and did engage in, cyberstalking and intestate threats.

The defendants, operating from the Dominican Republic, identified and sextorted victims using Facebook, WhatsApp, and other social media platforms. Almonte-Frías used her image to encourage victims in Puerto Rico to share online sexually explicit photos and videos (which were secretly recorded). Subsequently, defendant Díaz-Cuevas and other co-conspirators then extorted victims to send money under threat of exposing the compromising images to the victims’ family and friends. In some instances, the defendants created photo collages by combining the victim’s sexually explicit images with images of minors, thereby giving the false impression that victims were involved in sexual relationships with minors.

On multiple occasions, the victims paid the demanded amounts, emptied their accounts, and the defendants still carried out the threats and distributed the victims’ sexual images to the victims’ online network of friends and family members.

“These defendants ran a calculated scheme that preyed on trust, fear, and vulnerability, leaving lasting harm in its wake,” said Héctor Ramírez‑Carbó, Acting United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico. “Sextortion is a ruthless crime, and today’s prosecution makes clear that those who exploit victims—no matter where they hide—will be identified, pursued, and held to account.”

“In today’s ever-changing digital environment, criminals will develop creative ways to target victims and exploit them. Extortion is a serious crime that can cause lasting financial and psychological harm to its victims,” said Carlos R. Goris, Special Agent in Charge of FBI San Juan. “The FBI encourages all citizens to remain vigilant online and report to the authorities if you suspect you have been a victim of extortion. Your report will help law enforcement disrupt these networks and prevent others from becoming victims. The FBI demonstrates once again that no matter where you are, we will find you and bring you to justice.”

Almonte-Frías and Díaz-Cuevas are charged with conspiracy to cyberstalk and send interstate threats in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 371. The defendants made their initial court appearances on October 1, 2026 before U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcos E. López of the U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico. If convicted, they face a maximum penalty of five years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

The FBI in San Juan, Puerto Rico investigated the case.

The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, FBI Legal Attaché in Santo Domingo, the U.S. Marshals Service, and law enforcement partners in the Dominican Republic provided substantial assistance in securing the arrest and extradition to the United States of Almonte-Frías and Díaz-Cuevas.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Julián Radzinschi, of the Financial Fraud and Public Corruption Division, is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

title: Two Dominican Republic Nationals Extradited to Face Cyberstalking and Sextortion Conspiracy Charges in Puerto Rico

text:
WASHINGTON – Darae Vaughn, 31, of the District of Columbia, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 96 months in federal prison in connection with his role in a narcotics trafficking conspiracy that distributed fentanyl and crack cocaine in Northeast D.C., announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“Darae Vaughn trafficked fentanyl and crack cocaine while armed, putting lives at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Now he’s going to prison for eight years. If you push deadly drugs into our community while armed, you will be held accountable. You will go to prison.”

“Darae Vaughn trafficked fentanyl and crack cocaine while armed, putting lives at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Now he’s going to prison for eight years. If you push deadly drugs into our community while armed, you will be held accountable. You will go to prison.”

Vaughn, aka “Rae,” pleaded guilty June 30, 2026, before Judge Trevor N. McFadden to conspiracy to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl, to possession with intent to distribute 28 grams or more of cocaine base, and to distribution and possession of 10 grams or more of fentanyl. In addition to the 96-month prison term, Judge McFadden ordered Vaughn to serve five years of supervised release.

According to court documents, in March 2025 the FBI Safe Streets Task Force began an investigation into reports of narcotics trafficking on the 2000 block of 19th Place SE, particularly counterfeit M30 fentanyl pills.

The investigation revealed that from at least April 2025 through September 2025, during nine recorded transactions, Vaughn sold hundreds of fentanyl pills, and quantities of crack cocaine, carfentanyl, and methamphetamine while he was armed with a Glock 43x pistol.

In January 2025, codefendant Charles Dixon and Vaughn exchanged text messages discussing pills that Vaughn had supplied to Dixon. Dixon argued with Vaughn about how many pills Vaughn owed him. On April 8, 2025, Dixon participated in the sale of 96 fentanyl pills. On July 3, 2025, Dixon was involved in the sale of 163 fentanyl pills.

Dixon was sentenced on October 6 to 33 months in prison for his role in the conspiracy.

This investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Iris McCranie and Kate Naseef.

This case is part of the Department of Justice’s broader efforts to combat fentanyl trafficking and drug related violence in the District of Columbia. Fentanyl remains one of the deadliest substances circulating in the illegal drug supply, and counterfeit pills containing fentanyl pose extreme risks to unwitting users and the community at large.

NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit. On Friday, the agency released its final Request for Proposals inviting industry to submit plans for the next generation of commercial space stations.
“In alignment with the President’s National Space Policy, NASA is committed to maintaining a sustained American presence in low Earth orbit long after the International Space Station retires,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars. Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”
Building on the agency’s Ignition event earlier this year, NASA regularly has engaged with private industry to shape the agency’s future direction in low Earth orbit. This included publishing two Requests for Information in March to gather industry’s perspective on low Earth orbit destinations and transportation. The agency also published a draft Request for Proposals in July, followed by an industry day and one-on-one meetings that allowed interested companies to review and comment on the planned acquisition approach.
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” said Isaacman. “Since Ignition, we have spent a lot of time listening to industry and working through what it will take to make this transition successful. The opportunity is significant, but the economics ultimately have to work. We want to see credible plans, strong technical execution, and companies prepared to invest in destinations that can serve NASA while developing additional customers and markets of their own.”
Proposals are due Tuesday, Dec. 8, with contract awards expected in spring 2027.
Under the solicitation, NASA outlines requirements for companies interested in designing, building, testing, certifying, and operating commercial low Earth orbit destinations capable of providing end-to-end destination and transportation services for human spaceflight use.
NASA intends to award firm-fixed-price, multi-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contracts supporting development, certification, and services for continued low Earth orbit research and exploration. This will allow NASA to select two or more contractors through early development, followed by a competitive task order for final design, test, and evaluation, as well as certification and services from one or more contractors.
Learn more about NASA’s missions on the agency’s website:

DAVENPORT, Iowa – Rock Island men were sentenced to federal prison for conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance, distribution of a controlled substance, possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, and felon in possession of a firearm.

According to public court documents and evidence presented at sentencing, on June 12, 2025, all three men drove together to sell marijuana to a confidential source.

Daquez Deasante Howard, 22, remained in the car and possessed money from the drug sale, a loaded, Taurus pistol with an extended magazine, and 20.83 grams of marijuana on his seat. On July 8, 2026, Howard was sentenced to a 68-month prison term, followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Darryl Lee Smith, Jr., 23, was apprehended by police after he ran from the car and possessed a loaded revolver with the hammer cocked back. On May 13, 2026, Smith was sentenced to a 57-month prison term, followed by a three-year term of supervised release

Darryl Benard Shears, III,24, ran on foot, escaping the police. Inside the car, police found a loaded pistol, 35.10 grams of cocaine, 14.31grams of crack cocaine, and two functioning scales where Shears had been seated in the car before and after the drug deal. On June 29, 2025, Shears was arrested. Shears again attempted to flee from police on the Arsenal Bridge, crashing into multiple police cars, and jumping into the Mississippi river. Shears also possessed a loaded pistol with a round in the chamber. On October 8, 2026, Shears was sentenced to a 204-month prison term, followed by a six-year term of supervised release.

There is no parole in the federal system.

United States Attorney David C. Waterman of the Southern District of Iowa made the announcement. The Davenport Police Department investigated the case.

As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe.
